final.content:
# Comparative Analysis of Transitional Justice Mechanisms Following Mass Atrocities

## Introduction

Transitional justice comprises a heterogeneous set of mechanisms—judicial and non-judicial, domestic and international, retrospective and prospective—designed to address systematic human rights violations. Ruti Teitel's foundational framework characterizes the field as evolving in three "constitutional moments": post-war (e.g., Nuremberg), cold-war decolonization (e.g., truth commissions), and contemporary post-authoritarian/post-conflict transitions (e.g., ICC prosecutions) (https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/89c5/7d341b721b9ae0f4222a0f5fea3012c69f35.pdf). This report evaluates four mechanism families—Truth and Reconciliation Commissions (TRCs), international/hybrid prosecutorial tribunals, reparations programs, and lustration policies—against three normative criteria: (1) serving victims, (2) enabling democratic transitions, and (3) preventing recurrence of atrocities. Evidence is drawn principally from South Africa's TRC, Canada's residential schools TRC, the ICTY, ICC situations in Kenya and Sudan, German reparations for the Holocaust, the U.S. Civil Liberties Act of 1988, and the Czech, Polish, and German lustration regimes.

## 1. Truth and Reconciliation Commissions

### 1.1 South Africa

**Mechanism.** Established in 1995 under the Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act 34/1995. Operated through three committees: Human Rights Violations (victim testimony), Amnesty (perpetrator applications), and Reparation and Rehabilitation. Mandate: 1960–1994.

**Outcomes for victims.** The Human Rights Violations Committee received statements from approximately 21,676 deponents identified as victims (https://www.trc-inquiry.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Page-172-202.pdf). Of these, 17,428 applied for and received the once-off individual grant of R30,000 (https://www.trc-inquiry.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Page-172-202.pdf). The total paid was R497,798,781 in final grants (plus R53,165,325 in interim grants). The TRC had recommended approximately R126,000 per person over six years—a recommendation parliament halved (https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2020-11-08-the-unfinished-business-of-the-trc-is-killing-us-say-apartheids-victims/). The Centre for the Study of Violence and Reconciliation found the hearings' "greatest achievement" lay in restoring victim dignity through public testimony: "it feels like I got my sight back by coming here and telling my story" (https://sahistory.org.za/sites/default/files/volume5_0.pdf).

**However**, victim-evaluation research revealed mixed effects. A Khulumani Support Group survey of 20 survivors found that most became disillusioned despite initial enthusiasm; "eleven [of twenty] felt amnesty was unfair to victims," with nine calling it "wrong" and one fearing release of perpetrators (https://csvr.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2000/01/tellingitlikeitis-3.pdf). Rape victims were largely excluded from the "closed list" because sexual violence was not always defined as a political crime qualifying for amnesty (https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2020-11-08-the-unfinished-business-of-the-trc-is-killing-us-say-apartheids-victims/). The President's Fund remains the source of controversy: as of April 2016, ~R556 million had been disbursed to victims, with over R1 billion remaining, much redirected toward community programs rather than individual redress (https://groundup.news/article/apartheid-compensation-process-flawed-says-khulumani/).

**Democratic transition and prevention.** The TRC is credited with consolidating the post-1994 democratic settlement by establishing an "irrefutable" historical record (https://sahistory.org.za/sites/default/files/volume5_0.pdf) and by dismantling denial. However, scholars debate whether the TRC actually caused the post-1994 peace: "it is doubtful that the truth and reconciliation process was a cause of peace" given that 1990–94 violence had largely abated by 1996 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0022002706287115). The commission's most enduring contribution has been the integration of restorative language into South Africa's constitutional discourse, even as socioeconomic inequalities persist.

### 1.2 Canada (Residential Schools)

**Mechanism.** Active 2008–2015, embedded in the 2006 Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement (IRSSEA). Mandate: documented the experience of 150,000+ Indigenous children forced into 139 federally funded schools between the 1870s and 1996, classifying the system as "cultural genocide." Six-volume Final Report (December 2015) included 94 Calls to Action.

**Victim outcomes.** The TRC heard from 6,500 Survivors and witnesses, with at least 3,200 documented deaths of children in the schools—though Commissioner Sinclair maintained the true toll is "far higher" (https://thewalrus.ca/trc-introduction/). Survivor testimony served as the precursor to the federal September 30 National Day for Truth and Reconciliation (Call to Action 80, achieved 2021) and the Indigenous Languages Act (Calls 13/14, 2019). The TRC was preceded by the IRSSEA's Common Experience Payment ($10,000 for first year + $3,000/year thereafter) and Independent Assessment Process for severe abuse cases (https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1100100016575/1539866228414).

**Democratic transition and prevention.** Mixed picture. Government claims more than 85% of the 76 federal Calls to Action "completed or well underway" by 2025 (https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1524494530110/1557511412801). However, civil-society audits paint a darker picture: the Yellowhead Institute documented only 8 of 94 Calls fully implemented as of December 2020 (a regression from 9 the year prior), attributing failures to paternalism, anti-Indigenous racism, exclusion of Indigenous peoples from policy design, and insufficient resources (https://yellowheadinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/yi-trc-calls-to-action-update-full-report-2020.pdf). The Assembly of First Nations' 2023 Report Card records ongoing slow implementation. Critics argue reconciliation has become "performative" rather than structural (https://yellowheadinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/trc-2021-accountability-update-yellowhead-institute-special-report.pdf).

**Cross-cutting assessment.** South Africa and Canada share what Teitel calls the "dilemma of moderation"—the tension between restorative aspirations and retributive or distributive justice demands (https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/89c5/7d341b721b9ae0f4222a0f5fea3012c69f35.pdf). Both produced well-documented historical records and partial legislative commitments, but both failed to deliver reparations at the recommended scale. The TRC model performed best on establishing official truth and acknowledging harm—criteria emphasizing "human and civil dignity" rather than material redistribution.

## 2. Prosecutorial Tribunals

### 2.1 ICTY (Former Yugoslavia)

**Mechanism.** Established by UNSC Resolution 808 (1993) and Statute (827/1993) as a temporary ad hoc tribunal sitting in The Hague. Jurisdiction over war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide committed in the former Yugoslavia after 1991. Closed on 31 December 2017; functions transferred to the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT).

**Quantitative outcomes.** The ICTY indicted 161 individuals (https://www.icty.org/en/cases/key-figures-cases):
- 90 sentenced
- 19 acquitted
- 13 referred to national jurisdictions
- 37 proceedings terminated or indictments withdrawn (often due to death of accused)
- 2 awaiting retrial before the MICT
- Approximately 4,650 live witnesses testified, with court transcripts documenting testimony of more than 10,800 individuals (https://www.icty.org/sites/icty.org/files/images/content/Infographic_facts_figures_en.pdf).

**Victims and accountability.** The ICTY established beyond a reasonable doubt "crucial facts related to crimes committed in the former Yugoslavia," producing a permanent historical record that "made it impossible to deny that violations occurred" (https://www.icty.org/en/about/tribunal/achievements). Convictions including Milosevic, Karadžić, Mladić, Krajišnik, Plavšić, and Šešelj dismantled the previous "tradition of impunity." The Čelebići case established rape as torture under customary international law.

**Democratic transitions and prevention.** Mixed legacy. The "peace through justice" thesis held that ICTY indictments, combined with EU conditionality, pressured regional cooperation—the EU made ICTY cooperation "a sine qua non in accession negotiations" (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14683850701565973). Croatia's accession depended on such cooperation. State-level data from post-conflict societies 1982–2010 found international tribunals "do not appear to contribute to reducing the recurrence of civil war or improvements in human rights practices"—though neither did they exercise negative effects (https://sah.borca.ai/papers/146401203). The 2010 Gotovina/Markač and Haradinaj acquittals demonstrate the uneven impact: critics argue these "intensified tensions" between former Yugoslav successor states (https://gjis.journals.yorku.ca/index.php/gjis/article/download/36963/34931).

### 2.2 ICC Kenya (Post-Election Violence)

**Mechanism.** Prosecutor opened investigation proprio motu on 31 March 2010 into alleged crimes against humanity during the 2007–2008 post-election violence that killed ~1,300 people. Charges were confirmed on 23 January 2012 against four suspects (Kenyatta, Muthaura, Ruto, Sang); charges against Ali and Kosgey were not confirmed.

**Outcome 1: Kenyatta.** The Prosecution withdrew charges on 5 December 2014 because "the evidence has not improved to such an extent that Mr Kenyatta's alleged criminal responsibility can be proven beyond reasonable doubt" (https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/CourtRecords/CR2014_09939.PDF). Trial Chamber V(B) terminated proceedings on 13 March 2015. The Victims' Legal Representative described the withdrawal as a "betrayal" of thousands whose "lives had been torn asunder" (https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/CourtRecords/CR2014_09983.PDF).

**Outcome 2: Ruto and Sang.** On 5 April 2016 Trial Chamber V(A) vacated charges—noting that 17 prosecution witnesses had withdrawn cooperation due to intimidation and political interference—while explicitly declining to acquit, "without prejudice" to future re-prosecution (https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/ruto-and-sang-case-icc-trial-chamber-va-terminates-case-without-prejudice-re-prosecution). Prosecutor Bensouda condemned "deliberate and concerted efforts to derail this case through witness interference" that "denied the victims … the justice they so rightly deserve" (https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/statement-prosecutor-international-criminal-court-fatou-bensouda-regarding-trial-chambers).

**Assessment.** The Kenya cases illustrate the vulnerability of international prosecutions to non-cooperation and witness interference when the suspect state apparatus retains power. Both Kenyatta and Ruto won the 2013 election (Ruto remains Deputy President as of writing). No trial verdict was reached despite the ICC's collection of substantial evidence. This represents the most significant failure of international prosecutorial transitional justice to date in producing victim redress.

### 2.3 ICC Sudan (Darfur)

**Mechanism.** UNSC Resolution 1593 (2005) referred the Darfur situation to the ICC—the first time the Council exercised its Chapter VII referral power vis-à-vis a non-state party. Indictments: Ahmad Harun and Ali Kushayb (April 2007); first Al-Bashir warrant (4 March 2009) for crimes against humanity and war crimes; second warrant (12 July 2010) added three counts of genocide after the Appeals Chamber reversed the Pre-Trial Chamber's earlier refusal to include the charge (https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/CourtRecords/CR2010_04825.PDF). This was the first ICC indictment of a sitting head of state.

**Implementation failure.** Al-Bashir remained at large; Sudan categorically rejected the Court's jurisdiction. The African Union directed member states in 2009 to "withhold cooperation" with the ICC regarding Al-Bashir's arrest (https://exa.ai/library/publication/pzccxhpd5gx). Subsequent summits discussed collective AU withdrawal from the Rome Statute before being deferred (https://www.ispionline.it/en/publication/kenya-and-sudan-two-cases-shaped-africas-criticism-towards-icc-16454). Quantitative analysis indicated the indictment "accelerated patterns of obstruction and intimidation of peacekeeping actors, other third-party actors, and local staff associated with these," complicating UNAMID's mandate (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01436597.2019.1579640). Critics—including Julie Flint and Alex de Waal—argued the prosecution "endanger[ed] the people we wish to defend in Sudan" by collapsing peace-process leverage without compensating enforcement capacity (https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2013/3/25/the-enforcement-gap-how-the-international-criminal-court-failed-in-darfur).

**Assessment.** The ICC's enforcement gap—the absence of a dedicated police or detention apparatus—rendered the indictments symbolic rather than instrumental. Their effect on Sudan's policy of cooperation was negative rather than deterrent. No Sudaneses were tried for the Darfur atrocities during the relevant period, and mass violence in Darfur continued for years.

### 2.4 Synthesis: Tribunals' Performance

| Criterion | ICTY | ICC Kenya | ICC Sudan |
|-----------|------|-----------|-----------|
| Victim voices heard | ~10,800 witnesses (https://www.icty.org/sites/icty.org/files/images/content/Infographic_facts_figures_en.pdf) | Victims expressed "betrayal" | Victims largely unaddressed |
| Establishes historical record | Strong (settled Srebrenica facts, etc.) | Limited (no verdicts) | Limited (in absentia) |
| Democratic consolidation | Mixed (EU-linked accountability) | Negative (witnesses intimidated, political threats) | Negative (no enforcement, prolonged conflict) |
| Deterrence/recurrence | Studies show "no effect" either way (https://sah.borca.ai/papers/146401203) | Cannot assess (no verdict) | Conflict continued |

The broader 2025 statistical literature finds that states implementing any of trials, truth commissions, exile, or purge within five years of a prior mass atrocity experience a wait time "four times longer" until the next mass atrocity than those that did not (https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/routledg/cjhr/2025/00000024/00000002/art00007). However, this is an average effect across all mechanisms and does not endorse any single approach.

## 3. Reparations Programs

### 3.1 Germany's Holocaust Reparations

**Mechanism.** Architecture established by the 1952 Luxembourg Agreements between the FRG, Israel, and the Conference on Jewish Material Claims Against Germany ("Claims Conference") (https://2021-2025.state.gov/reports/just-act-report-to-congress/germany/):
- DM 3 billion (~$714 million at 1952 rates) to Israel in goods and services
- DM 450 million (~$107 million) to the Claims Conference for individual indemnification
- Federal Compensation Act (BEG, 1956): individual payments for personal injury, liberty, professional advancement, and property
- Federal Restitution Law (BRüG, 1957): restitution of movable property

**Quantitative trajectory.**
- Annual payments for Holocaust survivors have grown sharply: from ~€510 million ($557 million) in 2015 to a record $1.4 billion (€1.29 billion) for 2024—the largest single-year figure since reparations began more than seven decades ago (https://apnews.com/article/german-jews-holocaust-survivors-claims-conference-compensation-6e50867ada8a79d32d192c99020ee1cc).
- Total disbursements since 1952 exceed $90 billion (https://www.npr.org/2023/06/15/1182428154/germany-holocaust-survivors-payment-1-4-billion-nazi-victims).
- Composition of 2024 figures: $535 million direct to survivors (monthly pensions; hardship payments of €1,250 each to 128,000+ survivors); $888.9 million for home care and social welfare services delivered through ~300 agencies in 83 countries; increased funding for Holocaust education (https://www.jta.org/2023/06/14/global/germany-agrees-to-record-1-4-billion-in-annual-holocaust-reparations-as-survivors-age).
- As of mid-2019, approximately 25,000 survivors worldwide still received monthly BEG pensions (https://2021-2025.state.gov/reports/just-act-report-to-congress/germany/).

**Key quantitative observation.** Despite the comprehensive architecture, only ~25,000 of the original targeted population still receive direct monthly pensions, reflecting both survivor mortality and the limits of reparations in addressing harm at scale. Substantive reparations continued expanding through the 2000 German Foundation Initiative and additional agreements negotiated with Eastern European states (https://1997-2001.state.gov/policy_remarks/2000/000323_eizenstat_berlin.html).

### 3.2 United States: Japanese American Internment

**Mechanism.** Civil Liberties Act of 1988 (Pub. L. 100-383), sponsored by Rep. Norman Mineta (an internee) and Sen. Alan Simpson; signed by President Reagan on 10 August 1988. Conceded that WWII relocation was based on "race prejudice, war hysteria, and a failure of political leadership" rather than security (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Liberties_Act_of_1988).

**Quantitative outcomes.**
- $20,000 paid per surviving internee (equivalent to ~$46,000 in 2024 dollars).
- 82,219 recipients, totaling more than $1.6 billion; program closed 5 February 1999 (https://www.justice.gov/archive/opa/pr/1999/February/059cr.htm).
- An additional $5,000 paid to 145 Japanese Latin Americans (settled in Mochizuki litigation) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Liberties_Act_of_1988).
- $5 million annually for a public education fund to "discourage the occurrence of similar injustices and violations of civil liberties in the future" (https://uscode.ecfr.io/statutes/pl/100/383.pdf).

**Effectiveness.** A controlled experiment demonstrated that informational exposure to the Japanese American redress experience increased Asian American respondents' support for Black reparations "relative to a control condition, and national polling data on support for reparations" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11332238/). This points to the contagious symbolic-legitimizing function of reparations programs beyond direct material compensation.

### 3.3 Reparations Critique

Critical scholarship cautions that reparations can be "palliative"—offering limited material or symbolic redress without addressing structural injustices (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17502977.2022.2042650). The South African case exemplifies this: the President's Fund remains partially disbursed after 25 years, while perpetrators obtained amnesty. The "transformative reparations" literature suggests reparations are most effective when linked to non-temporary structural changes and meaningful victim participation in decision-making (https://www.elgaronline.com/view/journals/cilj/8/1/article-p39.xml). Symbolic reparations (memorialization, official apology, day of commemoration) play a recognized restorative role—Carlos Martín Beristain argues that "symbolic measures are aimed at recognizing the dignity of the victims, fostering the memory of relevant historical facts" (https://www.brandeis.edu/creativity-arts-social-transformation/news-events/pdfs/repairing_symbolic_reparations_greeley.pdf)—though risks include "ineffective, even detrimental monuments" when poorly designed.

## 4. Lustration Policies (Post-Communist Eastern Europe)

**Typology.** Research distinguishes three lustration archetypes (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/662648):
- **Dismissal** (Albania, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, unified Germany): barring those with collaboration from public positions;
- **Exposure** (Hungary, Poland, Romania): making secret-police collaboration records public without imposing categorical bans;
- **Confession** (Poland's 1997 Act): allowing tainted officials to retain positions if they voluntarily disclosed collaboration.

### 4.1 Czech Republic (1991 Act No. 451/1991)

The earliest and "semi-retributive" lustration regime banned former StB collaborators, agents, and communist party functionaries from specified public posts (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/law-and-social-inquiry/article/abs/lustration-laws-in-action-the-motives-and-evaluation-of-lustration-policy-in-the-czech-republic-and-poland-19892001/A54F46A5C8E41697959589830750116C). The Constitutional Court reviewed and moderated the law's most extreme provisions. Multiple extensions in 1995 and 2000 raised rule-of-law concerns, though evaluation research indicates a "relative success" within several years of passage (https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/D0651FBE5434D968F2F397C9F1754938/S1574019608004604a.pdf/lustration_and_lapse_of_time.pdf).

### 4.2 Poland (1997 Lustration Act)

Adopted "in the version of amendments Dz.u.99.42.428, Dz.u.99.57.618, Dz.u.99.62.681, Dz.u.99.63.701, Dz.u.00.43.488, Dz.u.00.50.600," the Polish model combined exposure of secret-police files with a confession pathway (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/law-and-social-inquiry/article/abs/lustration-laws-in-action-the-motives-and-evaluation-of-lustration-policy-in-the-czech-republic-and-poland-19892001/A54F46A5C8E41697959589830750116C). Late lustration programs in 2006 "expanded the scope and transparency measures associated with lustration as a form of transitional justice," covering "journalists, academics, business leaders, and others in 'positions of public trust'" (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/13510340902732581).

### 4.3 Germany (Unification-era)

The 1990 Unification Treaty allowed for dismissal of senior GDR party functionaries and Stasi collaborators from public office. The 1991 Stasi Records Act established the Federal Commissioner for Stasi Records, enabling vetting of judges, university professors, and schoolteachers. This produced "thousands" of discharges (https://files.core.ac.uk/download/pdf/41100396.pdf). Germany was not, however, directly comparable—it was absorbed into the FRG, providing institutional capacity others lacked.

### 4.4 Empirical Assessment

Nationwide survey experiments in the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Poland (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/662648) found:
- **Dismissal and confession systems increase citizens' trust in government and trust in tainted officials.**
- **Exposure systems reduce citizens' trust in tainted officials.**

Lustration was "unique to post-communist states and was not seen in any other transitional context," partly because "the ethnic wars overshadowed society's memories of communist wrongdoing" in the former Yugoslavia (https://https-sage-cnpereading-com-443.webvpn1.xju.edu.cn/doi/10.1177/08883254231163183).

**Limitations.** The 1995 ECtHR case of *Vogt v. Germany* (21 Eur. H.R. Rep. 205) held that some lustration approaches may violate freedom of expression under Article 10 ECHR. European Court of Human Rights jurisprudence has been "unsettled" on whether lustration laws survive contemporary scrutiny (https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/D0651FBE5434D968F2F397C9F1754938/S1574019608004604a.pdf/lustration_and_lapse_of_time.pdf), and the Council of Europe's 1996 Parliamentary Assembly resolution expressed concern over disproportionate bans.

## 5. Comparative Synthesis Against the Three Criteria

### 5.1 Serving Victims

| Mechanism | Strengths | Limitations |
|-----------|-----------|------------|
| TRCs | Restore dignity via public testimony; produce official recognition (https://sahistory.org.za/sites/default/files/volume5_0.pdf) | Monetary reparations chronically underfunded (South Africa: R30,000 vs. R126,000 recommended; Canada: 8–15 of 94 Calls implemented); conditional amnesty frustrates victims seeking punishment (https://csvr.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2000/01/tellingitlikeitis-3.pdf) |
| Tribunals | Provide voice; establish facts; deliver named-perpetrator accountability | Trials average 5+ years; victim participation rights inadequate (Kenya victims' "betrayal" complaint, https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/CourtRecords/CR2014_09983.PDF); few mid/low-level perpetrators reached (ICTY 90/161 sentenced for top leadership; remainder transferred/withdrawn) |
| Reparations | Material acknowledgement; survivor support (e.g., Germany: $1.4B annually for ~240,000 survivors, https://www.jta.org/2023/06/14/global/germany-agrees-to-record-1-4-billion-in-annual-holocaust-reparations-as-survivors-age) | Cannot heal trauma; coverage narrow; symbolism varies (Japanese Latin Americans only got $5,000 settlement) |
| Lustration | Signals state rejection of complicity; restores integrity of public institutions (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/662648) | Categorical bans harm individual tainted officials disproportionately; rule-of-law risks; *Vogt v. Germany* jurisprudence |

### 5.2 Enabling Democratic Transitions

**TRCs** stabilize transitions by domesticating conflict through ritualized truth-telling (South Africa's case demonstrates that the TRC served as "an instrument of national myth-making" that integrated restorative language into post-apartheid constitutionalism). Canada's experience shows that a TRC alone does not automatically produce structural change; political will and resources matter decisively.

**Prosecutorial tribunals** have inconsistent effects: the ICTY's most important external pressure came via EU accession conditionality, which instrumentalized cooperation (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14683850701565973). ICC interventions against sitting officials can destabilize democracy by prolonging conflict or provoking backlash (e.g., Sudan, Kenya), though they may in some cases deter abuses.

**Reparations** materially support democratic legitimacy by acknowledging state responsibility and redressing—ongoing symbolic and financial recognition undergirds Germany's postwar democratic stabilization. The U.S. Civil Liberties Act's official apology constitutes what Greiff has termed a "recognition function" essential to democratic reconciliation.

**Lustration** was most effective in the German and Czech cases, where strong democratic institutions and bounded scope coupled with international human rights frameworks (https://files.core.ac.uk/download/pdf/41100396.pdf). Late or expanded lustration programs risk "party-political instrumentalization" rather than democratic consolidation (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/13510340902732581).

### 5.3 Preventing Recurrence

**Statistical evidence (as of 2025):**
- Cross-national studies show that, after a mass atrocity, implementing any combination of trials, truth commissions, exile, or purge within five years extends the wait time to a subsequent mass atrocity by approximately 4× (https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/routledg/cjhr/2025/00000024/00000002/art00007).
- World Bank-UN analysis finds that "only prosecutions of low- and mid-level human rights violators are associated with a decrease in the likelihood of conflict recurrence," while high-ranking prosecutions show no clear net benefit; new constitutions and truth commissions are also positively associated with peace durability (https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/dev4peace/transitional-justice-rule-law-and-conflict-recurrence).
- A crucial distinction in the *International Studies Quarterly* (2017) finding: **motivation-addressing** mechanisms (truth commissions, comprehensive trials, reparations, amnesties) significantly reduce conflict recurrence by mitigating grievances; **opportunity-addressing** mechanisms (purges, exiles, selective trials of opposition) have little systematic effect (https://academic.oup.com/isq/article-abstract/61/3/690/4643613).
- Research on truth commissions specifically finds significant reductions in targeted mass killings (TMKs) following implementation, though issuance of final reports and recommendations for reforms alone is not associated with TMK reduction (https://researchconnect.suny.edu/en/publications/truth-commissions-and-the-prevention-of-targeted-mass-killings/).
- The Tufts analysis found that ICTY trials were historically associated with high expectations but produced "scant contribution" to prosecutions in domestic courts within the region (https://dl.tufts.edu/downloads/mw22vh255?filename=3484zt54v.pdf).

**Theoretical interpretation.** Teitel's "transitional justice in balance" argues that mechanisms should not be evaluated "at any cost"; the demand for justice must be "balanced with the need for peace, democracy, equitable development and the rule of law" (https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/89c5/7d341b721b9ae0f4222a0f5fea3012c69f35.pdf). Combined or sequenced mechanisms generally outperform single-instrument approaches.

## 6. Mechanism-by-Mechanism Verdict

### Truth and Reconciliation Commissions
**Best serve** victim dignification and historical reconciliation when paired with comprehensive reparations; **moderately serve** democratic consolidation; **credibly reduce** recurrence when final reports and reform recommendations materialize (per the SUNY mass-killing study). The South African model shows that partial implementation and conditional amnesty can erode victim trust. **Caveat:** Canada's trajectory exemplifies how implementation gaps can transform TRCs from transformation into performance.

### International Prosecutorial Tribunals
**Strongest at** establishing historical fact and breaking denial through documentary and testimonial evidence (ICTY: 161 indictments; ~10,800 witnesses; documented Srebrenica facts beyond dispute). **Weakest at** delivering timely justice: ICC Kenya trials collapsed due to witness interference; ICC Sudan produced no arrest despite multiple warrants. The 2010 *Science@home* finding shows that international tribunals "do not appear to contribute to reducing the recurrence of civil war"—although they do not harm either (https://sah.borca.ai/papers/146401203). Most credible recent work suggests that comprehensive (motivation-addressing) trials reduce recurrence, while selective opportunity-addressing prosecutions do not.

### Reparations Programs
**Most effective** at the symbolic-acknowledgment function: Germany's $90+ billion total and the U.S.'s $1.6 billion for Japanese Americans converted state wrongdoing into officially accepted responsibility. The Japanese American case shows measurable "contagion"—exposure to redress history increases support for ongoing reparative claims (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11332238/). **Limitation:** reparations cannot heal psychological or structural harm on their own; the South African case demonstrates how chronic implementation gaps can transform reparations from remedy into renewed grievance.

### Lustration Policies
**Distinctive strength:** Cheap, administratively feasible, and—as survey experiments demonstrate—dismissal and confession variants increase trust in both government and tainted officials alike (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/662648). **Distinctive weakness:** Post-1989 European experience is unique to post-communist settings; cross-regional generalization is limited. Long-running lustration raises ECHR concerns (https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/D0651FBE5434D968F2F397C9F1754938/S1574019608004604a.pdf/lustration_and_lapse_of_time.pdf).

## 7. Cross-Modal Conclusions

**First**, no mechanism is sufficient in isolation. The empirical record (motivation-addressing processes; 4× extended wait time to recurrence; World Bank-UN findings on constitutions) consistently shows that combined approaches—often truth commissions plus trials plus reparations, embedded within constitutional reform and human rights institutions—outperform single-mechanism strategies (https://academic.oup.com/isq/article-abstract/61/3/690/4643613; https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/routledg/cjhr/2025/00000024/00000002/art00007).

**Second**, the *ranking* of officials prosecuted matters: low- and mid-level prosecutions correlate with reduced recurrence; top-elite prosecutions (the dominant ICTY/ICC focus) demonstrate weaker and more conditional effects (https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/dev4peace/transitional-justice-rule-law-and-conflict-recurrence). This suggests a paradox: high-profile international tribunals' symbolic power coexists with their limited instrumental deterrent effect.

**Third**, mechanism effectiveness is highly context-dependent. International prosecution fails when states refuse cooperation (Sudan, ICC's 2013 enforcement gap, https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2013/3/25/the-enforcement-gap-how-the-international-criminal-court-failed-in-darfur). TRCs underperform when reparations are underfunded or excluded populations are large (South Africa's "closed list"). Lustration depends on the existence of a viable democratic core to absorb tainted personnel (Germany with FRG; Czech with civic dissidents; Poland with Solidarity networks).

**Fourth**, **victim-centering is the field's most underdeveloped operational dimension.** The ICC's own records reflect this: Kenya victims described the prosecution's withdrawal as a "betrayal" (https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/CourtRecords/CR2014_09983.PDF); CSVR research found that South African victims felt the TRC "failed" them on amnesty and reparations despite public testimony's emotional power (https://csvr.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2000/01/tellingitlikeitis-3.pdf). Reparations struggles in Canada and South Africa indicate that recommendations and resources must travel together.

**Fifth, prevention of recurrence** is best served by mechanisms that build enduring institutional counterweights—constitutional protections, independent judiciaries, human rights commissions—rather than one-off moments of accountability. The cross-national evidence indicates that the *motivation-addressing* purpose of mechanisms (mitigating grievances, signaling state commitment to peace) drives the durability effect, not their punitive content alone (https://academic.oup.com/isq/article-abstract/61/3/690/4643613). This insight, validated by the diversity of case studies here, suggests that lustration has a credible claim (Czech, German unification) when paired with institutional reform, and that truth commissions have a credible claim when followed by structural implementation. By contrast, ICC prosecutions without enforcement or followed by political backlash (Kenya, Sudan) generate diminishing demonstrable dividends.

In sum, the evidence accumulated across South Africa, Canada, the former Yugoslavia, Kenya, Sudan, Germany, the United States, and post-communist Central Europe supports a layered, sequenced, context-sensitive transitional justice strategy whose outcome metric should be motivation-addressing grievance reduction and institutional reform, with formal accountability pursued through mixed tribunals operating under feasible conditions of cooperation. The strongest single lesson is that attention to victim-centered design, comprehensive reparations, and follow-through on recommended reforms is the indispensable variable distinguishing mechanisms that consolidate democratic transitions from those that, despite extensive documentation and costly processes, leave underlying structural causes of violence largely intact.

# Process Tracing as Bayesian Updating vs. Causal-Diagram Inference: Methodological Tensions, Empirical Applications, and the Evolving Post-2010 Consensus

## I. Framing: Two Traditions, Shared Goals, Divergent Tools

The methodological conversation Andrew Bennett and Jeffrey Checkel consolidated in *Process Tracing: From Metaphor to Analytic Tool* (Cambridge, 2014) and the Bayesian/counterfactual program that runs from Judea Pearl's "causal calculus" papers (1995–present) through the work Pearl synthesizes in *The Book of Why* and that James Mahoney has explicitly grafted onto qualitative case research are now the two most influential frameworks for "mechanism-based" causal inference in political science (https://summit.sfu.ca/_flysystem/fedora/sfu_migrate/14884/SimonsWorkingPaper21.pdf). Both reject covering-law regularity as sufficient for explanation; both insist that causal claims require an account of *how* X produces Y; and both now routinely invoke counterfactual language. The tensions sit at three points: how a "mechanism" is defined and empirically grasped, how multiple causal pathways (equifinality) are identified and adjudicated, and how unobserved variables that confound interpretation are diagnosed and neutralized.

### Operationalization of "Causal Mechanism"

Bennett and Checkel (2014, p. 7) define process tracing as "the analysis of evidence on processes, sequences, and conjunctures of events within a case for the purposes of either developing or testing hypotheses about causal mechanisms that might causally explain the case." Critically, they drop the older "intervening variable" terminology because, as they note (p. 8-9), interceding events may be caused by additional forces, have amplifying or dampening effects, exhibit feedback, or function purely as diagnostic markers ("dye in a CAT scan") that do not transmit causal force to the outcome. A process-tracing mechanism is therefore a *theoretically specified part-configuration* of causal-process observations (CPOs), not a list of variables in a regression (pp. 7–11; cf. Collier, Brady, and Seawright's CPO/DSO distinction at https://summit.sfu.ca/_flysystem/fedora/sfu_migrate/14884/SimonsWorkingPaper21.pdf).

Pearl/Mahoney treat mechanisms as structurally isomorphic: a Bayesian network expressed as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) plus a set of structural equations, where each "mechanism" corresponds to the structural function assigned to an endogenous node, and unobserved "exogeneity terms" *U* capture noise or omitted forces that can be folded into functional-form uncertainty (Humphreys and Jacobs, "Qualitative Inference from Causal Models," 2017, pp. 7–8, https://macartan.github.io/assets/pdf/papers/2017_qualdag.pdf). Mahoney (2016, "Mechanisms, Bayesianism, and process tracing," *New Political Economy*) extends this by treating events as *sets of cases*, so that intervening events have membership rather than values, and Bayesian updating becomes a contraction of the domain of possible worlds (https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/routledg/cnpe/2016/00000021/00000005/art00008). Barrenechea and Mahoney (2019, "A Set-Theoretic Approach to Bayesian Process Tracing," *SMR*) restate Bayes' theorem as the narrowing of possible-world sets, defining "consequentialness" and "expectedness" of evidence analogously to Pearl's probabilistic restrictions but in set-theoretic language (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0049124117701489).

The operational consequence: for Bennett/Checkel, mechanism is empirically *inferred from within-case sequences and diagnostic markers*; for Pearl/Mahoney, it is *posited in the graph and used to define which observations would update beliefs*. Bennett and Checkel (pp. 23-26) explicitly ground their framework in scientific realism and pragmatist philosophy, while Mahoney's "toward a unified theory of causality" (2008, *CPS*) and his 2012 *SMR* essay on hoop/smoking-gun/straw-in-the-wind tests explicitly map process tracing onto counterfactual Bayesian logic. Bennett (2008, "Process Tracing: A Bayesian Perspective," Oxford Handbook) is the original bridge, demonstrating that hoop tests update weaker priors than smoking-gun tests — a formal claim later extended by Humphreys and Jacobs (2015).

### Equifinality in Comparative Case Studies

Bennett and Checkel (2014, p. 6) flag equifinality as one of the explicit problems their volume addresses: "criteria for how micro to go and how to deal with the problem of equifinality (the possibility that there may be multiple paths or combinations of different variables that can produce the same kind of outcome)." Their operational solution combines hoop tests, smoking-gun tests, and straw-in-the-wind tests (per Van Evera 1997) to discriminate among rival causal chains that terminate in the same outcome (https://summit.sfu.ca/_flysystem/fedora/sfu_migrate/14884/SimonsWorkingPaper21.pdf; Mahoney 2012, *SMR*, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0049124112437709). If two distinct hypotheses both imply the observed outcome, hoop tests can only refute, not confirm — leaving equifinality as a residual problem that the within-case sequence of intermediate events is supposed to resolve by tracing each mechanism's distinctive empirical fingerprint.

Charles Ragin's QCA tradition handles equifinality by design: "causation is an asymmetric, conjunctural, and equifinal phenomenon" (Ragin 2008; cf. https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-12982-7_7). Each row of the truth table corresponds to a *sufficient combination*, and Boolean minimization preserves distinct paths leading to the same outcome. Mahoney folds this into Bayesian logic by observing that the subset/superset relations of set theory *are* the quantitative limits of Bayesian inference as sample size shrinks (Mahoney 2016). Humphreys and Jacobs (2017, https://macartan.github.io/assets/pdf/papers/2017_qualdag.pdf) make the strongest claim for the Pearl/Mahoney side: process tracing and equifinality become formally tractable when the theory is encoded as a structural causal model — d-separation then tells you which observations block versus open informative paths, and equifinal configurations can in principle be enumerated as disjoint exhaustive alternatives. The crucial Bayesian advantage, per Fairfield and Charman (2017, *Political Analysis*, http://cpd.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/CPC_Fairfield_article.pdf), is that explicit Bayes logic forces the analyst to compare a hypothesis *H* against concrete rivals *H₁, H₂,…* rather than the vacuous complement ∼H, thereby addressing equifinality by demanding a specified competing recipe rather than leaving it implicit.

Bennett and Checkel, by contrast, treat rival hypotheses as data-elicited during research, accepting that the analyst may not enumerate all rivals up front. This is empirically flexible but allows "adversarial" hypotheses to be constructed after the fact — the precise failure mode Sherry Zaks (2020, "Updating Bayesian(s): A Critical Evaluation of Bayesian Process Tracing," *PA*, https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/abs/updating-bayesians-a-critical-evaluation-of-bayesian-process-tracing/3F9504656A884F380AE64151F5C8BE06) identifies as the most serious critique of dominant Bayesian practice (see Section IV below).

### Confounder Identification in Observational Data

Pearl's framework is the dominant formal apparatus for confounder identification. His back-door criterion (Pearl 1995, "A Causal Calculus for Statistical Research," https://proceedings.mlr.press/r0/pearl95a/pearl95a.pdf) provides a graphical test: a set Z "blocks" the back-door paths from X to Y if every such path contains a variable in Z and no collider is conditioned on; the front-door criterion identifies effects through mediating variables when back-door adjustment fails; the do-calculus gives three rules for transforming observational expressions *P(y|x)* into interventional ones *P(y|do(x))* (Pearl, "The Mathematics of Causal Inference," https://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r416.pdf). Pearl and Azaria Paz ("Confounding Equivalence in Causal Inference," https://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r343w-reprint.pdf) further show that two covariate sets have equal bias-reducing potential either if both are back-door admissible or if their Markov boundaries around the treatment are identical.

Waldner (2015), Humphreys and Jacobs (2017), and Mahoney (in Barrenechea and Mahoney 2019) import this apparatus into process tracing via DAGs. Waldner's "completeness standard" requires that researchers trace all distinguishable paths in the DAG, not just the ones implied by the favored hypothesis (Humphreys and Jacobs 2017, p. 4, https://macartan.github.io/assets/pdf/papers/2017_qualdag.pdf). Inside a single case, confounding is diagnosed through "d-separation": a candidate confounder Z is informative iff it is *not* d-separated from the query node by already-observed variables. Process tracing, in this view, is the mirror image of cross-case adjustment: where quantitative practice blocks dependence via conditioning, qualitative practice opens dependence via observation (Humphreys and Jacobs 2017, p. 5).

Bennett and Checkel's "best practices" criteria (their ten standards listed at https://summit.sfu.ca/_flysystem/fedora/sfu_migrate/14884/SimonsWorkingPaper21.pdf pp. 23-25) substitute a more craft-bound architecture: prioritizing rival hypotheses; treating within-case observations as evidence on the theoretical mechanism rather than as data-set observations; auditing for omitting, miscoding, or misinterfering with alternative explanations; and demanding "diagnostic" detail at each link in the chain. There is no graphical test; confounders are identified by theoretical argument about sequence, proximity, and diagnostic specificity. Mahoney and Vanderpol (2015, "Trace Your Data Before You Trace Your Theory"), not Bennett, are the ones to bring the DAG notion explicitly into the within-case workflow — illustrating that Pearl/Mahoney offers a formal apparatus the Bennett/Checkel version largely lacks.

## II. Empirical Application I — Skocpol's States and Social Revolutions (1979)

Skocpol's *States and Social Revolutions* (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_and_Social_Revolutions) compares France, Russia, and China using Mill's methods of agreement and difference, supplemented with "negative" cases (England, Prussia, Japan). The inferential machinery is interpretive process tracing combined with comparative-historical case selection (https://undsoc.org/2014/02/10/skocpol-on-the-chinese-revolution/). She posits two causal mechanisms — (a) state breakdown under international-military pressure combined with administrative weakness, and (b) peasant insurgency enabled by autonomous village communities — whose conjuncture yields social revolution (https://gotterdammerung.org/books/reviews/s/states-and-social-revolutions.html). Equifinality is theoretically neutralized: Skocpol insists on a conjunction, not an "either/or"; rivalry is between her structural account and Marxist/voluntarist accounts (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/states-and-social-revolutions/9481262B2BDA1BFFB3C9218DBD447190; https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/101503/1/International_Affairs_Skocpol_review.pdf).

Methodologically, the work can be read through all three lenses:

1. **Bennett/Checkel (2014)** would classify *States and Social Revolutions* as the canonical within-case process tracing applied at the macro-structural level, using sequences (state fiscal crisis → administrative collapse → elite defection → peasant mobilization → regime revolutionization) as the principal evidentiary base, with the negative cases serving as hoop tests for the necessity of each conjuncture (https://summit.sfu.ca/_flysystem/fedora/sfu_migrate/14884/SimonsWorkingPaper21.pdf pp. 13-18).
2. **Pearl/Mahoney** would re-render the theory as a DAG in which *international pressure* → *state breakdown* ← *administrative weakness* → *coercive incapacitation* → *peasant insurgency enabling conditions* → *social revolution*, with agrarian structure as a quasi-INUS condition. The Bayesian/DAG apparatus would highlight what Skocpol herself does not: the *U* (exogeneity) terms that absorb arguably non-trivial unobservables such as revolutionary ideology, leadership, and contingency. Waldner-style "completeness" would obligate tracing all distinguishable paths, including the Bonapartist state-reconstruction path that Skocpol narrates but does not theorize as causal.
3. The statistical/selection-bias critique is concisely stated by Sekhon (2004, "Quality Meets Quantity: Case Studies, Conditional Probability, and Counterfactuals," *Perspectives on Politics*, https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/perspectives-on-politics/article/abs/quality-meets-quantity-case-studies-conditional-probability-and-counterfactuals/59455A61B7AE3B48856C9C9341180025): Skocpol's theory is *deterministic* — she predicts a certain outcome given certain conjunctures — yet her negative-case evidence (England, Prussia, Japan) is consistent with her hypothesis only if the *probabilistic* version is endorsed; the data Bara Geddes assembled against the international-pressure hypothesis nonetheless support it when read probabilistically. Sekhon's deeper point is that *Skocpol's method converts her qualitative claims into a counterfactual conditional whose probability she never estimates*. This is precisely the deficit the Pearl/Mahoney framework addresses by making *P(Y|X)* and *P(Y|do(X))* formally distinct operations. Furthermore, Goldstone (1991) argues that Skocpol's central concepts (state, structure, crisis) are ambiguous in ways that under-determine the comparative move (https://ideas.repec.org/a/sae/jothpo/v4y1992i1p93-112.html) — a critique Bennett/Checkel's emphasis on within-case measurable diagnostic evidence answers more directly than Pearl's graphical rules, which themselves depend on correctly encoded causal knowledge.

The legacy assessment by Amenta, Binelli, and Chirot (2024, "The methodological legacies of Theda Skocpol's *States and Social Revolutions*," https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/02633957241245893) situates Skocpol's method as the empirical operationalization of the comparative-historical-analysis (CHA) framework she and Margaret Somers articulated in their 1980 article, with one forward-looking implication worth noting: "Skocpol the empirical scholar turns out to have been methodologically more advanced than Skocpol the methodologist." This is the standard reading that motivates the Bayesian/DAG reformulation two decades later.

## III. Empirical Application II — The QCA Tradition Following Ragin

QCA, as Ragin formalized in *The Comparative Method* (1987) and refined through *Fuzzy-Set Social Science* (2000) and "Configurational Comparative Analysis" (2009, https://sites.socsci.uci.edu/~cragin/fsQCA/download/Chapter5_CCA.pdf), pursues causal inference through set-theoretic subset relations. Causation is asymmetric, conjunctural, and equifinal by assumption (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-12982-7_7). Cases are members of fuzzy sets; consistency (analogous to within-set homogeneity) and coverage (analogous to empirical relevance, akin to explained variance) define which causal combinations are sufficient or necessary.

Two enduring tensions appear when QCA is compared with Bennett/Checkel process tracing and Pearl/Mahoney Bayesian inference.

First, *equifinality is structural rather than substantive*: QCA natively represents multiple sufficient combinations as OR-connected recipes, while process tracing must diagnose multiple paths by painstaking diagnostic observation. Schneider and Wagemann's extension to a two-step fsQCA on democratization (https://exa.ai/library/publication/y3w4vj35c9v) demonstrates the analytical leverage this provides for cases of "democratic regression within regime" versus "breakdown to hybrid regime." Mahoney's (2016) set-theoretic Bayesian reformulation shows that QCA's consistency/coverage criteria are first-order Bayesian approximations when priors are uniform and likelihoods are derived from consistency thresholds; the two techniques converge asymptotically (https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/routledg/cnpe/2016/00000021/00000005/art00008).

Second, *confounder identification is treated very differently*. Ragin's calibration procedure invites substantive/theoretical priors about set membership; Pearl's back-door criterion requires explicit closure of the causal DAG. Barrenechea and Mahoney (2019) argue that their set-theoretic reformulation of Bayes' theorem preserves the *inferential* logic of QCA while adding an evaluative apparatus for *within-case* process-tracing evidence. Schneider and Rohlfing ("A Unifying Framework for Causal Analysis in Set-Theoretic Multimethod Research," 2016, *SMR*, https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/0049124115626170) supply the explicit bridge: causal inference via case-level counterfactuals *integrates* QCA and process tracing, with QCA providing population-level sufficiency/necessity claims and process tracing adjudicating among within-case alternatives. They had already in 2013 outlined "combining QCA and process tracing in set-theoretic multi-method research" (*Sociological Methods & Research* 42:559-597).

The most pointed contemporary limitation of QCA, articulated by Baumgartner and others, concerns "robustness" of necessity/sufficiency claims when the underlying consistency threshold is permissive (Baumgartner 2022, and discussion at https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00491241211031268): uncertainty in QCA is *systematically under-specifi ed*, and consistency thresholds, PRI values, calibration, and back-to-case checks address it heuristically but without an underlying causal-inference architecture. The Bayesian/DAG response is to insist on the back-door, do-calculus, and explicit covariate sufficiency checks Pearl's framework provides — operations that QCA does not natively perform, though Rohlfing and Schneider (2013, *Political Research Quarterly* 66:220–235) have shown that "formalized case selection for process tracing after QCA" can reduce the ambiguity.

## IV. The Quantitative-Causal-Inference Critique Since 2010

Pearl's framework, while technically sharp, has been challenged from multiple directions in the past fifteen years; the methodological reverberations for process tracing protocols are the focus of this section.

**(a) Selection bias and identification without probability.** Pearl and Paz (1999–2014) extend the back-door criterion to selection diagrams and demonstrate that treatment-dependent covariates can be admissible (https://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r343w-reprint.pdf). The implication for case-study research: conditioning on a case-selection rule (the "selection-of-cases for study" variable, like "revolutions between 1789 and 1980") is itself a causal intervention that can bias estimates if unacknowledged. Bennett and Checkel's protocol documents do not systematically diagnose this; the Pearl-inspired Waldner completeness standard does, by demanding that selection into the case set be represented as part of the graph (Waldner 2015, discussed at https://macartan.github.io/assets/pdf/papers/2017_qualdag.pdf p. 4).

**(b) Post-treatment conditioning.** Pearl himself ("Conditioning on Post-treatment Variables," 2015, https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/jci-2015-0005/html) clarifies that Rule-2 of do-calculus *does* permit conditioning on post-treatment variables in some circumstances (when separation holds in the mutilated graph G_x̄), but warns that inappropriate conditioning — including on colliders affected by treatment — opens back-door paths. In a process-tracing context, treating an event that lies downstream of X as evidence about the cause of Y is exactly a post-treatment conditioning problem: if a researcher observes and codes the mediator, they may induce collider bias unless they use the right graph rule.

This critique has been absorbed, in formal terms, into the DAG-based process tracing framework of Humphreys and Jacobs (2017), which explicitly models mediators and moderators as graph nodes and requires that the researcher demonstrate d-separation of the query variable from the evidence variable before claiming "probative value." In less formal versions, the same insight animates the "veil of ignorance" process-tracing protocol (Luo et al., Symposium 2020, discussed in Checkel 2021, https://www.eui.eu/Documents/DepartmentsCentres/SPS/Profiles/Checkel/APSAAnnualConvention-CheckelPaper.0921.pdf pp. 2-5), in which a separate analyst evaluates evidence the researcher has pre-collected, eliminating (in principle) the bias introduced by post-treatment conditioning on evidence the researcher already knew was available. This is a direct methodological import of the qualitative-causal-inference critique.

**(c) The Zaks (2020) critique and Bayesian process tracing's gap.** Zaks' "Updating Bayesian(s)" (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/abs/updating-bayesians-a-critical-evaluation-of-bayesian-process-tracing/3F9504656A884F380AE64151F5C8BE06) systematically evaluates four strong claims made for explicit Bayesian process tracing (BPT):

1. It enables causal inference from iterative research.
2. The sequence in which evidence is evaluated is irrelevant.
3. It enables full engagement of rival explanations.
4. It prevents ad hoc hypothesizing and confirmation bias.

Zaks concludes that, on current practice, BPT "introduces more bias than it corrects for on numerous dimensions." Bennett, Charman, and Fairfield (2021, "Understanding Bayesianism: Fundamentals for Process Tracers," *PA* https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/abs/understanding-bayesianism-fundamentals-for-process-tracers/E543498F74EA03536A0693CE5BA5490C) counter that mutual exclusivity of hypotheses (MEE), proper handling of likelihoods on multiple hypotheses (rather than only H vs. ∼H), and iteration are achievable but require discipline the field has not consistently observed. Zaks' "Return to the Scene of the Crime" (https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/6F6C04ACD0E46D60E885BFD894A1C35E/S1047198721000243a.pdf/return_to_the_scene_of_the_crime_revisiting_process_tracing_bayesianism_and_murder.pdf) demonstrates, using a murder vignette, that BPT's step-by-step guidelines run into a series of specification problems in practice.

Checkel (2021), in his APSA address, summarizes the debate thus: "Bayesian process tracing is currently dominant," with 55% of process-tracing articles from January 2017 to August 2020 devoted in whole or part to formalization, mostly Bayesian (https://www.eui.eu/Documents/DepartmentsCentres/SPS/Profiles/Checkel/APSAAnnualConvention-CheckelPaper.0921.pdf p. 3). He identifies four outstanding problems: (i) the labeling controversy (the phrase "Bayesian process tracing" misleadingly applies the label to any qualitative Bayesian analysis, not to process tracing specifically); (ii) the inductive-mode problem (BPT cannot accommodate non-deductive mode because there are no theoretical priors); (iii) the arbitrary-probability problem (the three estimated probabilities required are subjectively assigned with no transparency mechanism); and (iv) the empirical-payload problem — Bayesian restatements of canonical studies (Wood 2003, Tannenwald 2007) "none of which demonstrates where the Bayesian approach improves the process tracing" (Checkel 2021, p. 5, citing Zaks 2021, p. 71).

## V. Empirical Application III — Recent Mixed-Methods Studies of Democratic Breakdown

The most active contemporary testing ground for integrating within-case evidence with cross-case statistical analysis is the literature on democratic backsliding, autocratization, and democratic breakdown. Three threads are worth noting:

(i) *Latin American backsliding, 1978–present.* A 2025 *Democratization* article (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13510347.2026.2703111) analyzes 27 episodes of democratic erosion in Latin America, combining a structured dataset of opposition strategic choices with case studies of Colombia and Mexico (survivors) versus Venezuela, Bolivia, and El Salvador (collapses). The dataset stage isolates associations involving party-system institutionalization and opposition composition; the case stage traces the *mechanism* by which opposition tactical choices translate institutional constraints into outcomes — a textbook sequential QCA + process-tracing MMR (Schneider-Rohlfing) deployment.

(ii) *Global QCA of authoritarian breakdown under mass contention, 1953–2024.* Braulio (2026, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7118179) applies fsQCA to 49 episodes and discovers the strong asymmetry: breakdown follows one necessary-but-not-sufficient combination (coercive defection + elite fragmentation without external support), while survival follows three distinct routes. This is equifinality in its most analytically tractable QCA form, and it directly mirrors the subset-superset logic Mahoney extends to Bayesian inference: the absence-of-external-support condition is the necessary back-door-controlled layer separating the breakdown recipe from the survival recipes.

(iii) *Administrative vs. coercive state capacity and democratic stability.* Andersen, Knutsen, and Skaaning (2025, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00323217251344758) provide a global analysis (1789–2020) identifying *administrative capacity* (meritocratic recruitment, impartial administration) as the robust predictor of incumbent-led democratic stability, while *coercive capacity* shows no robust association. The Pearl-Mahoney apparatus would re-read this finding as a back-door adjustment result: once the *administrative capacity* node is included, the *coercive capacity → breakdown* edge is blocked or attenuated. The Schneider-Wagemann tradition would read it through the two-step fsQCA, isolating "remote" (administrative) from "proximate" (coercive/elite) factors in the democratization breakdown literature going back to O'Donnell, Schmitter, and Linz, and refined by Maeda (2010).

In each, the within-case process-tracing step is taken up after the cross-case QCA/multiple-regression has whittled the solution space to a small number of paths. This is the architecture of set-theoretic MMR (Schneider and Rohlfing 2013, 2016) — and the practical answer to the question of how to integrate within-case evidence with cross-case statistical analysis.

## VI. The Emerging Methodological Consensus

Three elements of a near-consensus have crystallized in the post-2010 literature.

**First**, the dichotomy between "Bennett/Checkel narrative process tracing" and "Pearl/Mahoney Bayesian process tracing" has narrowed. Bennett and Checkel themselves recognize Bayesian logic as the dominant formal language (Bennett 2008; Checkel 2021). Mahoney and his collaborators recognize that process tracing must retain narrative-grounded diagnostic specificity that purely graphical representations compress. The standard textbook — Bennett and Checkel 2014, Beach and Pedersen's *Causal Case Study Methods* (2013, 2019) — now routinely includes Bayesian updating chapters; Humphreys and Jacobs (2017) explicitly wed within-case tracing to Bayesian-network DAGs.

**Second**, confounder identification is no longer treated as a problem that within-case tracing can finesse. The Cutting Edge advances of 2014–2022 — Waldner's completeness standard, the veil-of-ignorance protocol, Zaks' critique, Bennett–Charman–Fairfield's response, and the set-theoretic Bayesian reformulation — all converge on a stricter rule: the researcher must specify, in either graph or set-theoretic form, which variables condition the causal claim and which do not. The conventional "story plus narrative" process tracing that satisfied Bennett and Checkel's ten criteria in 2014 is now widely treated as necessary but insufficient.

**Third**, the practical integration of within-case with cross-case analysis follows the Schneider-Rohlfing (2016) MMR template: QCA or Bayesian regression establishes the *relevance* of mechanisms across a population; process tracing establishes *how* the mechanism operates in selected cases, including negative/least-likely cases (Levy 2008). Recent democratic-backsliding work (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13510347.2026.2703111; https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00471178251410728; https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00323217251344758) operationalizes this template directly. The older worry that qualitative case studies and large-N statistics are incommensurable has been largely retired in favor of explicit, sequential, and iterative designs.

The remaining points of contention are real but contained. (i) Subjectively assigned prior probabilities in BPT remain a credibility problem; the proposed remedies (transparency indices, peer-elicited priors, simulation-based calibration) are still pre-paradigmatic. (ii) The question of whether DAGs are *too* constraining — forcing causal knowledge onto researchers before they have done their fieldwork — is actively debated in interpretivist circles (Checkel 2021). (iii) The treatment of equifinality remains asymmetric: QCA handles it natively, Bayesian process tracing handles it via explicit hypothesis rivalry, and classical process tracing handles it via careful diagnostic differentiation of rival mechanisms (the result is the same but the epistemic economies differ).

Quantitatively, none of these debates can be settled by counting articles, but Checkel's bibliometric finding that 55% of process-tracing methodological output (Jan 2017 – Aug 2020) is devoted to formalization (https://www.eui.eu/Documents/DepartmentsCentres/SPS/Profiles/Checkel/APSAAnnualConvention-CheckelPaper.0921.pdf p. 3) tells us where the field's intellectual energy is flowing: toward ever more explicit, often Bayesian, often graph-based, but still fundamentally within-case mechanisms of causal inference.

---
