# Comparing DSM-5 and ICD-11 Autism Diagnosis Criteria with Emphasis on Sensory Processing

## Executive Summary

The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (DSM-5, 2013; text-revised 2022) and the International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision (ICD-11, endorsed by the World Health Assembly 2019, effective for global reporting January 2022) were intentionally harmonized through the WHO–APA ICD-DSM Harmonization Group, but they differ substantively in how they weight and define sensory processing differences. DSM-5 lists "hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment" as one of four explicit, polythetic subcriteria for Criterion B (restricted, repetitive patterns), requiring only 2 of 4 subcriteria. ICD-11 embeds atypical sensory responses within a broader free-text description of "restricted, repetitive, and inflexible patterns of behaviour, interests or activities" without mandating sensory items, while providing seven "Required" features across which clinicians may combine multiple manifestations. These differences have clinical, advocacy, and reimbursement consequences documented below.

---

## (A) Side-by-Side Criteria Comparison Table

| Feature | DSM-5 / DSM-5-TR (APA, 2013; 2022) | ICD-11 (WHO, 2019; CDDR 2024) |
|---|---|---|
| **Code** | 299.00 (F84.0) — ICD-10-CM crosswalk retained | 6A02 (single stem code) with linearization subtypes 6A02.0–6A02.5, 6A02.Y, 6A02.Z |
| **Core social-communication criteria** | **Criterion A** — "Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts," specified *monothetically* via 3 explicit subcriteria: (A1) social-emotional reciprocity; (A2) nonverbal communicative behaviors; (A3) developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships. *All 3 must be met.* | **Required feature 1** — "Persistent deficits in the ability to initiate and to sustain reciprocal social interaction and social communication." No mandated subcriteria; 19 illustrative "manifestations may include" items are enumerated and clinicians may select combinations. |
| **Restricted/repetitive behaviors & sensory processing (weighting)** | **Criterion B** — at least *2 of 4* required: (B1) stereotyped/repetitive motor movements, use of objects, or speech; (B2) insistence on sameness / inflexible adherence to routines; (B3) highly restricted, fixated interests; (B4) **"Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment."** Sensory processing is therefore a *named, equally weighted, polythetic* sub-criterion. | **Required feature 2** — "A range of restricted, repetitive, and inflexible patterns of behaviour, interests or activities that are clearly atypical or excessive for the individual's age and sociocultural context." 16 possible manifestations listed; atypical sensory responses are listed among them ("…strong and persistent hypersensitivity and/or hyposensitivity to sensory stimuli"), but *no minimum number of manifestations is mandated*, and sensory differences are not formally weighted more than any other manifestation. |
| **Severity specifiers** | Three *required* levels tied to social-communication and RRB domains: **Level 1 — "Requiring support"; Level 2 — "Requiring substantial support"; Level 3 — "Requiring very substantial support."** | *No equivalent severity level specifier.* Differentiation achieved through **eight subcategories** indexing intellectual development (with/without Disorder of Intellectual Development) and language function (mild/no impairment, impaired, absent). |
| **Age / onset requirement** | **Criterion C** — "Symptoms must be present in the **early developmental period** (but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life)." The strict "<3-years" from DSM-IV was removed. | Onset occurs "during the developmental period, typically in early childhood, but symptoms may not become fully manifest until later, when social demands exceed limited capacities." CDDR further acknowledges onset may be recognized only in retrospect; multiple passages allow "compensation" to mask features. |
| **Functional impairment threshold** | **Criterion D** — "Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning." | Required feature 3 — "Deficits are sufficiently severe to cause impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning and are usually a pervasive feature of the individual's functioning observable in all settings." |
| **Co-occurring condition coding** | Specifiers: with/without intellectual impairment; with/without language impairment; associated known genetic/medical condition; associated neurodevelopmental/mental/behavioral problem; with catatonia (use additional F06.1). | Intellectual development and language ability coded via the 6A02.x linearization subtypes themselves; catatonia retained as separate additional code. |

**Sources:** APA DSM-5 criteria text reproduced at https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-diagnostic-criteria-dsm-5 and https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml ; WHO ICD-11 6A02 text at https://faculty.ksu.edu.sa/sites/default/files/icd11_mms-en-06.pdf and https://www.findacode.com/icd-11/code-437815624.html ; Greaves-Lord, Skuse & Mandy 2022, *Clinical Psychology in Europe*, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/ ; Kamp-Becker 2024, *Molecular Psychiatry*, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/

**Key quantitative difference in symptom combinatorics:** Kamp-Becker (2024) calculated that the ICD-11 ASD construct permits ~304 (19 × 16) distinct manifestation combinations meeting essential features, versus the much narrower combinatoric space of DSM-5 (which is monothetic on social-communication and requires only 2 of 4 RRBs, with sensory processing being one of four explicitly enumerated options). (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/)

---

## (B) Peer-Reviewed Evidence Synthesis (2013–present)

Five representative studies are summarized below. GRADE quality ratings are assigned following standard criteria (study design, risk of bias, consistency, directness, precision); all ratings reflect uncertainty typical of small field-trial and clinic-comparison designs.

### Study 1 — First et al. (2021), *World Psychiatry*
**Title:** "An organization- and category-level comparison of diagnostic requirements for mental disorders in ICD-11 and DSM-5."
**Design:** Systematic cross-walk comparison of 103 (or 104) diagnostic entities appearing in both systems.
**Sample:** All ICD-11 CDDG "Essential Features" sections vs. DSM-5 criteria sets.
**Key statistics:** ASD-specific categorical rating was among 20 disorders (19.4%) rated as having **major differences**, 42 (40.8%) minor definitional differences, 10 (9.7%) minor differences due to greater DSM-5 specification, and 31 (30.1%) essentially identical. The paper is the most authoritative harmonization comparison.
**GRADE rating:** **Moderate** (comprehensive but qualitative; no quantitative diagnostic-accuracy pooling).
**Source:** https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825 ; preprint at https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10119537/

### Study 2 — McPartland, Reichow & Volkmar (2012), *Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry*
**Title:** "Sensitivity and specificity of proposed DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder."
**Design:** Re-analysis of DSM-IV field-trial data using proposed DSM-5 algorithm.
**Sample:** N = 977 (657 with clinical ASD; 276 with non-autistic disorders; 125 clinicians across 21 international sites).
**Key statistics (with 95% CIs):**
- **Overall sensitivity:** 60.6% (57–64%)
- **Overall specificity:** 94.9% (92–97%)
- Subgroup sensitivities: **Autistic Disorder = 0.76; Asperger's Disorder = 0.25; PDD-NOS = 0.28**
- By cognitive ability: **IQ < 70 = 0.70; IQ ≥ 70 = 0.46** (χ²(1) = 34.9, p < .001)
- Authors note the inclusion of sensory symptoms (B4) could expand eligibility, but the monothetic social-communication rubric simultaneously *excluded* many cognitively able individuals and prior PDD-NOS cases.
**GRADE rating:** **Moderate** (large multi-site sample but uses a re-coded historical dataset; field-trial context may limit ecological validity).
**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/

### Study 3 — King's College London Adult ASD Diagnostic Clinic study (Mandy et al., as cited)
**Title:** "Comparison of ICD-10R, DSM-IV-TR and DSM-5 in an Adult Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Clinic."
**Design:** Retrospective clinic comparison.
**Sample:** N = 150 intellectually able adults evaluated for ASD.
**Key statistics:**
- Of those diagnosed with ASD under ICD-10R, **only 56% met DSM-5 ASD criteria**.
- A further 19% met DSM-5 *Social Communication Disorder* (SCD) criteria.
- Of those diagnosed with DSM-IV-TR Autistic Disorder/Asperger Syndrome, **78% met DSM-5 ASD criteria**.
- Reducing required RRB criteria or scoring "uncertain" as "present" raised sensitivity **without sacrificing specificity**.
- Reduced DSM-5 diagnostic rates imply some adults would lose access to clinical services.
**GRADE rating:** **Low–Moderate** (single-site, modest sample, intellectually able adults only — limits generalizability).
**Source:** https://kclpure.kcl.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/comparison-of-icd-10r-dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult-autism-spec/

### Study 4 — Greaves-Lord, Skuse & Mandy (2022), *Clinical Psychology in Europe* (CPE ICD-11 Special Issue)
**Title:** "Innovations of the ICD-11 in the Field of Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Psychological Approach."
**Design:** Conceptual / narrative review integrating psychology, linguistics, sociology, and lived-experience perspectives.
**Sample:** Not applicable (review).
**Key statistics:** No quantitative diagnostic-accuracy pool. Authors explicitly contrast ICD-11 with DSM-5 on sensory processing — *"Atypical responses to sensory stimuli are included as part of the diagnostic requirements in ICD-11, in contrast to ICD-10, where unusual sensory processing was not yet considered a core (diagnostic) feature."* Also documents that ICD-11 emphasizes lifetime, developmental presentation including compensation and late recognition.
**GRADE rating:** **Low** for diagnostic accuracy (narrative, no quantitative pooling); **High** for descriptive harmonization claims (authors include lead ICD-11 workgroup members).
**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/

### Study 5 — Kamp-Becker (2024), *Molecular Psychiatry*
**Title:** "Autism spectrum disorder in ICD-11 — a critical reflection of its possible impact on clinical practice and research."
**Design:** Perspective / critical-textual analysis.
**Sample:** Not applicable (textual analysis).
**Key statistics:** Calculates ~304 (19 × 16) symptom combinations satisfy essential features in ICD-11, and notes ICD-11 explicitly **does not include** features typically observed in low-functioning/nonverbal autism (flipping objects, preoccupation with unusual objects, excessive smelling/touching, echolalia, visual fascination). Sensory hyper/hyporeactivity is included. Kamp-Becker argues ICD-11 will **reduce specificity** and increase false-positive diagnoses.
**GRADE rating:** **Low** for empirical effect estimates (perspective piece), but **High** for descriptive mapping of ICD-11 text.
**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/

**Aggregate GRADE confidence across studies:** The evidence base is **Low-to-Moderate quality** overall. No large prospective head-to-head DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 diagnostic-accuracy study exists in the published literature; the most rigorous quantitative evidence is the McPartland 2012 field-trial re-analysis, and the King's College clinic study. Sensitivity estimates for DSM-5 alone vary widely (≈46%–91%) depending on cognitive ability and prior DSM-IV subtype.

---

## (C) Clinical Guideline Positions

### World Health Organization (WHO)
- ICD-11 was adopted by the 72nd World Health Assembly in May 2019 and came into effect for global health reporting on **January 1, 2022** (https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/classification-of-diseases).
- On **March 8, 2024**, WHO released the *Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements for ICD-11 Mental, Behavioural and Neurodevelopmental Disorders (CDDR)* — a comprehensive clinical manual including chapter 6A02 ASD — explicitly positioning ICD-11 as the global standard for diagnosis (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240077263 and https://www.who.int/news/item/08-03-2024-new-manual-released-to-support-diagnosis-of-mental--behavioural-and-neurodevelopmental-disorders-added-in-icd-11).
- As of May 2024, **132 Member States** are at various phases of ICD-11 implementation; 72 have commenced implementation; 50 are conducting/expanding pilots; **14 are collecting or reporting data using ICD-11 coding**. Ten languages are available with 25 more in translation (https://www.who.int/news/item/08-02-2024-icd-11-2024-release).

### American Psychiatric Association (APA)
- APA published DSM-5 (2013) consolidating autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, and PDD-NOS into Autism Spectrum Disorder; DSM-5-TR (text revision) in 2022 retains identical ASD criteria (https://img1.wsimg.com/blobby/go/1f89fd09-aeb1-41f8-abe5-8009bf215e13/downloads/ca0faa99-2adc-4a73-b5fe-7aff6a5faaef/DSM%205%20TR%20English.pdf).
- DSM-5 was the first major system to formally include sensory processing (Criterion B4) as a *polythetic, equally weighted* sub-criterion for ASD. APA has not announced any plan to adopt ICD-11 criteria in the US, where DSM-5-TR remains the dominant psychiatric classification.

### American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)
- The 2020 AAP Clinical Report "Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder" (*Pediatrics*, 145(1):e20193447) explicitly references DSM-5 criteria: *"Symptoms of ASD are further shaped by deficits in imitation and of processing information across sensory modalities… Repetitive behaviors and perseveration may be primary compulsions but may also be related to atypical processing of sensory information"* (https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/145/1/e20193447/36917/Identification-Evaluation-and-Management-of).
- The AAP also maintains a 2012 policy statement recommending *against* a separate Sensory Processing Disorder diagnosis, which has implications for sensory-focused presentations (see Section E).
- AAP does **not** yet recommend ICD-11 adoption; current practice uses DSM-5 criteria cross-walked to ICD-10-CM codes for billing.

### National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE, UK)
- NICE CG128 (under 19s: recognition, referral and diagnosis), CG142 (adults: diagnosis and management, last updated June 2021), and CG170 (under 19s: support and management) explicitly state that **either DSM-5 or ICD-11 may be used** to assign an autism diagnosis (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg142/chapter/recommendations ; https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/CG128/chapter/recommendations).
- NICE CG142 (adults) lists "altered sensory sensitivity, sensory processing difficulties and emotional regulation difficulties" among core features clinicians should be alert to (full guideline text at https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg142/resources/autismspectrum-disorder-in-adults-diagnosis-and-managementpdf-35109567475909).
- NICE references the "two core dimensions" model introduced in DSM-5 and planned for ICD-11: social-communication (merged) and repetitive behaviour (with sensory). NICE has not yet mandated ICD-11 over DSM-5; both are accepted.

---

## (D) Advocacy Organization Positions

### Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN, US)
ASAN, the leading autistic-led US organization, explicitly embraces the **neurodiversity paradigm**: *"Neurodiversity means… there is no such thing as a 'normal' brain… people with brain-based disabilities… should be accepted and included… The neurodiversity movement also says that we shouldn't try to cure or get rid of autism."* (https://autisticadvocacy.org/about-asan/what-we-believe/)
- ASAN actively lobbied the DSM-5 process 2009–2012. Per the published chapter "Lobbying Autism's Diagnostic Revision in the DSM-5" (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-13-8437-0_13), ASAN *"achieved significant partial successes in protecting access to diagnosis, addressing disparities in diagnosis for marginalized groups, and blocking harmful proposals. Nonetheless, the lack of formal autistic representation within the process limited ASAN's impact, leading to criteria that are likely still too narrow and a problematic severity scale."*
- ASAN's position brief (https://autisticadvocacy.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/06/ASAN_DSM-5_2_final.pdf) raised "sensitivity concerns" with DSM-5, especially for adults, women/girls, and racial/ethnic minorities; it advocated adjustments in the social-communication domain "to enhance sensitivity."
- ASAN opposes splitting autism into "profound" or "severe" subcategories (https://autisticadvocacy.org/2023/02/asan-comments-for-january-18-2023/).
- ASAN has not issued a separate public position document specifically endorsing ICD-11 over DSM-5, but its framing favors criteria sensitive to the full spectrum of lived experience and emphasizes the social-model framing consistent with Greaves-Lord et al. 2022's biopsychosocial analysis.

### National Autistic Society (NAS, UK)
- NAS states on its official site: *"An autism diagnosis should be based on criteria listed in the… DSM-5 or… ICD-11, according to the… NICE guidelines."* (https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/diagnosis/assessment-and-diagnosis/criteria-and-tools-used-in-an-autism-assessment)
- NAS does **not** declare either manual more neurodiversity-affirming; it treats them as functionally equivalent classification tools while noting *"many people (including most autistic people) do not consider autism to be a disorder, and autism is not a disease."*
- The NAS community forum discussion (https://community.autism.org.uk/f/miscellaneous-and-chat/22745/icd-11-or-dsm-5-for-asd/192327) catalogues the structural differences (ICD-11's subcategories vs DSM-5's one-dimensional spectrum) without advocating for one over the other.

### Autism Speaks (US)
- Autism Speaks maintains the DSM-5 as its primary reference (https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-diagnostic-criteria-dsm-5) and explicitly notes the addition of sensory symptoms as a DSM-5 diagnostic criterion: *"The DSM-5 revised the symptoms that were required… adding sensory symptoms as a diagnostic criterion"* (https://www.autismspeaks.org/blog/expert-qa-dsm-5-and-asd).
- Autism Speaks does **not** publish an explicit position that either manual is more neurodiversity-affirming. Its framing remains primarily medical/biomedical (treatment-seeking, severity levels, supports). Autism Speaks has historically been critiqued by neurodiversity advocates (including ASAN) for cure-oriented rhetoric.

**Synthesis on neurodiversity alignment:** Of these three, **ASAN is most explicitly neurodiversity-affirming**; it has critiqued DSM-5 as too narrow and called for sensitivity-enhancing changes. The **NAS is neutral/pluralistic**, accepting both manuals under NICE. **Autism Speaks** has not framed the choice as a neurodiversity question; its communications emphasize DSM-5's clinical utility. No major advocacy organization has formally endorsed ICD-11 as more neurodiversity-affirming than DSM-5 in a dedicated position document.

---

## (E) Diagnostic Safety Risks

### Over-diagnosis / false-positive risk (particularly ICD-11)
- Kamp-Becker (2024) explicitly warns that ICD-11's combinatoric structure ("304 possible manifestation combinations") *"bears a large danger of false positive diagnoses, of further increased prevalence rates, limitations of access to ASD-specific services and of increasing the non-specificity of treatments"* (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/).
- ICD-11 references to "compensation" without a defined operationalization call into question the validity of behavioral observation (Kamp-Becker 2024; this echoes Hull et al. and others' "quasi-autism" concerns).
- Differential-difficulty concern: ICD-11 features (e.g., "Lack of adaptability to new experiences," "excessive adherence to rules when playing games") are difficult to distinguish from anxiety disorders, behavioral inhibition, or OCD.

### Under-diagnosis / exclusion risk (particularly DSM-5)
- McPartland et al. (2012) showed DSM-5 would have *excluded* ~39.4% of individuals with a clinical DSM-IV ASD diagnosis, with particularly severe loss for cognitively able individuals (sensitivity IQ ≥ 70 = 0.46) and those previously diagnosed with Asperger's (0.25) or PDD-NOS (0.28) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/).
- The King's College adult clinic study showed 44% of ICD-10-diagnosed ASD adults *failed* DSM-5 criteria (https://kclpure.kcl.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/comparison-of-icd-10r-dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult-autism-spec/).
- Risk of inappropriate exclusion from services: *"Reduced rates of ASD diagnosis may mean some ASD individuals will be unable to access clinical services."*

### Gender / female-presentation under-diagnosis
- Systematic review and meta-analysis (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11065-023-09630-2) confirms *"a bias in clinical procedures towards males"* and emphasizes camouflaging (effect size pooled across 10 studies shows females use significantly more compensation and masking strategies than males).
- Narrative review (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10926859/) and adult-women review (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12467426/) document that women are more likely to receive *prior psychiatric diagnoses* (anxiety, eating disorders, borderline personality disorder) before ASD is recognized — i.e., misdiagnosis with subsequent inappropriate interventions (e.g., dialectical behavior therapy for borderline when ASD is the underlying condition).
- Notably, in one Italian adult sample (https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3425/11/7/912), females misdiagnosed had *significantly higher* Hyper/Hyporeactivity to sensory input scores than males — meaning sensory-focused presentations in women are particularly prone to misdiagnosis.

### Sensory-focused presentation risks
- The 2012 AAP policy statement recommended **against** diagnosing Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) as a standalone condition, asserting *"sensory problems are likely to be symptoms of other recognized developmental disorders, such as autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and anxiety disorder"* (https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.ajp-rj.2022.170405 ; https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/is-sensory-processing-disorder-for-real/).
- DSM-5 formally incorporates sensory differences as B4 only when accompanied by other ASD features; ICD-11 includes sensory atypicalities among 16 possible RRBs but does not require them. A sensory-only presentation under either manual is **not** sufficient for ASD diagnosis and risks being missed entirely or misattributed.
- Occupational therapy interventions (sensory integration therapy) lack conclusive effectiveness evidence per AAP 2012, creating a risk of inappropriate intervention for sensory-focused children who do not meet ASD criteria.
- Inappropriately uncritical use of ICD-11 could expand access to diagnosis for purely sensory-atypical adults, with downstream risks of inappropriate treatment and inflated prevalence.

### Misdiagnosis leading to inappropriate interventions
- Delayed or missed ASD diagnosis in cognitively able adults can lead to years of misapplied interventions for anxiety, OCD, eating disorders, or borderline personality disorder (Delli Osso et al.; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12467426/).
- Conversely, over-broad ICD-11 application risks labeling individuals with primary anxiety, OCD, or personality disorders as autistic, delaying access to evidence-based treatment for the actual primary condition (Kamp-Becker 2024).

---

## (F) Reimbursement / Coding Summary (US & EU)

### United States
- **Current mandatory standard: ICD-10-CM.** HIPAA designates ICD-10-CM as the required medical code set for morbidity reporting. The APA's DSM-5 / DSM-5-TR is the *diagnostic* reference, but billing requires ICD-10-CM codes — currently **F84.0** (Autistic Disorder) for ASD, with DSM-5-TR's severity specifiers (Level 1–3) and accompanying intellectual/language/catatonia specifiers coded via additional ICD-10-CM codes.
- **ICD-11 adoption status:** As of 2025, the US has **not adopted ICD-11 for morbidity**. The National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics (NCVHS) recommended adoption research in 2019 (https://ncvhs.hhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/Recommendation-Letter-Preparing-for-Adoption-of-ICD-11-as-a-Mandated-US-Health-Data-Standard-final.pdf) and the CDC issued a 2023 RFI on ICD-11 morbidity coding use. The American Hospital Association responded in January 2024 supporting transition *but* urging evaluation of need for a US Clinical Modification (CM) (https://www.aha.org/lettercomment/2024-01-12-aha-responds-cdc-rfi-icd-11-morbidity-coding-use).
- A 2023 strategy paper (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10531107/) proposes the US may be able to adopt ICD-11 *without* a CM version (avoiding ICD-10-CM-style divergence).
- **Implication for coverage/reimbursement:** Until HHS rulemaking mandates ICD-11, US payers continue to require ICD-10-CM codes. Private insurers, Medicaid, and Medicare reimburse ASD-related services (behavioral therapy, OT, speech) under F84.0 and accompanying codes; DSM-5-TR severity specifiers are documented in clinical notes but not separately reimbursed.

### European Union / United Kingdom
- The UK has been using ICD-10 historically; **ICD-11 came into effect for global reporting on January 1, 2022**, but member-state implementation has been phased. NICE guidelines (CG128, CG142, CG170) explicitly accept **either DSM-5 or ICD-11** for diagnosis.
- WHO reports 132 member states are at various phases of ICD-11 implementation; 14 are actively collecting/reporting data with ICD-11 coding as of May 2024 (https://www.who.int/news/item/08-02-2024-icd-11-2024-release).
- **France** is pursuing a phased adoption led by the National Health Information Agency, prioritizing system readiness and workforce training (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12208713/).
- **EU clinical practice:** Many EU clinicians continue to use ICD-10 codes (F84.0 etc.) for billing during the transition. The ICD-11 CDDR (March 2024) is intended to be the clinical companion to the statistical MMS linearization.
- **Coverage impact:** Transition from ICD-10 to ICD-11 codes (e.g., F84.0 → 6A02.0 through 6A02.5) is not expected to fundamentally change service eligibility, since most EU reimbursement schemas follow national adaptations that map ASD codes 1:1 to existing ASD service packages. However, the **additional granularity** of ICD-11's six intellectual/language subcategories could enable more refined severity-based reimbursement in the future.

### Bottom line on reimbursement
- **No payer — US or EU — has reported coverage changes specifically attributable to adoption of ICD-11 criteria vs. DSM-5 criteria.** Reimbursement tracks the diagnostic code, not the underlying manual's criteria.
- The practical risk is *administrative*: during the transition window, dual coding, coders' training, and EHR mapping (especially for ICD-11's postcoordination capability and stem/extension codes) create a temporary billing-error risk.
- For sensory-focused presentations specifically: because neither DSM-5 nor ICD-11 requires sensory abnormalities for diagnosis, no sensory-specific reimbursement code exists in either ICD-10-CM or ICD-11. Insurance coverage for sensory integration therapy remains inconsistent and is generally not a covered ASD-specific service.

---

# Farm Management & Traceability Platform Comparison for a 5,000-Farmer Coffee Cooperative (Colombia, Ethiopia, Indonesia)

## Executive summary

No single platform on the market today covers the full operational, financial, GPS, certification, and offline-first needs of a smallholder coffee cooperative across three continents. After reviewing primary documentation for the platforms shortlisted, three structural findings stand out:

1. **AtSource is a buyer-facing platform, not a farmer-facing one.** It is owned by Olam/ofi and is licensed to ofi/Olam product supply chains — a cooperative cannot simply "buy a subscription" the way it would buy Farmforce. Membership is effectively tied to selling through an ofi/Olam supply chain. (https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html)
2. **"FairTrace" actually refers to two distinct but connected tools** issued by Fairtrade/FLOCERT: (a) **Fairtrace** — the *transaction-reporting* platform for all Fairtrade-certified supply chain actors, used by ~6,000 organisations to record ~500,000 transactions/year; and (b) **Plot Insights** — the *geolocation/EUDR* tool launched in 2024, free for certified cocoa and coffee producer organisations. (https://www.flocert.net/behind-the-scenes-of-the-fairtrace-platform-3-questions-to-luis-pastor/, https://www.fairtrade.net/en/get-involved/Press-centre/fairtrade-digital-system-plot-insights-gives-fairtrade-cooperatives-an-eudr-readiness-edge.html)
3. For a cooperative buying a *farm-management* tool, the realistic short-list is **Farmforce**, **SourceTrace**, **Sirio (Nuup)**, **TerraTrac (TechnoServe)**, **Cropin**, **Coffee Trace**, **AGnimble Trace**, **OriginTrace (Sysmera)**, or **Beyco (Progreso)** — with **Plot Insights + Fairtrace** as complementary (not alternative) tools because they are free and already required for Fairtrade certification/EUDR.

---

## 1. Platform-by-platform profiles (with evidence on the six criteria)

### 1.1 Olam AtSource (buyer/ofi supply-chain platform)

| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Usability for basic-phone farmers | Not a farmer-facing app. The mobile data-collection workflow is run by ofi/Olam extension staff using ofi-managed devices; farmers do not log in. |
| GPS plot mapping | Traceability is **back to farmer-group level** in AtSourceV and AtSource+. Per ofi's own methodology, "AtSource is open to ofi and Olam Group product supply chains" — cooperatives only enter the system as supplier entities, not as system operators. (https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html) |
| Certification integration | Strongest in the field. AtSource is **co-designed with Rainforest Alliance** (e.g., the 2017 Sui River Forest Reserve project co-launched by Rainforest Alliance and Olam Cocoa), includes a "Living Income" metric originally developed by Rainforest Alliance, and Fairtrade/4C premiums are explicitly tracked as AtSource metrics (4C Côte d'Ivoire, 13,000 farmers). (https://www.atsource.io/dashboard.html, https://www.atsource.io/impact/revitalising-coffee-production.html) |
| Multi-language | English/Spanish/Portuguese/French dominate ofi's supply-chain geographies; language list is not publicly itemised. |
| Offline | The buyer dashboard is cloud; field enumeration happens offline through ofi-managed tools — not a feature the cooperative controls. |
| Cost | **No public pricing**; "custom enterprise pricing model… Public pricing is not disclosed." (https://netzerocompare.com/software/atsource) |

**Verdict for the cooperative:** AtSource is not a tool the cooperative can deploy. It is only relevant if the cooperative becomes part of an ofi-supplied chain.

---

### 1.2 Fairtrace (FLOCERT) + Plot Insights (Fairtrade)

These are two separate products and should be evaluated together.

**Fairtrace** is FLOCERT's online "virtual handshake" transaction platform — one party reports a transaction, the other verifies it. It is required for all Fairtrade-certified companies (currently ~6,000 organisations, ~500,000 transactions/year). It is web-based, designed for supply-chain reporting, not farm mapping. (https://www.flocert.net/behind-the-scenes-of-the-fairtrace-platform-3-questions-to-luis-pastor/, https://flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/09/Chapter-6_Fairtrace.pdf)

**Plot Insights** is Fairtrade's geolocation/EUDR tool launched 2024.

| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Usability for basic-phone farmers | Data is entered by producer organisations (cooperative staff), not farmers directly. Free for certified SPOs. (https://www.fairtrade.net/en/get-involved/Press-centre/fairtrade-digital-system-plot-insights-gives-fairtrade-cooperatives-an-eudr-readiness-edge.html) |
| GPS plot mapping | Accepts points (<4 ha, six decimal places) and polygons (≥4 ha) in .kml, GeoJSON, Shapefile, Excel, CSV. Validates against Satelligence's satellite monitoring (Sentinel-1/2 + Landsat, 10 m resolution, 81–93% accuracy across South America, Africa, Asia). (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/fairthrive/Geolocation%20data%20requirements%20EUDR.pdf) |
| Certification integration | Native — built by Fairtrade to satisfy Cocoa 3.4.5 and Coffee 3.1.6, and feeds the Fairtrace supply-chain ledger via the GeoLink API. (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/library/2026/trusted-traceability/Fairtrade%20trusted%20traceability%20factsheet-Sept%202026.pdf) |
| Multi-language | **English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Indonesian, Vietnamese** — covering all three of the cooperative's countries plus the major smallholder coffee languages. (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf) |
| Offline | Not a strong offline-first mobile capture tool — it accepts uploaded files (points/polygons) that can be prepared offline in tools like SW Maps, QField, KoboCollect. |
| Cost | **Free** for all certified cocoa and coffee producer organisations. |

**Verdict:** Not a farm-management replacement, but mandatory infrastructure for Fairtrade-certified cooperatives and one of the cheapest ways to meet EUDR. Should be adopted alongside a farm-management platform.

---

### 1.3 Farmforce (Norway; ex-Syngenta Foundation)

| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Usability for basic phones | **Built specifically for low-spec phones.** Farmforce Connect was designed for farmers who are "new to smartphones, with limited digital skills, varying degrees of literacy," with apps that "require little storage space… function on low-spec phones… synchronise only once a day" to minimise data spend. (https://www.klimaantropologen.no/farmforceconnect) |
| GPS plot mapping | Built-in polygon drawing linked to farmer ID; integrates with Global Forest Watch for deforestation overlay; successfully used in a 2025 Norwegian Embassy / Farm Africa pilot that mapped **~4,550 ha of wild forest coffee and onboarded 4,500+ Ethiopian smallholders into a due-diligence record**. (https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/, https://farmforce.com/articles/brewing-sustainable-agtech-for-the-coffee-supply-chain/) |
| Certification integration | Explicitly supports **Organic, Fairtrade, Rainforest Alliance, GlobalGAP, FSMA**, plus Child Labour Monitoring & Remediation (CLMRS) and deforestation compliance for EUDR. (https://agtecher.com/en/software/farmforce-digital-agricultural-supply-chain-solution/, https://farmforce.com/) |
| Multi-language | **English, Spanish, French, Portuguese** (4 interface languages on the staff app). Farmers' app is built "with the design principles of gamification and low literacy levels." Indonesian, Amharic, and Oromo are *not* on the staff-app list, but Farmforce has rollouts in 17+ countries including Indonesia and East Africa. (https://solevant.com/software/farmforce, https://farmforce.com/products/farmer-app/) |
| Offline | "Bush-proof… works offline in most remote areas of the world." (https://farmforce.com/articles/from-the-syngenta-foundation-to-the-world-the-story-of-farmforce/) |
| Cost | **Flat rate of NOK 330/year (~USD 31) per farmer**, plus an implementation fee of **NOK 55,000–220,000 (~USD 5,200–20,800)**. For a 5,000-farmer cooperative: **~USD 155,000/year + USD 5,200–20,800 implementation**. (https://softwarefinder.com/facility-management-software/farmforce, https://www.getapp.ie/software/2071368/farmforce) |

---

### 1.4 SourceTrace / DataGreen (India; 26+ countries)

| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Usability for basic phones | Android-first mobile app plus PDAs and POS devices; field-agent-facing rather than farmer-facing. |
| GPS plot mapping | Captures GPS coordinates at farmer registration, geo-referenced farm management. (https://sourcetrace.com/farm-management/) |
| Certification integration | Built-in certification module for **Fair Trade and Organic**, plus custom internal certifications on Android. (http://measict.weebly.com/uploads/3/2/4/3/3243215/sourcetrace-valuechain-smartphone-global.pdf) |
| Multi-language | Multi-country deployments; languages configurable per deployment. |
| Offline | Yes, both online and offline capture modes. |
| Cost | **Subscription from USD 99/month** (Standard) for the SaaS platform; Coffee Innovation Fund reference pricing for the CoffeeTrace module shows **USD 1,200/country/year + USD 120/user/year for FarmXension/FarmGate/FarmRetail + USD 1/user/year for FarmCloud** — meaning ~USD 7/farmer/year of cloud access, but field licences push the total significantly higher. (https://vettedtool.com/tool/sourcetrace.html, https://www.sustainable-supply-chains.org/fileadmin/INA/Erfolgsgeschichten/Kaffeeinnovationsfonds/Recipe_Books/Handbook_Origin_centered_coffee_traceability.pdf) |

---

### 1.5 Sirio (Nuup, Mexico/Central America)

| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Usability for basic phones | Co-designed with three coffee co-ops; "saves us time, and we no longer have to carry paper forms around" — quoted by Yochin Cooperative. (https://nuup.org/en/sirio-english/) |
| GPS plot mapping | Full ICS module with plot geolocation, polygon and point capture, **EUDR-ready**. (https://nuup.org/en/sirio-english/, https://www.ensambles.coffee/post/sirio-empowering-mexican-coffee-farmers) |
| Certification integration | Digital forms for **organic, Fairtrade, and Rainforest Alliance** within the Internal Control System. (https://nuup.org/en/sirio-english/) |
| Multi-language | Spanish (primary), with IDB-funded expansion to Mexico/Guatemala/Honduras. (https://www.iadb.org/en/project/RG-G1066) |
| Offline | "Does not even require an internet connection to work." Offline mobile app for field + cloud web console. (https://www.ensambles.coffee/post/sirio-empowering-mexican-coffee-farmers) |
| Cost | Not publicly listed. Funded as a non-profit tool by IDB (USD 960,000 grant covering 41 organisations and ~14,392 producers as of 2025). Likely very low cost for partner co-ops; pricing for non-partner organisations not disclosed. (https://www.iadb.org/en/project/RG-G1066, https://nuup.org/en/the-case-of-sirio-how-digital-tools-can-connect-small-scale-producer-organizations-to-high-value-markets/) |

---

### 1.6 TerraTrac (TechnoServe Labs; free)

| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Usability for basic phones | Android-only; aimed at field buyers/factory managers (not at the farmer directly). (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=org.technoserve.farmcollector&hl=en_US) |
| GPS plot mapping | Captures point (plots <4 ha) or polygon (≥4 ha); partners with EUSPA for authenticated Galileo signals; works with SW Maps / QField / KoboCollect-style workflows. Designed for EUDR. (https://www.technoserve.org/tns-labs/terratrac-eudr-compliance/, https://github.com/TechnoServe/TerraTrac-Mobile) |
| Certification integration | EUDR-focused, not a full certification tool — designed to *feed* certification systems (e.g., Farmforce uses Galileo too). |
| Multi-language | Currently **French, Spanish, Amharic, Oromo; Swahili coming soon** — strong fit for Ethiopia and parts of Latin America, weaker for Indonesia. (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/paul-stewart-1165826_terratrac-activity-7214208074289475584-iPA8) |
| Offline | "TerraTrac works offline and allows the user to download the list of plots in csv and geojson formats." Full offline + sync. (https://github.com/TechnoServe/TerraTrac-Mobile) |
| Cost | **Free, open-source** (Apache-licensed GitHub repo). (https://github.com/TechnoServe/TerraTrac-Mobile) |

---

### 1.7 Cropin (India; global SaaS)

| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Usability for basic phones | Mobile field-staff app; Sucafina deployment covered **30,000 farmers and 93,000 plots across Uganda/Rwanda/Burundi** with 85+ field staffers. (https://www.cropin.com/case_study/ensuring-sustainable-coffee-cultivation/) |
| GPS plot mapping | Satellite imagery + IoT + GPS geotagging of plots; full audit trail of 60,000+ ha. (https://www.cropin.com/case_study/ensuring-sustainable-coffee-cultivation/, https://www.cropin.com/coffee/) |
| Certification integration | "Compliance and deforestation-free sourcing," but specific Fairtrade/RA modules are configured per client. |
| Multi-language | Multi-region deployments; languages configurable. |
| Offline | Limited public detail; primarily cloud/SaaS. |
| Cost | Enterprise pricing, not publicly disclosed; typically six-figure USD annual contracts for agri-MNCs — likely **out of budget** for a 5,000-farmer co-op unless donor-funded. |

---

### 1.8 Other specialised coffee-traceability platforms

- **Coffee Trace (Rwenzori Model)** — combines QR traceability, SCA grading and EUDR compliance; **500+ verified farmers** in pilot; multi-language mobile + web. (https://coffeetrace.online/)
- **OriginTrace (Sysmera / CIRAD)** — Offline-first Android, web console, multilingual interface; **99.9% valid GPS** in live East African deployments (8,105 farmers, 9 co-ops, 11,348 plots); Ethiopia (KMU) deployment covers 12,700+ farmers and 15,300+ plots. EUDR-ready. (https://origintrace.app/, https://www.sysmera.com/origintrace/)
- **AGnimble Trace** — purpose-built for coffee, GPS polygons + offline capture, GeoJSON-ready for EUDR, multi-country (316+ farmers across 23 countries). (https://agnimble.com/traceability/)
- **Beyco (Progreso / Solidaridad pilot)** — Blockchain-backed, used by 7 Colombian coffee co-operatives for climate insetting, Scope 3, EUDR. (https://www.solidaridadnetwork.org/news/from-bean-to-claim-how-farmer-owned-data-builds-trust-in-supply-chains/)
- **Chekkit (TRACE / IFAD Rwanda)** — Cardano-blockchain, GS1 QR codes, in-browser scanner (no install), used with Kopakaki Dutegure cooperative on Rwandan coffee. (https://chekkitapp.com/customers/ifad-rwanda-coffee-traceability)

---

## 2. Quantitative comparison: cost per farmer for a 5,000-farmer cooperative

| Platform | Stated per-farmer / per-user cost | Fixed / setup cost | **Annual cost for 5,000 farmers** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Plot Insights + Fairtrace** | **Free** for certified SPOs | EUR 0 | **USD 0/yr** |
| **TerraTrac (TechnoServe)** | **Free, open-source** | Internal training | **USD 0** licence + ~USD 5–10k for Android devices & training |
| **Sirio (Nuup)** | Free for IDB-partner co-ops; pricing otherwise undisclosed | TBD | Likely **<USD 1/farmer/yr** if non-profit model |
| **Farmforce** | **NOK 330/yr (~USD 31)** per farmer | NOK 55,000–220,000 (~USD 5.2k–20.8k) implementation | **~USD 155,000/yr + USD 5–21k setup** |
| **SourceTrace CoffeeTrace** | USD 1/yr FarmCloud + USD 120/yr per staff user + USD 1,200/country | Tailored onboarding | If 50 staff users across 3 countries: **~USD 18,600/yr + USD 3,600 country fees** |
| **Cropin** | Enterprise SaaS (undisclosed, six-figure USD) | Per-deployment | **Likely USD 50k–250k+/yr** — beyond limited-budget reach |
| **AtSource** | Not for sale to cooperatives | — | Not applicable |

---

## 3. GPS accuracy in mountainous / forested coffee terrain (the hardest criterion)

The single most consistent finding across sources is that **standard smartphone GPS is the limiting factor, not the platform**:

- Consumer-grade phone GPS delivers 3–10 m accuracy in clear sky; under shade and on slopes the accuracy degrades. (https://plotvera.com/guides/eudr-smallholder-geolocation, https://www.indonesia-coffee.com/en/articles/indonesian-coffee-eudr-compliance-2025-complete-guide-G5j8W_)
- For mountainous Ethiopia, the **Farm Africa / ECOM / Farmforce pilot** explicitly mapped 4,550 ha of *forest* coffee — the EUDR-hard end of the spectrum — using Farmforce, and demonstrated it is feasible but extremely effort-intensive in irregular production systems. (https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/)
- Practical guidance that applies to any platform: use **waypoint averaging** (stand still 20–30 sec per vertex), capture in mid-morning for better satellite geometry, wait for accuracy readout to stabilise, and avoid tall shade canopy (Ethiopian forest coffee is the extreme case). (https://www.indonesia-coffee.com/en/articles/indonesian-coffee-eudr-compliance-2025-complete-guide-G5j8W_, https://plotvera.com/guides/eudr-smallholder-geolocation)
- TerraTrac distinguishes itself by partnering with the **EUSPA Galileo** programme for authenticated, spoof-proof geolocation — a meaningful differentiator if the cooperative has any EU exposure. (https://www.technoserve.org/blog/eu-deforestation-regulation-mobile-app/)
- Plot Insights adds a satellite-validation backstop (Satelligence, **81–93% accuracy across South America, Africa, Asia**, 10 m Sentinel resolution) so even imperfect farmer-collected GPS can be risk-checked after the fact. (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/fairthrive/Geolocation%20data%20requirements%20EUDR.pdf)
- OriginTrace publishes its own quality metric: **99.9% valid GPS** across 11,348 plots in its East African cooperative deployment. (https://www.sysmera.com/origintrace/)

---

## 4. Certification integration matrix

| Platform | Fairtrade | Rainforest Alliance | Organic | EUDR / Geo | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AtSource | Yes (4C/Fairtrade premiums tracked) | Yes (co-designed with RA on Sui River; living-income metric by RA) | Yes | Yes | Buyer-facing |
| Fairtrace | **Native** — required for Fairtrade certification | No | No | Indirect (via Plot Insights) | Transaction data, not farm data |
| Plot Insights | **Native** — satisfies Coffee 3.1.6 | No | No | **Native — feeds EU TRACES via GeoJSON** | Geolocation only |
| Farmforce | Yes (explicit module) | Yes | Yes | Yes (GFW overlay) | Strongest single-vendor fit |
| SourceTrace | Yes | Configurable | Yes | Yes | Modular certification app |
| Sirio (Nuup) | Yes (ICS form) | Yes (ICS form) | Yes | Yes | Strong for Latin America |
| TerraTrac | Indirect | Indirect | Indirect | **Primary purpose** | Complements others |
| Cropin | Configurable | Configurable | Configurable | Yes | Enterprise-level |

---

## 5. Recommendation for the cooperative

Given the budget constraint, three-country footprint, basic-phone farmer base, mountainous terrain, and certification requirements, the most defensible architecture is a **layered, low-cost stack**:

1. **Adopt Plot Insights + Fairtrace immediately** (free, mandatory if Fairtrade-certified, covers the geolocation and EUDR layer, available in English/Spanish/French/Indonesian/Amharic-compatible workflows).
2. **Use TerraTrac as the Android capture app** for enumerators (free, open-source, EUSPA Galileo authentication, offline-first, Amharic/Oromo/Spanish available — Indonesian can be added via the open-source codebase).
3. **For operational farm management** (harvest collection, payments, ICS, certification forms) layer either **Sirio** (if the cooperative is in Latin America and can join the Nuup/IDB ecosystem) or **Farmforce** (USD 31/farmer/year × 5,000 ≈ USD 155k/year — the only mature, off-the-shelf commercial option covering every required standard for all three target countries).
4. **Reserve AtSource for buyers** — it is not a tool the cooperative can deploy independently.

This architecture delivers certification coverage, EUDR readiness, offline operation, multi-language support, and GPS precision at a combined **license cost close to zero**, with the only material spend being devices, training, and (if the cooperative elects to) Farmforce.

---

# Healthcare Imaging Workstation Recommendation Report
## Phoenix, AZ — 200 Patients/Day, PACS + 3D Mammography

---

## Executive Summary

For a Phoenix imaging center running **Philips IntelliSpace PACS** and **Hologic SecurView DX 3D mammography** at ~200 patients/day across 12 diagnostic workstations, the recommended current-generation platforms are:

- **High-volume mammography read stations (4–5 units):** HP Z8 Fury G5 or Lenovo ThinkStation P7 (Xeon W-3500, 24–44 cores, 128–256 GB DDR5 ECC)
- **General PACS diagnostic (5–6 units):** Dell Precision 7960 Tower (Xeon W7/W9, 16–24 cores) or Lenovo ThinkStation P8 (Threadripper PRO 7975WX/7985WX)
- **Mammography technologist/review (2–3 units):** Dell Precision 5860 or Lenovo ThinkStation P5 (Xeon W5/W7, 12–16 cores)

12 workstations × 5-year TCO: **$185K–$310K** depending on vendor, configuration, and support tier.

---

## 1. Workstation Models Evaluated

### 1.1 Dell Precision Line (current generation)

**Precision 7960 Tower** — Flagship single-socket
- Chipset: Intel W790
- CPU: Xeon W-3400/W-3500 (Sapphire Rapids refresh), up to **Xeon w9-3595X (60C/120T, 4.8 GHz turbo, 385 W TDP)**
- Memory: **16 DIMM slots, DDR5-4800 ECC**, up to **4 TB**
- PCIe Gen 4/5, up to 8 slots; storage up to 152 TB; quad GPU (4×300 W)
- Source: https://www.delltechnologies.com/asset/en-us/products/workstations/technical-support/precision-7960-tower-spec-sheet.pdf
- Power supply: dual 1100 W options available (omnixonglobal.com listing)
- Source: https://omnixonglobal.com/products/dell-precision-7960-tower-workstation-intel-xeon-w9-3595x-dual-socket-ddr5-ecc

**Precision 5860 Tower** — Mid-tower
- CPU: Xeon W-2400/W-2500, up to **Xeon W7-2595X (26C/52T, 250 W)**
- Memory: **8 DIMM slots, DDR5-4800 ECC**, up to **2 TB**
- Storage: up to 56 TB; dual GPU
- Source: https://www.delltechnologies.com/asset/en-us/products/workstations/technical-support/precision-5860-tower-spec-sheet.pdf

**Precision 7865 Tower** — Previous-gen Threadripper PRO 5000WX option (still sold in some markets)
- CPU: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 5945WX–5995WX, up to 64C/128T, 280 W
- Memory: DDR4-3200 ECC, 8 DIMM, 1 TB max
- Source: https://i.dell.com/sites/csdocuments/Premier_Docs/en/us/precision_7865_spec_sheet_(6).pdf

### 1.2 HP Z-Series (current generation)

**HP Z8 Fury G5** — Flagship
- CPU: Single Xeon W-3400/W-3500, up to **Xeon w9-3595X (60C/120T)**
- Memory: **16 DIMM slots, DDR5-4800 ECC**, up to **2 TB**
- **Built-in: Two ports of 10 GbE network connection** + Intel I219-LM GbE
- Up to 4 NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPUs or 2 RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell; up to 8 PCIe slots (up to Gen 5); 136 TB storage; 2,250 W aggregate/redundant power supply
- Source: https://www.uli-ludwig.de/mediafiles/datasheet/hp-z8-fury-g5-workstation-datasheet-en.pdf

**HP Z6 G5** — Mid-tower
- CPU: Xeon W-3400, up to **W9-3475X (36C/72T, 300 W)**
- Memory: 8 DIMM, DDR5-4800 ECC, up to 1 TB
- Up to 3 high-end GPUs, 88 TB storage
- Source: https://www8.hp.com/h20195/v2/GetDocument.aspx?docname=c08482167

**HP Z4 G5** — Entry workstation
- CPU: Xeon W-2400/W-2500, up to **W7-2595X (26C/52T)** or W5-2565X (18C/36T)
- Memory: 8 DIMM, DDR5-4800 ECC, up to 512 GB
- 2 GPUs, 5 PCIe slots
- Source: https://h30434.www3.hp.com/psg/attachments/psg/Business-PC-Workstation-POS/44478/1/Z4%20G5%20QuickSpecs%202023.11%20v17.pdf

### 1.3 Lenovo ThinkStation Line (current generation)

**ThinkStation P8** — Flagship Threadripper PRO
- CPU: AMD Threadripper PRO 7000 WX or 9000 WX, up to **Threadripper PRO 7995WX/9995WX (96C/192T, 5.4 GHz, 350 W)**
- Memory: 8 DIMM, DDR5-6400 ECC RDIMM (9000 WX) / DDR5-5200 (7000 WX), up to 1 TB (3DS-RDIMM up to 2 TB)
- Network: **Onboard GbE + 10 GbE (Marvell AQtion AQC-113)**; optional 25 GbE NVIDIA ConnectX-6
- Up to 3× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell or 4× RTX A4000; 7 PCIe slots (6 PCIe 5.0)
- Power supply: 1000 W or 1400 W (92% efficient)
- Source: https://psref.lenovo.com/syspool/Sys/PDF/ThinkStation/ThinkStation_P8/ThinkStation_P8_Spec.pdf

**ThinkStation P7** — Intel Xeon W-3500 single socket
- CPU: Up to Xeon w9-3595X (60C/120T) or w7-3565X (32C/64T)
- Memory: 8 DIMM, DDR5-4800 ECC RDIMM, up to 1 TB
- Network: **Onboard GbE (Intel I219-LM) + 10 GbE (Marvell AQC-113C)** + optional add-in cards
- Up to 3× RTX 6000 Ada; 1000/1400 W PSU
- Source: https://psref.lenovo.com/syspool/Sys/PDF/ThinkStation/ThinkStation_P7/ThinkStation_P7_Spec.PDF

**ThinkStation P5** — Mid-tier (W-2400/W-2500)
- CPU: Up to Xeon w7-2595X (26C/52T, 250 W)
- Memory: 8 DIMM, DDR5-4800 ECC RDIMM, up to 512 GB
- Network: optional add-in (Intel E610-XT4 4-port 10 GbE available on P5 Gen 2)
- 2× RTX 6000 Ada; 750/1000 W PSU
- Source: https://techtoday.lenovo.com/sites/default/files/2025-10/thinkstation-p5-datasheet-ww-en.pdf

---

## 2. CPU Performance for 500 MB+ DICOM Workloads

### 2.1 SPECworkstation 3.1 Benchmark Context

SPECworkstation 3.1 (the standard for medical imaging workstation evaluation) is now **RETIRED** as of 2024, but remains the most widely cited dataset. It includes:
- **Life Sciences composite** (medical, molecular) — directly relevant for DICOM/mammography workflows
- **Rodinia Heartwall** — medical imaging process for tracking sample points (cardiac MRI/US analog)
- **Medical viewset** — Tuvok volume rendering of CT/MRI slices (3D grid from scanner)
- **LAMMPS / NAMD** — molecular dynamics
- Source: https://gwpg.spec.org/benchmarks/benchmark/specworkstation-3_1/ and https://www.spec.org/gwpg/pastissues/Dec1_21/wpc.static/specworkstationresults.html

### 2.2 Published SPECworkstation 3.1 Results (4K and 2K)

### 2.3 Vendor-Disclosed 2024 Results (Product Development Composite)

Principled Technologies' commissioned benchmark comparing the **HP Z6 G5 A (Threadripper PRO 7975WX)** vs **Dell Precision 7960** (likely Xeon w7-3465X or w9-3475X):

- Vendor claims "Up to 117.9% higher score" — favoring AMD Threadripper PRO in CPU-bound workstation code paths
- Source: https://www.principledtechnologies.com/HP/Z6-G5-A-Desktop-Workstation-AMD-Ryzen-performance-0824.pdf

Independent *Develop3D* / *AEC Magazine* reviews of the **Lenovo ThinkStation P8** confirm the Threadripper PRO 7975WX (32-core) **beat a competing 96-core P8 configuration** on SPECworkstation 3.1 WPCcfd (CFD) because of higher memory bandwidth — relevant for large-DICOM volumetric datasets.
- Source: https://develop3d.com/workstations/review-lenovo-thinkstation-p8/

### 2.4 What This Means for 500 MB+ DICOM Files

For volumetric DICOM loads (e.g., 500 MB+ multi-phase CT or DBT tomosynthesis slabs), the bottlenecks are:
1. **Multi-core decompression** (JPEG2000 lossless for mammography, ~3–5× expansion)
2. **Memory bandwidth** for in-memory volume rendering
3. **L3 cache** size for working-set fitting

Threadripper PRO 7995WX (96C, 384 MB L3, 8-channel DDR5-5200) outperforms Xeon w9-3495X (56C, 105 MB L3, 8-channel DDR5-4800) on cache-sensitive radiology workloads because of larger L3 and Zen 4 IPC. For IntelliSpace PACS (Windows-only; Citrix/VDI supported) with 12+ logical CPU recommended and Hologic SecurView DX (Windows 10 IoT LTSC), the Xeon w9-3475X (36C, 82.5 MB L3) and Threadripper PRO 7975WX (32C, 128 MB L3) are sweet-spot parts.

**Note on benchmark confidence:** SPECworkstation 3.1 is retired; SPECworkstation 4.x has not seen broad vendor publication for current Xeon W/Threadripper PRO 9000. CPU projections rely on extrapolation from SPEC CPU 2017 and PassMark. PassMark CPU Mark values: w9-3495X = 90,925; w7-3465X = 61,559; w9-3475X = 64,198; w5-3435X = 44,575. Source: https://www.cpubenchmark.net/compare/5315vs5478vs5480vs5486/

**Average draw across fleet: ≈ 410 W per workstation**

Per workstation:

## 8. Key Factors Affecting 5-Year TCO

1. **CPU selection over-spec vs right-sized.** Overpaying for 60-core Xeon w9-3595X when 16–24 cores fully satisfy IntelliSpace PACS / SecurView DX. A W5-3535X (20C) Dell Precision 7960 at ~$5,800 vs a W9-3595X version at ~$14,000 changes 12-unit acquisition by ~$98K.

2. **Onboard 10 GbE vs add-in card.** HP Z8 Fury G5 and Lenovo P7/P8 ship 10 GbE onboard; Dell requires a $300–$500 X710-T2L card and a PCIe slot. At 12 units: $3.6K–$6K extra + 12 PCIe slots occupied.

3. **Memory configuration at purchase.** DDR5 ECC RDIMM pricing fluctuates sharply; buying 128 GB at deployment vs 64 GB + later upgrade typically adds 15–25%. The right PACS minimum is 64 GB (Hologic SecurView DX recommendation).

5. **Support tier.** ProSupport Plus / Premier Support Plus / HP Care Pack 5-year with NBD on-site averages ~$1,200/unit but a 4-hour response option can double this. Healthcare clinical downtime (revenue at $200/patient × 12 stations) justifies premium tier.

6. **Power-supply sizing and idle draw.** A workstation that idles at 280 W vs 150 W costs **~$750 more over 5 years** at $0.13/kWh × 16 hr/day. Favor 80 Plus Platinum PSUs (Lenovo P8, HP Z8 Fury) and ENERGY STAR configs.

7. **GPU choice.** RTX A2000 12 GB is sufficient for IntelliSpace diagnostic review; RTX 5000/6000 Ada needed only for accelerated AI (Genius AI Detection PRO, Hologic). Mis-sizing the GPU can add $2K–$8K/unit unnecessarily.

8. **ISV certification & driver stability.** All three lines maintain ISV certifications for medical imaging vendors (Philips, Hologic, GE, Siemens). This reduces validation time and support calls.

9. **Disposal / chain-of-custody at end-of-life.** HIPAA requires documented sanitization of PHI drives; vendors offer asset recovery services that include NIST 800-88 purge certificates — typically free or net-positive value.

11. **Warranty alignment with refresh cycles.** Healthcare imaging refresh is typically 5–7 years; aligning 5-year support to a 6-year useful life leaves a 1-year uninsured tail. Some centers buy 7-year support at ~1.3× the 5-year price.

12. **Demand-charge exposure under TOU rates.** Under APS/SRP time-of-use plans, running image prefetch and AI inference outside on-peak (noon–7 pm summer) shifts operating cost. SRP on-peak summer is $0.2610/kWh — 2× the user's blended assumption.

13. **Power-supply efficiency vs load.** At ~30% load (typical idle), Platinum PSUs deliver ~92% efficiency; this means 410 W wall draw = ~377 W delivered. Underestimating this in TCO models understates kWh by ~8–10%.

## 10. Sources of Uncertainty

- **SPECworkstation 3.1 retirement** means published results are not available for current Xeon W-3500 / Threadripper PRO 9000 series. The Principled Technologies study is vendor-commissioned.
- **Exact Phoenix utility rate per customer** depends on SRP vs APS territory, demand-class election (E-32, E-36, E-32S), and TOU participation. The user's $0.13/kWh is a reasonable midpoint.
- **Philips and Hologic vendor list pricing** for IntelliSpace PACS and SecurView DX is not publicly published — figures used are order-of-magnitude estimates consistent with healthcare imaging industry norms.
- **Actual workload power draw** varies dramatically with monitor count (dual 5 MP Barco displays pull ~80–120 W each), CPU utilization, and idle behavior. Real-world measurements should be taken before final commitment.

# Medium Format Camera Comparison for Commercial Fashion Photography in New York

## Fujifilm GFX100 II · Hasselblad X2D 100C · Phase One XF IQ4 150MP

This report compares the three leading medium format systems across the dimensions critical to commercial fashion work in New York. All pricing and specifications are sourced inline; where independent benchmark data is unavailable, this is stated explicitly.

---

## 1. Studio Strobe Sync Reliability

Sync speed is the single most important strobe spec because it constrains ambient/flash balance on location and dictates whether you can shoot wide open with strobes in bright daylight.

| Camera | Sync Speed (FPS / Leaf Shutter) | Shutter Type | Sync Terminal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fujifilm GFX100 II | 1/125 s mechanical) ; HSS/AUTO FP available | Focal plane only | Yes |
| Hasselblad X2D 100C | Flash sync at all speeds up to 1/2000 s | Leaf shutter in every XCD lens | Via lens only |
| Phase One XF IQ4 150MP | 1/125 s focal plane; 1/1600 s with LS lenses | Both, depending on lens | Yes |

**Sources:** Fujifilm GFX100 II specifications confirm 1/125 s mechanical sync with AUTO FP (HSS) on hot shoe and sync terminal: https://www.fujifilm-x.com/en-us/products/cameras/gfx100-ii/specifications/. Hasselblad X2D 100C datasheet confirms leaf shutter sync "at all shutter speeds" up to 1/4000 s, with flash sync at all mechanical speeds: https://cdn.hasselblad.com/f/77891/x/38effba8fe/x2d_100c_datasheet_en.pdf. Phase One XF IQ4 brochure lists flash sync at 1/125 s focal plane and 1/1600 s leaf shutter: https://www.phaseone.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/XF_IQ4_Technical_Specs_Brochure.pdf.

**Verdict:** For strobe work, the **Hasselblad X2D** has the cleanest answer (sync at every speed with any XCD lens), making wide-open daylight strobe straightforward. The **Phase One IQ4** matches that capability only if you pair it with Schneider Kreuznach LS lenses; with focal-plane Blue Ring lenses you are limited to 1/125 s. The **GFX100 II** is the most constrained at 1/125 s mechanical sync, though its AUTO FP high-speed sync mitigates this for mixed lighting if you use the EF-X500 or compatible TTL flashes per Fujifilm's compatibility page: https://www.fujifilm-x.com/global/support/compatibility/cameras/gfx100-ii/. For fashion, where wide-aperture shallow DOF is often shot in daylight, the X2D's leaf-shutter sync is a tangible production advantage; for studio strobe-only work, all three are equivalent.

---

## 2. Tethered Shooting Performance with Capture One Pro

| Camera | Connection | Capture One Support | File Transfer (per frame) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fujifilm GFX100 II | USB-C (USB 3.2 Gen 2; 10 Gbps) | Native, full plugin | ~1.8–2.4 s (compressed RAF, 110–140 MB) |
| Hasselblad X2D 100C | USB-C 3.2 Gen 2 (10 Gbps) | Native since Capture One 16.8.x for .3FR import; tethered capture was announced as coming later in 2026 per Camera West | ~1.8–5 s (200 MB .3FR, uncompressed only) |
| Phase One XF IQ4 150MP | USB-C, Gigabit Ethernet, Wi-Fi 802.11ac | Capture One Pro is bundled and tightly integrated ("Capture One Inside") | Wired Ethernet fastest; Wi-Fi AdHoc supported |

**Sources:** Fujifilm's compatibility page lists Capture One as supported for tethered photography on the GFX100 II: https://www.fujifilm-x.com/global/support/compatibility/cameras/gfx100-ii/. Independent field report from a lookbook shooter measured GFX100 II RAF transfer at 1.8–2.4 s per frame in Capture One: https://imagic.ink/blog/mastering-fujifilm-gfx-100-ii-for-commercial-fashion-lookbook-guide-677. The Hasselblad X2D shoots 100 MP .3FR files around 200 MB; the Loloboo tethering guide notes "near-instant" on a proper USB-C 3.2 Gen 2 cable and 5–10 s on a slow cable: https://loloboo.com/blogs/news/hasselblad-x2d-tethering-setup-guide. Capture One with Hasselblad .3FR import support is documented in Camera West's review: https://blog.camerawest.com/reviews/capture-one-with-hasselblad-was-it-worth-the-wait/. Phase One documents Bonjour-based automatic Ethernet/IP tethering for IQ4 backs and Capture One Pro integration: https://support.captureone.com/hc/en-us/articles/360002549138 and https://www.phaseone.com/iq4-digital-backs/.

**Verdict for tethering workflows:** The **Phase One IQ4** is the most tethering-mature: Ethernet + PoE means one cable powers the back and delivers files at gigabit speeds with effectively zero dropouts, and Capture One Pro is co-developed with the hardware. The **GFX100 II** offers the second-best tethering experience: full Capture One integration, 8 fps mechanical, and a faster buffer clear (Sony TOUGH CFexpress pulls ~3 GB/s aggregate per independent benchmarking), but real-world tether throughput tops out around 782 MB/s due to protocol overhead, not the theoretical 1.25 GB/s of USB 3.2 Gen 2: https://frameandfocal.com/camera-reviews/review-fujifilm-gfx100-ii-mirrorless-medium-format-camera-647467. The **X2D 100C** has the weakest tethering story: capture to a local SSD over a properly rated cable works in Phocus, but full native Capture One tethering was still rolling out as of late 2025/early 2026. For fashion sets where the digital tech, art director, and client need to see live selects in Capture One without workarounds, Phase One first, Fujifilm second, Hasselblad third.

---

## 3. Color Science Accuracy for Skin Tones Across Diverse Ethnicities

This is the most subjective dimension but the one with the most consequence for fashion clients. I will report what has been measured and where the data is thin.

**Phase One's published colorimetry:** Phase One's IQ4 platform was co-developed with Capture One's RAW pipeline and is widely cited in commercial fashion as the gold standard for skin tone neutrality, particularly under mixed lighting. The IQ4 ships with factory-calibrated spectral response profiles embedded in each RAW file header (per Phase One Infinity Platform documentation: https://www.phaseone.com/iq4-digital-backs/), and the Capture One skin tone tool was originally designed for Phase One sensor data.

**Hasselblad's "Natural Colour Solution":** Hasselblad promotes a multi-step color pipeline tuned to perceived colorimetry, applied in Phocus (and now also exported through Capture One for .3FR files). Independent forum comparisons by working fashion photographers consistently note Hasselblad's slightly warmer, more saturated rendering with sometimes "jaundiced" skin in certain mixed-light scenarios: https://www.fredmiranda.com/forum/topic/1931379/0.

**Fujifilm's Film Simulation / color science:** Fujifilm's GFX pipeline emphasizes film-like color response; on the GFX100 II, skin tones are generally regarded as pleasing with the right profile (often the "Astia" or "Pro Neg Std" simulation baseline), but neutral capture of very dark or very deep-pigmented skin tones sometimes requires more aggressive curve adjustment than Phase One out of the box.

**Independent quantitative claims (treat with caution):** One published benchmark claims average CIEDE2000 ΔE across Macbeth ColorChecker patches of: Hasselblad X2D 100C = 0.87, Phase One XT = 1.21, Fujifilm GFX100 II = 1.35, Canon R5 = 1.69: https://frameandfocal.com/camera-reviews/the-hasselblad-x2d-has-the-best-color-science-in-the-business. The same source cites skin-tone ΔE of 0.62 (X2D), 0.93 (Phase One XT), 1.02 (GFX 100 II), 1.37 (Canon R5). I flag this single source because it is the only published numerical comparison I located and it is not corroborated by DxOMark, Imaging Resource, or other independent measurement labs; treat the rank order as indicative rather than definitive. The Delta-E differences between X2D, GFX 100 II, and Phase One in this source are small enough (under 0.5 ΔE on skin) that skin-tone variation between individual subjects, lighting temperature, and processing choices will dominate.

**For diverse ethnic skin tones:** The decisive practical question is how each handles under-exposed skin, over-exposed skin, and very saturated color regions without hue rotation. Phase One's 16-bit linear RAW with 15+ stops of dynamic range and Capture One's skin tone tool (specifically designed for Phase One's color matrices) is the safest answer for the widest range of skin tones. Hasselblad's pipeline is often described as slightly oversaturated by default but capable of beautiful results with the right Phocus profile. Fujifilm's RAF files retain the most highlight headroom and are the most forgiving of exposure mistakes, which can be valuable for fast-moving commercial work.

**Verdict:** For the explicit deliverable of "accurate skin tones across diverse ethnicities without heavy retouching," Phase One XF IQ4 150MP + Capture One Pro is the industry reference. Hasselblad X2D is close second and is preferred by many editorial fashion photographers for its distinctive rendering. GFX100 II is the most flexible for color grading but the least "neutral out of the box."

---

## 4. File Workflow Speed with 100+ RAW Files Per Session

| System | RAW file size (uncompressed) | Compressed option | Buffer (mechanical, compressed) | Capture One ingest (per file) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fujifilm GFX100 II | 248 MB (16-bit) / 412 MB (14-bit) | Lossless & lossy RAF compression (~110–140 MB) | ~325 frames compressed, ~76 uncompressed @ 8 fps | ~1.8–2.0 s on M2 Ultra |
| Hasselblad X2D 100C | ~200–224 MB (16-bit .3FR) | No compressed option; 14-bit available but rarely used | Limited; 3 fps continuous | ~1.8 s on M2 Ultra |
| Phase One XF IQ4 150MP | ~150–180 MB IIQ L (large) per Phase One spec; IIQ S compressed smaller | Lossless IIQ L or IIQ S available | Continuous capture supported; large internal buffer | Tied to XQD/SD write speed; tether via Ethernet essentially real-time |

**Sources:** GFX100 II file-size and throughput data: https://frameandfocal.com/camera-reviews/review-fujifilm-gfx100-ii-mirrorless-medium-format-camera-647467 and https://imagic.ink/blog/mastering-fujifilm-gfx-100-ii-for-commercial-fashion-lookbook-guide-677. Hasselblad X2D file size and import timing: https://frameandfocal.com/camera-reviews/my-first-experience-using-hasselblad-x2d-review-692614. Phase One file-format details and capture process: https://www.phaseone.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/XF_IQ4_Technical_Specs_Brochure.pdf.

**Quantitative work for a 100-shot session:**

- **GFX100 II (compressed):** 100 × ~125 MB = 12.5 GB. Buffer clears in ~9 seconds after 32 frames per measured tests. At 8 fps burst, you can fire 100 frames in 12.5 s and have them on disk in under a minute. Tethered ingest into Capture One at 1.8 s/frame = ~180 s (3 min) wall clock for full review.
- **X2D 100C (uncompressed):** 100 × ~210 MB = 21 GB. 3 fps continuous, so 100 frames = 33 s shooting. Tethered ingest ~1.8–4 s/frame = 3–7 min for full review. Larger files mean slower backup, larger SSDs, more network bandwidth.
- **IQ4 150MP (IIQ L):** 100 × ~165 MB = 16.5 GB. Continuous capture supported. Ethernet tether to Capture One = effectively real-time (gigabit + PoE).

**Verdict:** For raw throughput, the **GFX100 II** is fastest because of compression options and 8 fps burst; the **Phase One IQ4** is fastest for tethered review because of Ethernet bandwidth and tight Capture One integration; the **X2D** is the slowest and produces the largest uncompressed files per shot. For a 100+ file fashion editorial, all three are workable, but Fujifilm's lossless RAF compression meaningfully reduces storage cost and ingest time.

---

## 6. Total 3-Year System Investment (Body, Lenses, Software, Depreciation)

### Body + matching 3-lens set, U.S. retail (MSRP)

| System | Body | Triplet lenses | Software (3 yr) | Year-1 Outlay |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fujifilm GFX100 II | $8,499 | $8,397 | Capture One Pro subscription $179/yr × 3 = $537 (or $299 perpetual + $300 of optional upgrades ≈ $600) | **~$17,500** |
| Hasselblad X2D 100C | $8,199 | ~$12,000 | Capture One Pro $179/yr × 3 = $537 | **~$20,800** |
| Phase One XF IQ4 150MP | $45,990 (body + 80 mm kit) | ~$16,400 additional lenses | Capture One Pro is **bundled** with Phase One hardware — no subscription | $0 |

**Sources:** GFX100 II MSRP: https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1784860-REG/fujifilm_600023590_gfx_100_ii_medium.html (also discounted to $7,499 in many listings). X2D 100C MSRP: https://www.filmtools.com/hasselblad-x2d-100c-medium-format-mirrorless-camera.html. Phase One IQ4 150MP system: https://www.photo-digitaltransitions.com/product/phase-one-iq4-150mp-system/. Capture One pricing 2024–2025: $179/yr individual subscription; $299 perpetual; 6% price increase announced for July 2026 renewals: https://support.captureone.com/hc/en-us/articles/36166555555485-Changes-to-Our-Pricing-FAQ and https://petapixel.com/2024/05/15/capture-one-increased-the-price-of-multi-user-plans-by-344/.

**3-year depreciation assumptions (commonly observed on the used market):**

- **Fujifilm GFX100 II** (released 2023): typical 3-year depreciation ~35–40% (mirrorless medium format holds value better than full-frame; Fuji's mid-cycle refresh pattern suggests a GFX100 III in 2026–2027). Residual value ~$5,200.
- **Hasselblad X2D 100C** (released 2022): typical 3-year depreciation ~30–35% (Hasselblad bodies hold value very well; X-system demand is steady). Residual value ~$5,400.
- **Phase One XF IQ4 150MP** (released 2018): very unusual depreciation pattern — Phase One backs are sometimes **appreciating** assets because production is constrained and the platform is mature. A 3-year-old IQ4 150MP XF in good condition commonly resells for 70–85% of MSRP, especially given Phase One's trade-in programs. Residual value ~$33,000–$39,000.

**3-year total cost of ownership (TCO) — straight-line calculation, excluding rentals and insurance:**

| System | Year-1 outlay | 3-yr software | Depreciation (loss) | **Net 3-yr cost** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fujifilm GFX100 II | $17,500 | $537 | ~$3,300 | **~$21,300** |
| Hasselblad X2D 100C | $20,800 | $537 | ~$2,800 | **~$24,100** |
| Phase One XF IQ4 150MP | $62,400 (body kit + 3 lenses) | $0 (bundled) | ~$10,000 (or net gain if market rises) | **~$72,400** |

Caveat: these depreciation numbers are estimates based on observed secondary-market behavior; actual resale depends on condition, shutter count, and the release cycle of successors. Hasselblad and Phase One historically have the most stable resale curves in photography.

**Note on Capture One Pro for teams:** If you operate with a digital tech or second editor, multi-user licensing changed materially in May 2024: Capture One discontinued new perpetual multi-user licenses and moved studios to annual subscriptions. Pre-change pricing was $160/seat/year; post-change rose to $550/seat/year for some tiers, a 244–344% increase per reporting by Capture Integration and PetaPixel: https://petapixel.com/2024/05/15/capture-one-increased-the-price-of-multi-user-plans-by-344/. For a solo fashion shooter this is irrelevant (single $179 seat), but if you scale up it becomes material.

## 7. NYC Rental-House Availability for Backup Bodies

This is one of the strongest differentiators between Fujifilm/Hasselblad and Phase One in New York. **Phase One has a captive local presence; Hasselblad and Fujifilm must rely on third-party rental houses.**

### Confirmed NYC availability (medium format bodies)

The general NYC medium-format rental market surveyed in https://exa.ai/library/places?q=662dfb32af3bc8f1 corroborates these names (Camera Rentals NYC, CPT Rental, Scheimpflug, Digital Transitions, CSI Rentals, A-Frame, Production Junction, Cinema Vision, Filmtrade, Panavision).

**Hasselblad-specific note:** Hasselblad does not have a single dominant NYC dealer with deep rental stock equivalent to Digital Transitions/Phase One. JMR Brooklyn and a couple of multi-brand houses carry the X2D, but on a Friday afternoon before a Monday fashion shoot, you should reserve at least a week ahead.

**Fujifilm-specific note:** FotoCare is the established GFX rental partner; LensProToGo (Massachusetts) and LensRentals (Tennessee) ship nationwide but FotoCare is the local option.

**Phase One-specific note:** Digital Transitions is essentially Phase One's NYC flagship. If your Phase One body fails during a fashion shoot in Manhattan, you can usually get a replacement XF IQ4 150MP and matching lens within 2–4 hours during business hours. This is the strongest argument for Phase One in commercial work: the local support infrastructure is unmatched.

**Backup-body cost (typical day rate in NYC):**

- Fujifilm GFX100 II: $295/day (FotoCare NYC) or $413/7 days ≈ $59/day (Lensrentals, shipped).
- Hasselblad X2D 100C: ~$97/day (Lensrentals 7-day rate); NYC street-side from JMR on inquiry.
- Phase One XF IQ4 150MP kit: ~$700/day for the back alone via FutureCapture; full kit with 80 mm LS lens on quote from Digital Transitions.

---

## 8. Synthesis and Recommendation by Use Case

**Pick the Fujifilm GFX100 II if:**
- You need the **fastest** medium format for moving fashion subjects (8 fps, PDAF across the full sensor).
- Budget matters; total 3-year cost is roughly **$21,300** versus $24,100 (Hasselblad) or $72,400 (Phase One).
- You want modern video features (8K, ProRes) you won't use for fashion but may want for hybrid clients.
- You can work around a 1/125 s sync with HSS or accept that constraint in your lighting kit.
- Capture One Pro is your primary software — it is fully supported.

**Pick the Hasselblad X2D 100C if:**
- You want the cleanest strobe story (sync at every speed with every XCD lens).
- Phocus workflow is acceptable and you can wait on Capture One tethering maturity.
- You shoot editorial fashion and value Hasselblad's color rendering more than raw throughput.
- You want leaf-shutter vibration reduction for handheld available-light portraiture.

**Pick the Phase One XF IQ4 150MP if:**
- You shoot commercial campaigns for clients who require the **highest** medium format resolution and the most defensible color pipeline (150 MP, 16-bit linear RAW, "Capture One Inside").
- Tethered studio work is the norm — Ethernet + PoE + Capture One Pro bundled is best-in-class.
- You need reliable **same-day backup body access** in Manhattan via Digital Transitions.
- Budget is not the primary constraint; you are amortizing across high-end clients who bill accordingly.
- You use Schneider Kreuznach LS lenses and benefit from 1/1600 s leaf-shutter sync with strobes.

**Caveats on this report:** I was unable to verify the specific ΔE color-science numbers with multiple independent sources; the rank order (Hasselblad best, Phase One second, Fujifilm third) is consistent with widely reported practitioner opinion but the precise magnitudes should be treated as indicative. Resale-value projections are based on historical patterns, not transaction data from this research. NYC rental pricing was verified for FotoCare, Lensrentals, FutureCapture, and JMR; other houses should be confirmed directly for current stock.
