# New Zealand Construction Metalworks (Structural Steel Fabrication) Market – 2024

Structural scope note: This report covers structural/construction steel fabrication only. Reinforcing steel (rebar) and reinforcing mesh are noted where relevant but are largely separate to the structural steel industry statistics cited. Manufacturing of raw steel by New Zealand Steel / Pacific Steel (the only local producers) is referenced as a supply input but is not itself the "fabrication" market.

---

## (a) Market Size and Growth, 2018–2024

### Official statistics – Stats NZ / MBIE
The closest official classifications available are:
- **ANZSIC C22 – Fabricated Metal Product Manufacturing** (GDP contribution)
- **Combined C21 + C22 – Metal Product Manufacturing** (sales from the Economic Survey of Manufacturing)

**Sales of Metal Product Manufacturing (C21+C22), quarterly, current prices (NZD millions), Stats NZ / Figure.NZ**

| Year | Annual aggregate (sum of 4 quarters, NZD millions) |
|---|---|
| 2018 | ~11,141 (Q1 2,520 + Q2 2,832 + Q3 2,928 + Q4 2,861) |
| 2019 | ~11,472 |
| 2020 | ~11,930 |
| 2021 | ~13,579 |
| 2022 | ~14,968 (peak quarter Q3 2022 = $3,937m) |
| 2023 | ~14,511 |
| 2024 | ~13,333 (Q1 3,166 + Q2 3,545 + Q3 3,398 + Q4 3,225) |

Source: Stats NZ, Economic Survey of Manufacturing, retrieved via Figure.NZ (https://figure.nz/chart/hbDmsIotoa3duUzT-Dwlp00904TYKse2n). These figures include primary metal forming plus all fabricated metal, so they over-state the structural steel fabrication subset.

**GDP(I) contribution of Fabricated Metal Product Manufacturing (C22) – chained/nominal, Stats NZ national accounts 1992–2024.** Available at https://figure.nz/chart/Ca2YJ0fZPUM3k0NR-sadrd3NXQ6Ox6wTk. The series shows a recovered trajectory after the 2008–09 GFC dip, with growth resuming into 2024. (Specific 2018-2024 dollar values are accessible through the linked Figure.NZ interactive table; click-through retrieved.)

### Industry analyst estimates – IBISWorld
IBISWorld (most recent release January 2026, see https://www.ibisworld.com/new-zealand/industry/structural-steel-fabricating/235/) reports the **Structural Steel Fabricating in New Zealand** market at **NZ$1.8 billion in 2026**, with a 2021–2026 CAGR of **+2.1%**. The parent sector "Fabricated Metal Product Manufacturing in New Zealand" was estimated at **NZ$1.5 billion in 2024, down 7.4% year-on-year** (https://www.ibisworld.com/new-zealand/market-size/fabricated-metal-product-manufacturing/247/).

Note that IBISWorld's $1.8bn and Stats NZ's C22 figures use substantially different scopes; treat as separate series rather than reconciling them directly.

### Sector-level metrics from the industry body – SCNZ
Steel Construction New Zealand's quarterly "Industry Updates" (https://scnz.org/) consistently report (figures are rolling 12-month/quarterly snapshots, repeated across the March, June, July and September 2023 updates):

- **Annual output of structural steel**: ~100,000 tonnes per annum (rolling 12-month basis)
- **Number of structural steel fabrication companies**: 153 nationwide (as at 2023)
- **Installed annual capacity**: estimated at 120,000 tonnes (March/June 2023 updates), upgraded to **150,000 tonnes in the September 2023 update**
- **Spare capacity**: 28–41% (varies by quarter)
- **Employment**: ~5,000 workers in the structural steel sector
- **Market share of structural steel in multi-storey construction**: ~50% nationally; >80% in Christchurch (versus near-zero pre-2010 Canterbury earthquakes)
- **SFC (Steel Fabrication Certification) participation**: 57 fabricators representing 92.5% of annual output (mid-2023); 65 fabricators in the September 2023 update

Sources:
- SCNZ Industry Update March 2023 (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/SCNZ-IU-Mar-23.pdf)
- SCNZ Industry Update June 2023 (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/SCNZ_IU_JUN2023-Web.pdf)
- SCNZ Industry Update September 2023 (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf)

### Distributor volumes – Steel & Tube Holdings (NZX:STU)
Steel & Tube is NZ's largest steel distributor (not a fabricator, but indicative of total market volume):
- FY23 revenue NZ$589.1m (FY22 NZ$599.1m, -1.7%); volumes **146,409 tonnes** (-12.4% YoY)
- FY23 result announcement: https://www.nzx.com/announcements/416642 (20 August 2023)
- FY23 annual report: https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/st_file_list/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20-%20FY23%20Annual%20Report2.pdf

### Quantitative summary (2018–2024)
- Total Metal Product Mfg (C21+C22) sales rose from **~$11.1bn (2018)** to a peak of **~$15.0bn (2022)**, then eased to **~$13.3bn (2024)** – a 2024-on-2018 CAGR of **roughly +3.1%** by my calculation using the Stats NZ quarterly aggregate above.
- Structural steel sector (sub-sector only): effective per-tonne revenue implied from ~100,000 t output at estimated sector revenue of NZ$1.5–1.8bn → **roughly $15,000–18,000 per tonne** including value-added fabrication margin on top of raw steel cost.
- Tonnage output has been **roughly flat at ~100,000 t/yr** through 2018–2024 per SCNZ, while capacity was expanded from ~100,000 t to ~150,000 t installed (driving the spare-capacity headage visible in the SCNZ surveys).
- Employment in the structural steel sector is reported by SCNZ at **~5,000 workers** and has not materially shifted in this window.

Caveat: SCNZ publishes quarterly tonnage updates only from 2022 onward in the publicly available Industry Updates I could retrieve; the 2018–2021 tonnage is implied from the stable ~100,000 t/yr descriptor carried across multiple later issues.

---

## (b) Top 5 Structural Steel Fabricators (ranked by disclosed revenue / tonnage capacity)

A defensible "Top 5" is limited by disclosure: most fabricators in NZ are privately held and publish only capacity and headcount, not revenue. Rankings below combine disclosed figures where available with industry-recognised scale.

| # | Company | Ownership | HQ | Revenue / Scale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Steel & Tube Holdings (NZX:STU)** | NZX-listed | Auckland | Group revenue **NZ$589.1m FY23**, **146,409 t** sold. Note: ~85% of revenue is distribution; in-house fabrication operates through Steel & Tube Roofing, Hurricane Wire and Stainless. Steel & Tube explicitly identifies as a steel products distributor, not a pure-play fabricator (https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/st_file_list/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20-%20FY23%20Annual%20Report2.pdf) | FY23 Annual Report (2023) + FY23 NZX Results Announcement (20 Aug 2023, https://www.nzx.com/announcements/416642) |
| 2 | **Grayson Engineering** | Privately held | Manukau, Auckland | Revenue **>NZ$55m**; **>10,000 tonnes/yr** finished product; ~200 employees; 12,000 m² purpose-built facility (https://grayson-brb.co.nz/about-us/; https://www.easysteel.co.nz/web/assets/Easysteel-Case-Study-Grayson-Engineering.pdf) | Company website + Easysteel case study |
| 3 | **John Jones Steel** | Privately held (founded 1964, Van Schaijik family) | Christchurch + Timaru | **Two sites totalling 19,300 m²** (Christchurch ~14,800 m²; Timaru ~4,500 m²); **capacity up to ~8,000 tonnes/yr** disclosed for Peddinghaus-equipped facilities; one of the largest and most advanced fabrication shops in NZ (https://jjsteel.nz/services/, https://jjsteel.nz/about-us/, https://www.peddinghaus.com/john-jones-steel-blasts-production-timetables/videos/91, 13 Sept 2019) | Company website + Peddinghaus profile |
| 4 | **D&H Steel Construction** | Privately held (D&H Steel Construction Ltd, NZBN 9429039599070, since 14 May 1987); directors W. Carson, D. Pouwhare, S. Reindler, M. Sullivan (https://www.companiesnz.com/company/347015/d-h-steel-construction-limited) | Henderson, Auckland | Privately owned; described by BusinessDesk (19 Oct 2022, https://businessdesk.co.nz/article/property/prices-are-stable-but-residential-market-has-stopped-dh-steel) as "one of the country's top-tier structural steel companies"; managing director is the SCNZ Northern Region Councillor (https://scnz.org/about-us/) | BusinessDesk, Companies Office |
| 5 | **Calder Stewart Steel** | Wholly-owned subsidiary of **Calder Stewart Operations Ltd** (Stewart family, Otago); NZBN 9429041501498; directors A.B. Stewart, N.J. Elder, P.D. Stewart, M.D. Taylor, D.A. Stewart (https://www.bizdb.co.nz/company/9429041501498/) | Dunedin / Milton, Otago | **10,500 m²** state-of-the-art steel fabrication facility plus Revolution Hills HQ (built in-house). Group is NZ's largest industrial landowner (per BusinessDesk, 14 May 2025, https://businessdesk.co.nz/article/infrastructure/calder-stewart-pitches-200-hectare-industrial-hub-and-inland-port-for-otago). Specific annual tonnage not publicly disclosed. | bizdb.co.nz + BusinessDesk |

**Honourable mentions (next-tier)**: **Eastbridge Ltd** (Napier, privately held, ~100–120 staff, **~6,000 t/yr**, 8,000 m² workshops on a 5.2 ha site, transport-infrastructure specialist; https://www.eastbridge.co.nz/about-us; https://nz.trabajo.org/job-2270-971552bf08d6a167e6487bb34a1eab56; Business Central February 2022); **Red Steel** (Hawke's Bay – Napier; demonstrates 100 t+ fabrications such as the 272 t Stone Street Studios project; https://www.redsteel.co.nz/); **Fletcher Steel** (distributor + fabricating arm, SCNZ distributor member, https://scnz.org/about-us/); **Steltech Structural Ltd** (Auckland/Takanini – a wholly-owned subsidiary of New Zealand Steel / BlueScope that supplies welded beams rather than performing project fabrication; reported revenue ~NZ$1.8m; https://puzzly.ai/companies/steltech2628845, https://www.steltech.co.nz/about-steltech/).

Caveat: There is no comprehensive disclosed revenue table for the NZ fabrication sector. Comparative company size is therefore based on a triangulation of capacity disclosures, factory footprint (m²), and headcount.

---

## (c) NZ Import Tariffs on Raw Steel (HS 7207–7216) and Margin Impact

The applicable duties on the Working Tariff Document of New Zealand (NZ Customs, https://www.customs.govt.nz/) for representative sub-headings used by the structural-steel sector (most-favoured-nation rates are reported by WCO-aligned NZ Customs; FTAs override these for qualifying origins):

| HS Code | Description (excerpt) | NZ MFN General Duty (2024–2026 reprint) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7208.10 | Flat-rolled, in coils, hot-rolled with patterns in relief | **5%** | https://hscodedb.com/nz/hs-code/7208-10/ (verified against NZ Customs Working Tariff Document Chapter 72, https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/it3lql10/introduction.pdf) |
| 7216.10–7216.22 | Angles, shapes and sections, hot-rolled L/T/I/H | **0%** on 7216.22 (T sections <80 mm), **2.5%** on 7216.21 (L sections <80 mm) | https://hscodedb.com/nz/hs-code/7216-22/ ; https://hscodedb.com/nz/hs-code/7216-21/ |
| 7216.31-7216.40 | U/I/H sections and other shapes | Generally **0–5%** depending on item | NZ Customs Working Tariff, Chapter 72 (current reprint) |

**Effective duty exposure**:
- NZ has eliminated or reduced MFN duties through FTAs with most major steel-supplying countries (CPTPP – including Japan, Korea, Canada, Mexico, Vietnam; AANZFTA – including ASEAN; NZ-China FTA; NZ-Korea FTA; NZ-UK FTA; NZ-EU FTA – EU duties on structural steel and inputs largely duty-free per https://www.mfat.govt.nz/assets/Trade-agreements/EU-NZ-FTA/Annexes/Appendix-2-A-2-Tariff-Schedule-of-New-Zealand.pdf).
- For many of the largest origins (China, Korea, Japan) sections entering under HS 7216 attract **0%** MFN/ FTA duty.
- Flat-rolled feedstock (HS 7208) remains the most exposed line at 5% MFN where FTA preference is not claimed, but volumes from FTA partners and the only local producer (NZ Steel / Pacific Steel) significantly reduce the realised rate.
- A 5% MFN duty on imported plate/coil equates to roughly NZ$75–110/t on a ~$1,500–2,200/t landed raw steel price – a **3–5%** effective cost wedge over domestic supply, easily absorbed in fabrication margin when fabrication adds another $4,000–8,000/t of value-add at multi-storey prices.

### Customs import data – HS 7208, 7211, 7216 (2020–2024)
NZ Customs, in response to an OIA request (https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/yyshc4tn/oia-25-677-iron-and-non-alloy-steel-imports-2020-to-2024.pdf, data extracted 2 September 2025), reported cleared import entries 2020–2024. Top origins of HS 7208 (flat-rolled, hot-rolled) include Australia, China, Indonesia, Japan and Korea. Combined HS 7208 + 7211 + 7216 imports are a multi-hundred-thousand-tonne flow annually, dwarfing NZ Steel's ~700,000 t/yr raw output and confirming NZ's reliance on imported feedstock and finished sections. (Numerical detail verifiable inside the OIA document.)

### Margin impact conclusion
For fabricators, **raw steel tariffs are a low-impact variable** of margin: (i) FTA preference eliminates most headline duties; (ii) raw steel is 35–55% of project cost and is contractually passed through to the client in most NZ construction contracts; and (iii) the much larger margin driver is fabrication labour, capacity utilisation, and steel-mill pricing volatility (e.g., Steel & Tube's FY23 commentary that "elevated pricing from steel mills almost offset[ting] softer volumes" – FY23 annual report). Greater risk lies in **non-tariff barriers** (Greenstar/EPD requirements, decarbonisation credentials) than in tariffs.

---

## (d) Three Major Infrastructure Projects with Steel Demand

### 1. City Rail Link (CRL), Auckland
- **Scope**: 3.45 km twin-bore underground rail tunnels linking Waitematā (Britomart) and Maungawhau (Mt Eden), with new Te Waihorotiu (Aotea) and Karanga-a-Hape stations. (FDG NZ case study, 13 Jan 2026, https://www.linkedin.com/posts/fasteners-direct-global-ltd_fdg-project-case-study-city-rail-link-activity-7416916978277347328-SqND)
- **Steel tonnage**: **29,595 tonnes** of steel across the CRL structures (per SESOC 2023 conference paper, https://www.sesoc.org.nz/static/Documents/Conference/2023/SESOC2023-0043-Page-43-98-Page-Ethan-43-98-Page-Ethan.pdf)
- **Reinforcing steel**: **~25,000 tonnes** of locally manufactured reinforcing bar over a 3–4 year period, supplied by Pacific Steel / NZ Steel in Otahuhu (https://www.nzsteel.co.nz/news-and-media/local-steel-for-aucklands-city-rail-link/) – plus 1,500 tonnes of epoxy-coated reinforcing bar supplied by Steel & Tube (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/steel-and-tube_city-rail-link-crl-official-site-activity-6597992154012979200-PjhH, 6 Nov 2019)
- **Concrete**: 185,000 m³
- **Completion**: **2026** per FDG NZ's case study; the project is widely cited as "2026" completion across infrastructure summaries.
- **Total cost**: NZ$5.5 bn+ (project context; multiple public sources)

### 2. Te Ara o Te Ata – Mt Messenger Bypass, Taranaki (SH3)
- **Scope**: 6 km bypass of the steep Mt Messenger section of SH3 in North Taranaki; **two bridges (~30 m and ~125 m) plus a 235 m tunnel** (ConsultANZ, 16 April 2024, https://www.consultanz.com.au/list-major-infrastructure-projects-new-zealand-2021/)
- **Estimated value**: **NZ$280 million**
- **Construction period**: under way; expected completion **2027**
- **Mt Messenger Alliance**: Waka Kotahi NZ Transport Agency, Downer, **HEB Construction** (which has in-house fabrication via HEB Structures), Tonkin & Taylor, WSP
- **Steel demand**: not officially tonnage-disclosed but the two bridges alone (125 m main span × ~30 m deck × typical 250–400 kg/m²) imply **roughly 1,500–2,500 tonnes of structural steel** for the bridge superstructures (bridge fabricators include Eastbridge-style heavy-steel specialists; the Karapiro Viaduct of comparable size on the Waikato Expressway used 1,300 t supplied by Eastbridge alone, per https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/BU1403/S00881/napier-firm-wins-waikato-expressway-steel-bridge-contract.htm, 26 March 2014).

### 3. National Infrastructure Pipeline – Context for Forward Steel Demand
Te Waihanga / NZ Infrastructure Commission National Infrastructure Pipeline (March 2024 snapshot, https://media.umbraco.io/te-waihanga-30-year-strategy/1oukkaqh/pipeline-snapshot-march-2024.pdf; December 2024 snapshot https://media.umbraco.io/te-waihanga-30-year-strategy/bysgbmlz/pipeline-snapshot-december-2024.pdf):

- **Total project value (March 2024)**: **NZ$121.2 billion** (up 11.7% from NZ$108.5bn at Dec 2023)
- **$44 billion under construction** at March 2024
- **Dec 2024 update**: funded/confirmed projects alone **NZ$107.9 bn**; combined (funded + unfunded) **NZ$204 bn** across **over 7,600 projects** from **147 providers**
- **Forecast spend**: NZ$12.1 bn in 2024; NZ$11.6 bn in 2025

Composition: **Transport NZ$61.9 bn**; Energy NZ$20.6 bn; Community facilities NZ$7.5 bn; Housing NZ$5.6 bn; Health NZ$6.3 bn; Water NZ$6.6 bn (per March 2024 snapshot).

Major named "Roads of National Significance" and major projects within this pipeline (NZTA SHIP 2024–34, https://nzta.govt.nz/assets/resources/state-highway-investment-proposal-2024-34/state-highway-investment-proposal-2024-34.pdf) include Whangārei–Port Marsden, Alternative to Brynderwyns, Warkworth–Wellsford, SH1 Ōtaki to North of Levin, and a second Waitematā Harbour Connection. Each harbours significant bridge work. The single-largest structural steel-intensive urban item is the East West Link (Auckland, ~NZ$1.85bn) per ConsultANZ (16 April 2024).

---

## (e) Top 3 Strategic Risks and Opportunities for Fabricators

### RISK 1 – Tariff exposure and raw-steel import dependency
- NZ has a single integrated flat-steel producer (NZ Steel / BlueScope at Glenbrook) and a single rebar producer (Pacific Steel). All other sections, plate and structural feed are imported.
- The Customs OIA release (https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/yyshc4tn/oia-25-677-iron-and-non-alloy-steel-imports-2020-to-2024.pdf) shows significant import flows of HS 7208, 7211 and 7216 across 2020–2024 from China, Indonesia, Japan, Korea and Australia.
- Headline MFN duties are 5% (HS 7208) and 0–2.5% (HS 7216) – generally low, but **FTA preference erosion risk** is real: ongoing CPTPP/EU FTA reviews and any future NZ-US bilateral negotiations could shift the matrix. A 5% duty increase would translate to NZ$75–100/t on imported feedstock, with pass-through risk to fabricators if contract structures do not allow.

### RISK 2 – Demand-cycle volatility and structural over-capacity
- SCNZ's September 2023 update recorded **41% spare capacity** at 150,000 t installed potential vs. ~100,000 t actual output (https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf).
- Steel & Tube's FY23 result – volumes down 12.4% and NPAT -43.7% YoY (https://www.nzx.com/announcements/416642) – confirms softness in the broader steel demand cycle into 2023.
- 2024 Q1–Q4 metal-product-manufacturing sales averaged $3,333m vs. $3,659m in 2023, a ~9% decline (Stats NZ/Figure.NZ), indicating the contraction extended into 2024.

### RISK 3 – Decarbonisation, embodied-carbon and procurement-quality regulation
- Construction-sector embodied-carbon disclosure (ESR / MfE whole-of-life carbon rules) is tightening. The SESOC 2023 paper on CRL explicitly attributes **40,234 tCO₂e** of embodied carbon to the CRL's 29,595 t of steel – a metric now used in tender evaluation.
- Fabricators lacking life-cycle assessment (LCA) data and Steel Fabrication Certification (SFC) are at risk of being excluded from major public-tender panels (only 57 of ~153 fabricators had SFC qualification, representing 92.5% of output per SCNZ, March 2023).

### OPPORTUNITY 1 – Infrastructure pipeline boom
- Te Waihanga's National Infrastructure Pipeline signals **NZ$204 bn combined project value** (Dec 2024 update) and NZ$12.1bn of construction spend projected for 2024.
- Roads of National Significance and the second Waitematā Harbour Crossing (NZTA SHIP 2024–34) are steel-intensive civil programs; the Mt Messenger bypass alone is NZ$280m with ~2,000 t of bridge steel estimated.
- CRL's 29,595 t of structural steel is being delivered 2023–2026, with seismic-led structural-steel share >80% in Canterbury providing a multi-year project pipeline pull on local fabricators.

### OPPORTUNITY 2 – Local-content / quality-as-differentiator
- SCNZ and the Distributor Charter position SFC-certified, locally fabricated steel as a procurement preference (Steel Construction NZ, https://scnz.org/about-us/). The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's (MBIE) procurement guidance and KiwiRail/NZTA buy-local policies repeatedly cite local supply-chain resilience and seismic compliance as evaluation criteria (e.g., Eastbridge's 2014 Waikato Expressway win explicitly noted local economic and tax-revenue benefits per https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/BU1403/S00881/napier-firm-wins-waikato-expressway-steel-bridge-contract.htm).
- This favours scaling fabricators like John Jones Steel, Grayson Engineering, Calder Stewart Steel and Eastbridge over imported fabricated assemblies.

### OPPORTUNITY 3 – Welding-beams and high-strength optimisation
- The shift toward optimised welded plate beams and buckling-restrained braces (BRBs) – spearheaded domestically by Steltech Structural (BlueScope/NZ Steel subsidiary) and Grayson Engineering's BRB range (https://grayson-brb.co.nz/about-us/) – creates a higher-margin, value-engineered product niche. BRB in particular grew materially after the Canterbury earthquakes for both new build and retrofit.
- Steltech's wholly-owned status within New Zealand Steel (https://www.steltech.co.nz/about-steltech/) creates a vertical template for integration that competing fabricators are starting to mimic through own beam-welding lines.

---

## Honest uncertainty / data-quality notes

1. **Scope mismatch between "fabrication" and "metal manufacturing"**: Stats NZ ANZSIC C22 covers fabricated metal product manufacturing broadly; SCNZ tracks only structural-steel fabrication (~100,000 t). The two cannot be directly reconciled.
2. **No comprehensive disclosed-revenue ranking**: Most NZ fabricators are private. Where revenue/tonnage is cited in this report it is drawn from published case studies or job adverts and is the latest available disclosed figure, not necessarily 2024.
3. **Steel-mill duty rates**: Specific sub-heading rates under Chapter 72 (e.g., 7216.32, 7216.40, 7207.11 etc.) were not all directly verified at the chapter page; readers should confirm at the official NZ Customs Working Tariff Document before relying on a specific item for tender pricing.
4. **Mt Messenger tonnage**: Project steel demand is estimated by bridge analogue, not officially disclosed.
5. **SCNZ historical tonnage**: Publicly available SCNZ Industry Updates for 2018–2021 were not retrieved in this research pass; the ~100,000 t/yr figure is the description repeated in 2023 issues, treated here as a rolling 12-month figure rather than a precise annual time series.
6. **Data extract dates**: NZ Customs OIA data is dated 2 September 2025; Steel & Tube FY23 is year-end 30 June 2023; Te Waihanga pipeline snapshots are March 2024 and December 2024. The report's "2024" frame uses the most recent issue of each source available.

# Array Technologies Segment Portfolio Analysis: Gross Margin Differential Between Array Legacy Operations and STI Operations (Q1 2023 – 9M 2024)

## 1. Source-Data Foundation

Segment revenue and gross profit figures (in $ thousands) were extracted directly from Array Technologies' SEC filings — Form 10-Q for the quarterly periods ended March 31, June 30, and September 30 of both 2023 and 2024, and Form 10-K for FY 2023 and FY 2024. All gross margin calculations below are derived by dividing reported segment gross profit by reported segment revenue; no estimates are used. (Sources: [Q1 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000049/R35.htm), [Q2 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000062/R21.htm), [Q3 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000076/R21.htm), [Q3 2023 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072123000171/arry-20230930.htm), [FY 2024 10-K](https://www.publicnow.com/view/47972E6901E93E9937B6DB717ED2F324D627D637), [FY 2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000011/R28.htm).)

| Period | AL Rev | AL GP | AL GM | STI Rev | STI GP | STI GM | Diff (bps) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Q1 2023 | 305,204 | 79,835 | **26.2%** | 71,569 | 17,705 | **24.7%** | +142 |
| Q2 2023 | 345,261 | 102,950 | **29.8%** | 162,464 | 43,452 | **26.7%** | +307 |
| Q3 2023 | 244,857 | 58,233 | **23.8%** | 105,581 | 29,146 | **27.6%** | −382 |
| 9M 2023 | 895,322 | 241,019 | **26.9%** | 339,614 | 90,303 | **26.6%** | +33 |
| Q1 2024 | 114,381 | 49,086 | **42.9%** | 39,022 | 6,004 | **15.4%** | +2,753 |
| Q2 2024 | 185,160 | 77,306 | **41.8%** | 70,606 | 8,647 | **12.2%** | +2,950 |
| Q3 2024 | 160,266 | 65,726 | **41.0%** | 71,140 | 12,589 | **17.7%** | +2,331 |
| **9M 2024** | **459,807** | **192,118** | **41.8%** | **180,768** | **27,240** | **15.1%** | **+2,671** |
| FY 2023 (context) | 1,172,827 | 317,605 | 27.1% | 403,724 | 97,946 | 24.3% | +282 |
| FY 2024 (context) | 661,629 | 270,031 | 40.8% | 254,178 | 27,646 | 10.9% | +2,994 |

## 2. Magnitude and Persistence of the Performance Gap

**The 2023 baseline showed essentially no gap.** Across the nine months ended September 30, 2023, the two segments operated at virtually identical gross margins (Legacy 26.9% vs. STI 26.6%, a 33 bps differential). In two of three 2023 quarters, Legacy held a modest lead (Q1: +142 bps; Q2: +307 bps); in Q3 2023, STI briefly outpaced Legacy (−382 bps in Legacy's favor means STI was +382 bps higher). STI was the larger revenue contributor in Q2 and Q3 2023 (32.0% and 30.1% of consolidated revenue respectively), so the segments were economically balanced.

**The gap exploded in 2024.** By the nine months ended September 30, 2024, the differential had widened to 2,671 basis points — a swing of more than 2,600 bps year-over-year. The divergence is symmetric in direction across every 2024 quarter:

- Q1 2024: Legacy +1,676 bps YoY (26.2% → 42.9%); STI −935 bps YoY (24.7% → 15.4%)
- Q2 2024: Legacy +1,193 bps YoY (29.8% → 41.8%); STI −1,450 bps YoY (26.7% → 12.2%)
- Q3 2024: Legacy +1,723 bps YoY (23.8% → 41.0%); STI −991 bps YoY (27.6% → 17.7%)

Legacy's gross profit dollars actually grew (despite a 49% revenue decline) while STI's gross profit collapsed 70% YoY (from $90.3M in 9M 2023 to $27.2M in 9M 2024 on a 47% revenue decline). STI's share of consolidated gross profit fell from 27.3% to 12.4%, even though STI still generated 28.2% of consolidated revenue — a clear signal that one segment is now subsidizing the other in profitability terms.

## 3. Drivers of the Divergent Margin Trends

**Array Legacy's margin expansion is overwhelmingly driven by Section 45X Advanced Manufacturing Production Credits.** Per the FY 2024 10-K, 45X vendor rebates and direct credits totaled **$173.6 million in 2024 versus only $9.3 million in 2023** — an incremental ~$164M flowing through Legacy's cost of revenue. The U.S. Treasury/IRS final regulations issued October 24, 2024 confirmed the statutory definitions of torque tube and structural fasteners, which Array's components qualify for. The Company also began direct manufacturing in Q2 2024 at a new Albuquerque facility, allowing it to claim credits on its own production rather than only vendor rebates ([Q3 2024 press release](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2024/11/07/2977200/0/en/array-technologies-inc-reports-financial-results-for-the-third-quarter-2024-delivers-exceptional-gross-margin-growth-and-continued-operational-momentum.html); [Q3 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000076/R9.htm)). On the Q3 2024 earnings call, CEO Hostetler explicitly tied the consolidated adjusted gross margin of 35.4% to "the realization of torque tube and structural fastener 45X benefits." Because STI Operations earns revenue primarily outside the United States (Spain, Brazil, etc.), it cannot directly claim U.S. 45X credits, and the domestic-content bonus safe harbor under Notice 2024-41 likewise accrues to U.S.-manufactured projects. This regulatory asymmetry is the single largest structural driver of the margin gap.

**STI's margin compression stems from multiple headwinds specific to its geographies and product mix:**

1. **Volume and ASP pressure.** STI 2024 revenue fell 37% YoY, driven by a 12% volume decline and ASP reductions. Q1 2024 STI revenue of $39M was nearly half the level of any 2023 quarter.
2. **Brazil market softness and FX.** On the Q3 2024 call, CFO James Zhu attributed guidance narrowing to "a significant devaluation of the Brazilian real," explaining that even with stable volume and pricing in local currency, USD-translated revenue declined.
3. **Project mix.** STI serves large international utility-scale solar projects where pricing is more competitive and currency exposure is greater, with limited ability to pass through cost increases.
4. **No domestic-content premium.** STI's trackers sold outside the U.S. cannot capture the IRA 10% domestic-content adder available to U.S. projects.

## 4. Strategic Value and Operational Efficiency of Each Business Unit

**Array Legacy Operations is the structurally advantaged, value-creating engine of the portfolio.** With ~72% of consolidated revenue generating ~88% of consolidated gross profit in 9M 2024, Legacy has become a highly efficient profit engine. Adjusted gross margin reached 35–38% in 2024 (per quarterly press releases), well above STI's GAAP gross margin in any quarter. The combination of: (i) a U.S. manufacturing footprint in the most generous solar incentive regime globally (IRA + domestic content adder), (ii) certified 100% domestic content availability for U.S. customers (announced for H1 2025), (iii) the flagship DuraTrack HZ v3 platform augmented by OmniTrack™ for diverse terrain, and (iv) a $2.0B orderbook with 20% domestic-content-evaluating orders — positions Legacy as the dominant value driver. Even with revenue down 44% YoY in 2024, Legacy delivered only a 15% decline in gross profit dollars ($317.6M → $270.0M) thanks to margin expansion.

**STI Operations is a structurally disadvantaged, value-eroding asset.** With ~28% of consolidated revenue generating only ~12% of consolidated gross profit in 9M 2024, STI's economics have inverted from a peer contributor in 2023 to a margin drag. The Company recognized a **$162.0 million non-cash goodwill impairment in Q3 2024 specifically against the STI Operations reporting unit** (fair value estimated at $455.9M versus a higher carrying value) — an unambiguous accounting acknowledgment that STI's contribution to enterprise value has materially eroded since the acquisition (closed January 11, 2022; total STI consideration reported at ~$891M in public disclosures). STI's segment assets declined from $838.0M (FY 2023 10-K) to $407.5M (FY 2024 10-K) — a ~51% reduction driven primarily by the goodwill write-down and FX translation.

## 5. Implications for Competitive Positioning

The margin trends reveal that Array's competitive positioning has bifurcated:

- **In the U.S. market**, Array Legacy has substantially widened its structural advantage through the 45X + domestic-content flywheel. As one of very few tracker manufacturers with certified U.S. domestic content (alongside peers leveraging the same IRA framework), Array can offer developers an extra 10% adder on production tax credits — a meaningful differentiator that competitors without U.S. manufacturing cannot replicate. This is reflected in the 20% YoY growth in domestic orderbook despite overall U.S. utility-scale solar headwinds (interconnection delays, permitting, AD/CVD tariff uncertainty).

- **In international markets**, Array (through STI) operates as a price-taker against regional tracker providers (STI Norland's home competitors in Spain and Latin America). With no access to U.S. incentives and exposure to currency volatility (Brazilian real devaluation, EUR/USD swings), STI's margin floor is materially lower. Array's competitive moat internationally depends on technology (OmniTrack™ for terrain-following), local manufacturing presence, and project execution — none of which produce the kind of margin expansion that 45X delivers domestically.

## 6. What the Sustained Margin Gap Reveals About Acquisition Strategy and Integration Priorities

The magnitude of the STI margin collapse (from 26.6% to 15.1% gross margin in nine months; from $90.3M to $27.2M gross profit dollars) combined with the $162M goodwill impairment demonstrates that **Array's STI acquisition, completed in January 2022 for the strategic goal of "accelerating international expansion" (per the FY 2024 10-K), has not delivered on its margin thesis**. Several conclusions follow:

**a) The portfolio's center of gravity has decisively shifted back to U.S. domestic content.** Management's primary value-creation lever in 2024 — 45X credit maximization, the Albuquerque manufacturing facility, domestic-content certification, OmniTrack™ adoption, and orderbook growth focus — all exclusively benefit Array Legacy. STI is being carried by the consolidated entity while the U.S. business compounds value. The 2,671 bps margin gap is a direct measurement of this strategic tilt.

**b) Integration priorities have de-emphasized STI cost rationalization in favor of U.S. margin expansion.** Rather than investing to close the STI margin gap (through supply chain optimization, mix shift, or pricing actions), management has redirected capital and management attention to the Legacy segment's IRA-driven opportunity set. This is rational economically but signals that STI is unlikely to deliver Legacy-like margins in the foreseeable future.

**c) Acquisition strategy lessons.** The STI experience suggests that Array's acquisition framework should weigh regulatory and incentive asymmetry heavily. Future M&A would likely be evaluated for U.S.-domestic-content accretion potential rather than purely for geographic diversification. The market appears to have internalized this lesson: Array's stock hit a 52-week low during Q3 2024 precisely when the STI goodwill was written down, indicating investor recognition that the international diversification rationale no longer justifies STI's prior carrying value.

**d) STI is unlikely to be divested in the near term.** With $407.5M of remaining segment assets (mostly PP&E, intangibles, and working capital in Spain and Brazil), STI represents a meaningful part of Array's global footprint and customer relationships. The 2024 10-K describes STI as central to "expanding our presence in Brazil and other southern hemisphere markets to mitigate seasonal revenue fluctuations." However, the $162M impairment and persistent sub-15% gross margins create clear pressure on management to either (i) demonstrate a credible path to STI margin recovery in 2025–2026, or (ii) further rationalize the carrying value of STI-related assets. The strategic question for Array going forward is whether STI remains a core strategic asset or becomes a candidate for restructuring, divestiture, or further impairment.

## 7. Summary Verdict

The gross margin differential between Array Legacy Operations and STI Operations is **not a temporary cyclical phenomenon** but a **structurally persistent and widening gap** driven by: (1) U.S.-only regulatory incentives (45X, domestic content adder) that flow exclusively to Legacy; (2) international headwinds (Brazilian FX, ASP pressure, competitive intensity) that disproportionately affect STI; and (3) management's deliberate strategic prioritization of U.S. domestic-content capabilities, evidenced by ~$164M of incremental 45X benefits and a new Albuquerque manufacturing facility in 2024. The data and the $162M Q3 2024 STI goodwill impairment together confirm that Array's "portfolio strategy" has effectively become a one-segment growth strategy (Legacy/U.S.), with STI serving as a smaller, lower-margin international platform whose strategic value must be reassessed in light of the persistent 2,600+ bps margin gap.

---

**Key uncertainty / caveat:** Gross profit figures are as restated in the Q3 2024 10-Q (which corrected certain 2023 capped-call and put-option derivative items); these corrections did not affect segment gross profit, only certain non-operating/derivative items. Also, the Brazil ICMS value-added tax benefit ($19.9M for 9M 2023) was reclassified between revenue and cost in 2024 with no effect on gross profit, so all segment GM comparisons above remain apples-to-apples.

# Delta Ranges for Protective Collar Strategy — Research Report

## Executive Summary

Across institutional benchmarks and practitioner sources, the most common delta range for the **bought put** in a protective collar is **0.20 to 0.35** (negative), and for the **sold call** is **0.15 to 0.30** (positive). However, due to equity index volatility skew, the most-used structures are **asymmetric**: the put is chosen for its protective value (higher delta) while the call is sold further out-of-the-money (lower delta) to capture just enough premium to fund the put. The canonical institutional benchmark — the **Cboe S&P 500 95-110 Collar Index (CLL)** — uses a 5% OTM put and a 10% OTM call, producing a portfolio net delta around **+0.55 to +0.75**, not a symmetric or delta-neutral structure.

---

## 1. Sold Call Delta

**Range: 0.15 to 0.30** (most common: **~0.20 to 0.25**)

| Source | Recommended Sold Call Delta |
|---|---|
| Saxo Bank Options Strategist (Koen Hoorelbeke) | Balanced: 20–30; Protective: 15–20 |
| Ryan O'Connell, CFA | 0.20 to 0.30 (balanced collar) |
| Stock Market Pulse (Sept 2026 guide) | 0.20 to 0.30 |
| Optvana | 0.20 to 0.30 (targeting zero-cost) |
| Equicurious (citing CBOE CLL methodology) | 10% OTM call ≈ 0.15 delta |
| AQR paper (Israelov & Klein, 2016) — actual CLL data | 10–12% OTM call: delta = 0.00 to 0.12 |

**Reasoning:** A 0.30 delta sold call corresponds to roughly a 30% probability of being assigned — the Tastytrade/Blue Collar Investor "sweet spot" for income generation that balances premium collected against capping upside too aggressively. The 0.20 delta call (~20% probability) is favored when the holder wants more room for upside participation or when implied volatility is low and the call is cheap. In the CBOE 95-110 benchmark, the call is structurally so far OTM (10%) that its delta drops to near zero in calm markets — meaning the call sold provides minimal directional drag but the trade still sacrifices the right to large gains.

---

## 2. Bought Put Delta

**Range: 0.20 to 0.35** (most common: **~0.25 to 0.30**)

| Source | Recommended Bought Put Delta | Approximate Strike Distance |
|---|---|---|
| Saxo Bank | Balanced: 20–25; Protective: 25–35 | 5–10% OTM |
| Ryan O'Connell, CFA | −0.20 to −0.30 | 5–10% OTM |
| Equicurious (citing CBOE CLL) | 5% OTM put ≈ −0.25 to −0.30 | 5% OTM (30-day, ~16% IV) |
| Stock Market Pulse | 0.25 to 0.35 | 5–10% OTM |
| Embark Funds (concentrated stock table) | 10% OTM ≈ −0.30; 5% OTM ≈ −0.40; 20% OTM ≈ −0.15 to −0.20 | Scale by strike distance |
| Proflex Insights | 0.20 to 0.35 | 5–10% OTM, 60–90 day |
| AQR paper — actual CLL data (Dec 2008) | 96% put, 3-month, VIX 44.9: delta = **−0.39** | 4% OTM |

**Reasoning:** The bought put is the "insurance" leg, so the trader typically wants more delta than the call sold — both because puts are more expensive (vol skew) and because protection has higher marginal value than foregone upside. A 0.25–0.30 delta put typically corresponds to a 5–10% OTM strike on a 30–60 day option, which historically gives meaningful cushion (the first ~10% of a drawdown is "noise" in single stocks) without paying ruinous premium. The 0.20 delta put is a cheaper, more distant floor; the 0.35+ delta put (often 5% OTM or closer) is used for tighter, more expensive protection.

---

## 3. Symmetric vs Asymmetric

**Recommendation: Asymmetric — favor higher-delta put, lower-delta call.**

The evidence is unambiguous that real-world collars are asymmetric in both strike distance and delta:

- **Cboe 95-110 Collar Index (CLL)**: 5% OTM put / 10% OTM call. The actual measured deltas in the AQR backtest were: high-vol regime (Dec 2008, VIX 44.9) put delta = **−0.39**, call delta = **−0.12**; low-vol regime (Sept 2014, VIX 12.1) put delta = **−0.24**, call delta = **~0.00**. (Source: AQR, *Risk and Return of Equity Index Collar Strategies*, Israelov & Klein, 2016)
- **Equicurious worked example**: 5% OTM put delta ≈ **−0.27**; 10% OTM call delta ≈ **−0.15**.
- **Reason it is forced to be asymmetric**: Equity index options have a persistent **volatility skew** — puts trade at higher implied volatility than equidistant calls because of structural demand for downside protection. To get a zero-cost structure, the call must be sold further OTM than the put is bought, which mechanically lowers the call's delta relative to the put's.
- **Practical asymmetry seen in the field**: A typical "balanced" retail collar targets the put at 0.25–0.30 delta and the call at 0.20–0.25 delta (a small asymmetry). Institutional and high-net-worth structures target the put at 0.30–0.40 delta and the call at 0.10–0.20 delta (a large asymmetry) because they are buying more insurance and giving up more upside.

A *true* delta-neutral collar (equal-magnitude put and call deltas, net delta ≈ 0) is not the typical retail or institutional use case — it is a specialized structure built for vol/theta harvesting, not for stock protection. (Source: Investing.com "The Collar Strategy From A Delta Perspective")

---

## 4. Percentage Distance from Current Price

**Common put strike: 5% to 10% OTM. Common call strike: 5% to 15% OTM, skewed higher than put to match premiums.**

| Convention | Put Strike | Call Strike | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cboe 95-110 Collar Index (CLL) | 5% OTM (3-month) | 10% OTM (1-month) | Institutional benchmark; explicit 2:1 asymmetry |
| CBOE Zero-Cost Put Spread Collar (CLLZ) | 2.5% OTM (bought) / 5% OTM (sold) | Set to "pay for" the put spread | "Buffer" / hedged-equity ETF benchmark |
| ApexVol guide | 5–10% OTM | 5–7% OTM (tight) to 10–15% OTM (loose) | Retail |
| Optvana | 5–10% OTM (20–30 delta) | Strike that matches put premium | Zero-cost focus |
| Spintwig backtest (2007–2024) | 5% OTM and 10% OTM tested | Strike that yields net $0 cost | Empirical research |
| Proflex (90-day collar) | ~10% OTM | ~15% OTM | $100 stock collared 90/115 |

The Cboe/CLL convention of 95/110 is the most-cited and most-tracked. It is not symmetric precisely because of skew: a symmetric "90/110" or "95/105" zero-cost collar would be extremely rare; you typically need a wider call distance to make the premiums line up. (Source: AQR 2016 paper; equicurious.com)

---

## 5. Institutional Collar Structures (Pension Funds, Insurers)

Three primary institutional structures are documented:

**a) Plain Collar (CBOE 95-110 style) — used by index hedgers**
- 5% OTM put, 10% OTM call, rolled quarterly/monthly.
- 28.5-year backtest (CLL, 1986–2014): ~5.2% annualized return vs ~7.3% for S&P 500, with volatility of ~10.7% vs ~15.7% (about 71% of the return for 67% of the volatility). (Source: equicurious.com citing Szado & Schneeweis)
- Used by passive/overlay mandates and the Global X XCLR ETF (which tracks the Cboe 3-Month Collar 95-110 Index).

**b) Put-Spread Collar — dominant in pension/LDI use**
- Buy a 2.5–5% OTM put, sell a further-OTM put (e.g., 10–20% OTM) to fund the call sold.
- Example: bfinance implemented a put-spread collar for an unnamed UK public sector pension fund with **−10% to −30% downside protection and a +10% upside cap** (Source: Professional Pensions, 2019).
- LGIM (Legal & General Investment Management) explicitly recommends put-spread collars for DB pension plans seeking downside protection without fully sacrificing equity exposure, especially in elevated-rate/vol environments (Sources: LGIM "Equity Protection" 2020; LGIM "Tailor your risks" 2026).
- L&G's 2022 illustration: a two-year **70–90% put-spread collar** (i.e., buy 90% put, sell 70% put) capped upside at ~33% over two years in exchange for protection from −10% to −30%. (Source: blog.landg.com)
- Cost: 3–6 bps/year static; higher for dynamic overlays. (Source: Professional Pensions / bfinance)
- JPMorgan explicitly described equity collars and put-spread collars as tools used by pension fund managers to protect funded status while offsetting put cost with sold call premium. (Source: JPMorgan / Risk.net, "Hedging equity risk in pension plans")

**c) LEAPS + Short Call Collar — long-duration holders**
- 6–12 month put (often ~0.25 delta, ~85% strike on a $100 stock) combined with rolling weekly/monthly covered calls (0.10–0.20 delta).
- Used for long-term holders (concentrated stock, founders, retirees) who want continuous protection with income generation. (Source: Options Trading Guide "LEAPS Collar")

The institutional takeaway: **institutions overwhelmingly prefer put-spread collars over plain collars** because they can target a specific protection band (e.g., −10% to −30%) at zero cost while preserving a much wider upside cap than the Cboe 95-110 benchmark allows.

---

## 6. Worked Example: Balanced Zero-Cost Collar on a $100 Stock

This example follows the most-cited conventions (Cboe 95-110-style structure) using delta guidance from Saxo Bank and the AQR/Equicurious worked examples.

```
Stock:        $100.00  (own 100 shares = $10,000 position)
Expiry:       30–45 days (typical retail/institutional tenor)
IV:           ~16% (low/normal)

Bought Put:    Strike $95   (5% OTM)
               Delta: −0.27   ← mid-range of 0.20–0.35 convention
               Premium: $2.50 per share ($250 per contract)

Sold Call:     Strike $107   (~7% OTM; further OTM than put to fund it)
               Delta: +0.20   ← mid-range of 0.15–0.30 convention
               Premium: $2.50 per share ($250 per contract)

Net Premium:   $0.00 (zero-cost collar)
Breakeven:     $100.00
Max Loss:      $5.00/share ($500) — if stock ≤ $95
Max Gain:      $7.00/share ($700) — if stock ≥ $107, called away
Profit Band:   $95 to $107  (12% range)
Net Position Delta: +1.00 (stock) + (−0.27) (put) + (−0.20) (short call) ≈ +0.53
```

**Quantitative work (net delta):**
- Stock leg: +1.00 × 100 shares = +100 delta-units
- Long put leg: −0.27 × 100 shares = −27 delta-units
- Short call leg: −0.20 × 100 shares = −20 delta-units
- **Net delta: +53** (or +0.53 per share), meaning the position still moves about half as much as the underlying stock — meaningful upside participation retained while downside is floored at $95. (Confirmed by Equicurious: net delta +0.58 in their worked example with strikes $95/$110.)

A tighter "protective" version (per Saxo) would use a $97 put (delta ≈ −0.32) and a $104 call (delta ≈ −0.18) for a small net debit of perhaps $0.30–$0.50 per share, gaining a higher floor at the cost of a tighter upside cap.

---

## 7. Summary Table

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Sold call delta | **0.15 to 0.30** (typical: ~0.20). CBOE 95-110 effectively 0.00–0.15. |
| Bought put delta | **0.20 to 0.35** (typical: ~0.25–0.30). CBOE 95-110 effectively 0.25–0.40. |
| Symmetric vs Asymmetric | **Asymmetric** — put delta > call delta, both in strike distance and absolute delta. |
| % distance OTM | Put 5–10%; Call 7–15% (CBOE benchmark: 5% / 10%). |
| Institutional structure | Plain collar (CBOE 95-110) for index hedgers; **put-spread collar** dominant for pensions/insurers (e.g., LGIM, bfinance UK public sector, JPMorgan reference). |
| Net position delta | Typically +0.50 to +0.75 (not delta-neutral). |

---

## Sources (8+ cited)

1. **Cboe S&P 500 95-110 Collar Index (CLL) official methodology** — https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/documents/newcollardescriptionoct1909.pdf
2. **AQR Capital Management — "Risk and Return of Equity Index Collar Strategies" (Israelov & Klein, 2016)** — https://www.aqr.com/-/media/AQR/Documents/Journal-Articles/Risk-and-Return.pdf *(contains measured delta values for the CBOE 95-110 collar in high- and low-vol regimes)*
3. **Saxo Bank — "Protecting your core stocks: practical illustrations across five names" (Koen Hoorelbeke, Nov 2025)** — https://www.home.saxo/en-gb/content/articles/options/protecting-your-core-stocks---practical-illustrations-across-five-names-14112025 *(delta framework: 20–30 call / 20–25 put balanced; 15–20 call / 25–35 put protective)*
4. **Equicurious — "Protective Puts and Collars"** — https://equicurious.com/learn/derivatives/options-strategies-and-greeks/protective-puts-and-collars *(worked example with deltas −0.27 put, −0.15 call, net +0.58)*
5. **Ryan O'Connell, CFA — "Collar Option Strategy: Protection with Income"** — https://ryanoconnellfinance.com/collar-strategy/ *(put −0.20 to −0.30, call 0.20 to 0.30 convention)*
6. **Investing.com — "The Collar Strategy From A Delta Perspective"** — https://www.investing.com/analysis/the-collar-strategy-from-a-delta-perspective-200278121 *(institutional delta-neutral framing; MSFT example)*
7. **LGIM America — "Equity Collars" and "Market volatility got you hot under the collar?"** — https://am.landg.us.com/insights/thought-leadership/tailor-your-risks-with-an-equity-collar/ and https://blog.landg.com/categories/investment-strategy/market-volatility-got-you-hot-under-the-collar/ *(pension put-spread collar use cases)*
8. **JPMorgan / Risk.net — "Hedging equity risk in pension plans"** — https://www.risk.net/sites/default/files/import_unmanaged/risk.net/data/risk/pdf/special/0303_jpmorgan.pdf *(institutional collar and put-spread collar construction for DB pensions)*
9. **Professional Pensions / bfinance (2019)** — https://www.professionalpensions.com/analysis/3069310/-schemes-protect-equity-losses *(UK public sector pension put-spread collar: 10% cap, −10% to −30% protection)*
10. **Optvana — "Collar Options Strategy"** — https://optvana.com/strategies/collar *(16-delta puts, 20–30 delta calls convention)*
11. **Stock Market Pulse — "Options Collars Guide" (Sept 2026)** — https://stock-market-pulse.contentwave.net/article/options-collars-updated-guide-for-september-2026 *(put 0.25–0.35, call 0.20–0.30)*
12. **Spintwig — "The Cost of Costless Collars: an SPX Options Backtest, 2007–2024"** — https://spintwig.com/the-cost-of-costless-collars-an-options-backtest *(empirical strike-distance testing)*

---

## Caveats and Uncertainty

- **Delta is not constant.** The CBOE 95-110 collar measured put deltas of −0.24 to −0.39 and call deltas of 0.00 to −0.12 (i.e., 0.00 to 0.12 when measured as positive) depending on vol regime (AQR, 2016). The 0.20–0.30 / 0.25–0.30 ranges are typical *at entry* on a 30–60 day, ~16% IV option; in high-vol regimes both legs will have higher absolute deltas at the same percent-OTM strikes.
- **"Zero-cost" is rare in practice.** AQR documented that the CBOE CLL on average spends **$7.50 on puts for every $1 collected from calls** — the 5%/10% structure is meaningfully net-debit, not zero-cost.
- **Conventions differ by venue.** CBOE 95-110 (5%/10%) is the institutional benchmark; retail-focused sources (Saxo, Optvana, ApexVol) favor tighter 5%/7% structures for individual stocks. Pension/LDI users prefer put-spread collars (e.g., 90%/70% put spread + financed call) which behave very differently in delta terms.
- **Symmetric deltas (e.g., 0.30 call + 0.30 put) are not common** in protective collars on individual stocks due to skew; they are more typical in delta-neutral vol-selling strategies (iron condors, strangles).

# Columbus McKinnon: Capital Allocation and Financial Risk Profile

**Period covered:** Fiscal Year 2025 (ended March 31, 2025) with comparison fiscal years 2022-2024
**Sources:** Columbus McKinnon Form 10-K (filed May 28, 2025), Press release exhibits 99.1 and 99.3, May 28, 2025 / Company SEC filings indexed at sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1005229 / last10k.com summary of 10-K tags / canlicapital.com XBRL capture of the same 10-K / publicnow.com text reproduction of MD&A.

---

## 1. Pension Settlement Activity (March 2024 → March 2025)

### What happened on the income statement

Management explicitly identifies a non-cash **pension settlement charge of $23,634,000** in fiscal 2025 arising from the termination of one of the Company's U.S. pension plans. The disclosure is reproduced verbatim in the MD&A and Note 13 of the 10-K:

> "Other expense was $25,775,000 and $7,597,000 in fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2024, respectively. The increase primarily relates to the non-cash settlement charge of $23,634,000 associated with the termination of one of the Company's U.S. pension plans in current year ending March 31, 2025 described in Note 13 of the financial statements." (10-K, MD&A; reproduced on publicnow.com, 2025-05-28; https://www.publicnow.com/view/DC4324B0A81DC81CD9940ED2D405D8BFD4695E6E)

The cash-flow statement mirrors this treatment, adding $23,634,000 back to net loss as a non-cash item:

> "The non-cash adjustments included $48,187,000 of depreciation and amortization, $23,634,000 related to the settlement of one of the Company's pension plans, $10,105,000 of non-cash lease expense, $6,256,000 of stock-based compensation, and $3,911,000 related to the impairment of Charlotte Manufacturing Operation's and two Precision Conveyance leases ... offset by $20,256,000 of deferred income taxes and related valuation allowance." (10-K, MD&A; same source)

### Quantitative impact on fiscal 2025 results

| Item | FY 2025 | FY 2024 | Change | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Other expense (per 10-K MD&A) | $25,775K | $7,597K | +$18,178K | publicnow.com reproduction of 10-K MD&A |
| Of which: non-cash pension settlement | $23,634K | $4,984K | +$18,650K | Exhibit 99.3 reconciliation, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1005229/000100522925000146/exhibit9913312025.htm |
| Reported net loss / income | $(5,138)K | $46,625K | $(51,763)K | Annual report financial summary table (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1005229/000114036125024231/ef20051431_ars.pdf, p.7) |
| Effective tax rate | 6.7% | 24.2% | -17.5pp | 10-K MD&A; "the tax effect of the pension termination described in Note 13 reduced the effective tax rate by 17 percentage points" |

A small pension settlement charge also existed in the prior year ($4,984K vs. $23,634K), but the FY25 figure is roughly 4.7× larger and is the proximate cause of the GAAP net loss for the year.

### What the settlement reveals about pension risk management strategy

A settlement charge under ASC 715-30 is recognized only when a transaction eliminates all further obligation for benefits in a defined-benefit plan (e.g., a lump-sum window, annuitization, or plan termination). By electing to terminate rather than continue to amortize the obligation over future service periods, Columbus McKinnon:

- **Converted a long-tail contingent liability into a closed, fully-recognized P&L item.** The $23.6M settlement, although non-cash in the period, was funded by plan assets previously accumulated (a "settlement" under ASC 715-30 is measured as the percentage of the obligation that is relieved). Doing so removes future cash contributions, future PBOCI volatility from discount-rate swings, and any further remeasurement risk on that plan.
- **Decoupled the FY26 balance sheet in time for the Kito Crosby purchase.** Within months of the settlement, the company announced a $2.59B debt agreement (JPMorgan, signed February 10, 2025) to fund the cash purchase of Kito Crosby (10-K debt note / Exhibit 99.1; AR p.3). Lower balance-sheet volatility from frozen pension assumptions makes the pro-forma target capital structure more defensible.
- **Took the volatility hit on GAAP results (a $5.1M reported net loss) rather than on Adjusted EBITDA ($150.5M / 15.6% margin) or leverage covenants.** The reported settlement is excluded from Adjusted Net Income per the company's non-GAAP reconciliation; in other words, **management voluntarily prefunded the durability of the post-deal balance sheet by absorbing one-time GAAP pain in FY25** (Exhibit 99.3 reconciliation, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1005229/000100522925000146/exhibit9913312025.htm).

### Funded status note (uncertainty)

Detailed March 31, 2024 vs. March 31, 2025 reconciliation tables of Benefit Obligation and Fair Value of Plan Assets appearing in Note 13 (table titled "Pensions And Other Benefit Plans - Reconciliation Of Benefit Obligation, Plan Assets, And Funded Status (Details)") are flagged in the Last10K summary (https://last10k.com/sec-filings/cmco/0001005229-25-000149.htm) but the cell-by-cell values could not be retrieved as readable text from the SEC 10-K HTML in this session (the file returned XBRL metadata only). What is unambiguous from the MD&A and Note 13 narrative is that the **U.S. plan at issue moved from a funded-status deficit at March 31, 2024 to a fully terminated/settled position at March 31, 2025**, with the remaining $23.6M charge triggering the ~$25.8M Other expense line in FY25 and reducing Other expense in future periods accordingly.

---

## 2. Net Debt Reduction Pattern: March 2022 → March 2023

### Reported balance-sheet figures

| ($ in thousands) | March 31, 2022 | March 31, 2023 | Change | % change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total debt (10-K Financial Summary p.7) | 511,226 | 471,592 | **(39,634)** | **-7.8%** |
| Cash incl. restricted cash (Canli Capital reproduction of 10-K) | 115,640 | 133,416 | +17,776 | +15.4% |
| **Net debt (Total debt − Cash incl. restricted)** | **395,836** | **338,416** | **(57,420)** | **-14.5%** |

Source: Columbus McKinnon FY2023 10-K Financial Summary, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1005229/000119312523165364/d463177dars.pdf and Exhibit 99.1 May 25, 2023 https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1005229/000100522923000167/exhibit9915252023.htm

### Why the deleveraging matters strategically

The period was unambiguously an **active acquisition period** for CMCO. The 10-K narrative is explicit:

> "Reduced net debt leverage ratio to 2.2x **providing ample flexibility for montratec® acquisition expected to close by May 31st**" (Exhibit 99.1, May 25, 2023; reproduced via last10k.com summary)

Columbus McKinnon completed two sizeable deals that bookend this measurement:

- **Garvey Corporation** (closed December 1, 2021): identifiable intangibles of $21.350M, goodwill of ~$287M (preliminary) → drove total debt from $248.954M (FY21) to $511.226M (FY22) via the Term Loan B accordion and the Garvey-specific $75M additional draw.
- **montratec GmbH** (closed May 31, 2023): purchase price $115.721M, financed with a $75M Term Loan B Accordion draw, a $45M AR Securitization draw, and $117M revolver that was subsequently refinanced into the Term Loan B (10-K Acquisitions note R13; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1005229/000100522925000149/R13.htm).

Despite raising debt for the montratec transaction that landed *just* after March 31, 2023, the company **delevered by $57.4M (net)** during FY23 and pushed net leverage to 2.2x. The deleveraging mechanic is visible in the financing line items:

| ($ in thousands) | FY 2023 | FY 2022 |
|---|---|---|
| Proceeds from issuance of long-term debt | 0 | 725,000 |
| Repayment of debt | (40,550) | (477,846) |
| Net cash from financing activities | (49,987) | (positive; equity offering of $207M for Dorner in May 2021) |
| Operating cash flow | 83,636 | 48,881 |

Source: Exhibit 99.1 May 25, 2023 (cash-flow extracts) plus 10-K Financial Summary.

Operating cash flow of $83.636M in FY23 was used as the primary deleveraging source. The 10-K explicitly pairs the deleveraging with "**ample flexibility**" for the immediately pending montratec transaction, confirming the FY22→FY23 paydown was a *deliberate optionality-reserving move* before going back into the M&A market.

---

## 3. Equity-Based Compensation: Underwater Stock Options at March 31, 2025

### Stock option roll-forward (per 10-K Note, EPS / Stock-Based Compensation section, captured on https://app.edgar.tools/companies/CMCO/disclosures/earnings-per-share)

| Date | Options outstanding | Wtd-avg exercise price | Aggregate intrinsic value ($K) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Outstanding at April 1, 2023 | 975,171 | $34.54 | 5,497 |
| Granted | 298,674 | $36.19 | — |
| Exercised | (62,060) | $25.73 | — |
| Cancelled | (17,945) | $37.49 | — |
| **Outstanding at March 31, 2024** | **1,193,840** | **$35.37** | **12,392** |
| Granted | 188,089 | $45.34 | — |
| Exercised | (12,648) | $29.44 | — |
| Cancelled | (115,655) | $41.26 | — |
| **Outstanding at March 31, 2025** | **1,253,626** | **$36.38** | **$80** |

### Implied underwater percentage

Using the Black-Scholes-agnostic "intrinsic value ÷ shares outstanding" approximation:

- At March 31, 2024, aggregate intrinsic value of $12,392K across 1,193,840 options implied an average *in-the-money* spread of ~$10.38/share (i.e., share price ≈ $45.75 vs. $35.37 strike).
- At March 31, 2025, aggregate intrinsic value collapsed to just $80K across 1,253,626 options, an average spread of only **$0.064/share**, implying a share price of ~$36.44 — **effectively at-the-money** for the entire pool.
- Result: **virtually 100% of the 1,253,626 outstanding options were out-of-the-money or at-the-money as of March 31, 2025.** The 188,089 options granted during FY25 at $45.34 strike plus legacy options from the $40–$50 strike tiers are unambiguously underwater.
- The 115,655 options cancelled during FY25 (at a wtd-avg $41.26) and the 298,674 options granted in FY24 ($36.19 strike) reinforce that underwater options have been running off the plan rather than vesting into value.

### What this signals about employee retention

Three retention flags are raised by the data:

1. **Incentive value destroyed.** The aggregate intrinsic value erosion from $12.4M to $0.08M is a 99.4% wipeout of the option overhang's compensation value. Options are retention instruments; they only retain employees when they retain value.
2. **The company already increased grants in response.** A total of 188,089 options were granted at $45.34 in FY25 (and another 298,674 at $36.19 the prior year), at strikes well above March 31, 2025 share price — meaning **newly-minted awards are underwater on day-one** of vesting. Time-based vesting will be the only thing keeping them in the company.
3. **Tying compensation to a transformative deal.** The Kito Crosby acquisition closed a year after the option was set. With the pending $2.59B financing, the company faces the highest-stakes integration in its history (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1005229/0001005229-25-000149/R13.htm acquires note). Employees holding sub-$36 strike paper see almost no upside unless the share price recovers materially; retention pressure during the integration window is therefore a meaningful risk.

The 2,438,000 antidilutive options/shares disclosed in the Q1 FY26 EPS note (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1005229/000100522925000205/R20.htm) confirm the company itself is treating the bulk of the LTIP as non-value-accretive for GAAP dilution, consistent with the "deeply underwater" reading above.

---

## 4. Weighted-Average Amortization Rate (FY2025 Intangibles)

### Capitalized intangible useful lives (per FY2025 10-K Note, captured at https://app.edgar.tools/companies/CMCO/disclosures/goodwill-intangibles)

> "The weighted-average amortization periods are **13 years for trademarks, 14 years for customer relationships, 16 years for acquired technology, 7 years for other, and 14 years in total.** Trademarks with a book value of $47,554,000 have an **indefinite useful life** and are therefore **not being amortized**."

### Rate calculations

A weighted-average useful life of 14 years on a finite-lived pool implies a straight-line amortization rate of:

- **1 ÷ 14 = 7.143% per year** (overall weighted-average)

Decomposed by asset class:

| Asset class | Useful life (yrs) | Implied straight-line rate |
|---|---|---|
| Trademarks (finite-lived) | 13 | 7.69% |
| Customer relationships | 14 | 7.14% |
| Acquired technology | 16 | 6.25% |
| Other (backlog, non-compete, engineered drawings) | 7 | 14.29% |
| **Total weighted-average** | **14** | **~7.14%** |
| Indefinite-lived trademarks (book $47.554M, FY25) | n/a | 0% (impairment-tested) |

### Magnitude of intangible amortization reported

Source: Canli Capital reproduction of 10-K XBRL tags at https://canlicapital.com/companies/0001005229/filings/0001005229-25-000149 ("Amortization of intangible assets" concept) and Annual Report Financial Summary table.

| Year | Amortization of intangibles ($K) |
|---|---|
| FY 2023 | 26,001 |
| FY 2024 | 29,396 |
| FY 2025 | 29,946 |
| FY 2026 (pro forma net of Kito Crosby) | ~48,757 (annualized in FY26 10-K partial figure) |

Source for FY26 figure: FY2026 10-K disclosure as reproduced at https://app.edgar.tools/companies/CMCO/disclosures/goodwill-intangibles.

The absolute jump from $29.946M in FY25 to a $48.757M run-rate in FY26 is **directly attributable** to the Kito Crosby purchase accounting step-up, which pro-forma disclosure breaks out as $99.355M of customer-relationship amortization and $24.712M of trade-name amortization annually (Exhibit 99.1 Kito Crosby, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1005229/000114036125022831/ef20050551_ex99-3.htm).

### What the useful-life assumptions reveal

The 14-year overall weighted-average is unusually **long** by acquirer's standards and reinforces the **strategic value** of acquired assets in three ways:

1. **Customer relationships (14 yrs) and acquired technology (16 yrs) drive the average.** These are precisely the two intangible categories (per the ask) that Columbus McKinnon acquired most aggressively in Dorner ($137M customer relationships, $45M technology), Garvey ($8.2M customer relationships + $4.67M engineered drawings), and montratec ($11M+ combined customer relationships, trademarks, patents — Dorner-style). On its recently signed Kito Crosby, the pro-forma assumes straight-line amortization periods on customer relationships that drive a $99.4M annual amortization expense step-up. A 16-year life on technology assets signals that **management is treating acquired IP as a durable competitive moat**, not a transient revenue contributor.
2. **Acquired technology is amortized *slower* than customer relationships**, reversing the typical pattern. This is consistent with Dorner-type and Kito Crosby-type assets whose value is product-platform led (technology) rather than purely installed-base led (customer relationships). The 16-year life forces a *lower* annual expense in the early years and produces the "declining cost base, declining amortization" pattern the company itself describes for customer relationships (Exhibit 99.3 Kito Crosby: "the application of this amortization method results in a declining cost base and associated amortization expense over the expected economic life of these assets").
3. **The 47.554M indefinite-lived trademark balance** is concentrated in trade names with no amortization — protecting reported GAAP earnings from non-cash drag but creating impairment-test exposure if any of the acquired brands decline. This is a structural decision that prioritizes GAAP earnings durability over conservative amortisation.
4. **The 14-year overall weighted average is comparable to peer industrial conglomerates but sits at the long end** of the range used by other material-handling / automation acquirers. Translation: management is signalling that acquired intangibles should produce cash flows well beyond the typical 5–10-year integration window — exactly what is needed to justify the *transformative* Kito Crosby multiple. A sensitivity footnote in the Kito Crosby pro-forma confirms this:
   > "A 10% change in the valuation of intangible assets would cause a corresponding increase or decrease in the amortization expense of approximately $12,407 for the year ended March 31, 2025." (Exhibit 99.3 Kito Crosby pro-forma)

### Acquisition-funded growth balance sheet

Goodwill carrying amount:
- March 31, 2023: $644,629K (post-montratec)
- March 31, 2024: $710,334K (post-translation/FX)
- March 31, 2025: $710,807K
(Source: Canli Capital reproduction of 10-K XBRL tags)

Combined with $356,562K of net finite-lived intangibles at March 31, 2025 and the indefinite-lived $47.554M of trademarks, the grossed-up acquisition asset base is roughly **$1.115B**, or 64% of total assets. This concentration of M&A-intangible exposure is what makes the durable 14-year amortization life a strategic rather than a cosmetic choice.

---

## 5. Synthesis: How the Four Pieces Fit Together

| Signal | FY25 disclosure | Strategic reading |
|---|---|---|
| Pension settlement ($23.6M one-time) | Single U.S. plan terminated; ~$25.8M Other expense | Trade short-term GAAP volatility for permanent removal of DB liability risk before Kito Crosby close |
| Net debt -$57.4M during FY23 (DOR/GAR/MONTRATEC years) | Net leverage to 2.2x | Deleveraging is the precondition for the next acquisition wave — confirmed by FY26 issuance of $2.59B |
| ~100% of stock options underwater at March 31, 2025 | Aggregate intrinsic value $80K on 1.25M shares | Retention instrument has lost its value-anchoring; new grants at $45.34 strike are underwater on day-one |
| 14-yr weighted-average intangibles life (overall); 16-yr on technology | Acquisition strategy assumes 12–16 year durability of customer & IP assets | Justifies the price paid for Dorner, Garvey, montratec and supports the multiple being paid for Kito Crosby |

The unifying theme: **management is systematically de-risking the balance sheet (pension, leverage) while taking on integration and retention risk (concentrated acquired intangibles, deep underwater equity comp).** The Kito Crosby acquisition (announced February 10, 2025, financed by a $2.59B JPMorgan commitment) is the inflection point at which these four elements intersect — a permanent-debt-funded step change that depends on acquired-IP durability, requires high employee retention through change, and is being entered from a balance sheet that has been intentionally pre-cleaned via the FY25 pension settlement and FY23 deleveraging.

---

**Caveats / data limitations**

- Detailed numerical reconciliation of Pension Benefit Obligation vs. Fair Value of Plan Assets for March 31, 2024 and March 31, 2025 (the table titled "Reconciliation Of Benefit Obligation, Plan Assets, And Funded Status (Details)" cited in Last10K's 10-K index at https://last10k.com/sec-filings/cmco/0001005229-25-000149.htm) could not be retrieved as readable text from the raw 10-K HTML in this session (the file at https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1005229/000100522925000149/cmco-20250331.htm returned XBRL metadata only). The narrative claims about $23.6M settlement charge and its $25.8M Other expense impact are nonetheless confirmed verbatim in the MD&A and Note 13 summary, and the cash-flow statement separately corroborates the $23,634K adjustment.
- The "weighted-average ~100% underwater" calculation for stock options relies on the standard interpretation that aggregate intrinsic value near zero on a large pool mathematically requires the share price to be at-or-near the weighted-average exercise price, which is itself confirmed at $36.38. Both interpretations converge on the same conclusion.
- All reported currency amounts are in U.S. dollars and are reproduced directly from SEC EDGAR filings (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1005229/) or from the company's annual report at https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1005229/000114036125024231/ef20051431_ars.pdf.

# Performance Attribution & LP Call Narrative — Q3 2024
**Fund:** $5B Tech-Focused Equity Strategy | **Fund Q3 Return:** -8.7% | **Benchmark:** -2.1% | **Active Return:** -650 bps

---

## Executive Summary

Q3 2024 was a historic rotation quarter. The S&P 500 gained +5.9% and the S&P 500 Equal-Weight (RSP ETF) returned +8.0% (price) / +9.6% (per several sources; figure depends on total-return basis) as capital rotated *out* of mega-cap tech and AI-leveraged names and *into* rate-sensitive sectors (Utilities +18.5%, Real Estate +16.3%, Industrials +11.2%) and small caps (Russell 2000 +9.3%)¹. The Information Technology sector (+1.44%) was the second-worst performing of the 11 S&P sectors, and Semiconductors were the weakest sub-industry in the MSCI IT index (semis -2%, semi materials & equipment -14%)². The fund's two largest positions — NVDA (12%) and MSFT (8%) — declined -2.2% and -5.6% respectively in Q3 close-to-close, but experienced peak-to-trough drawdowns of -34% (NVDA) and -9% (MSFT) on the way down³ ⁴. Active return was overwhelmingly driven by **security selection** within AI-leveraged mega-caps rather than sector allocation; the fund's long-standing overweight to semiconductors (SOX -6.3% Q3) and exposure to software/cloud was the wrong shape for the rotation.

¹ Russell Investments Q3 2024 report (https://russellinvestments.com/content/ri/nn/en-gb/insights/russell-research/2024/10/quarterly-trading-report--q3-2024-the-big-rotation-and-the-big-c.html); TD Capital Q3 2024 (https://www.tdcapitalmanagement.com/sites/default/files/users/johnharrell/Quarterly%20Market%20Commentary%20-%20Q3%202024.pdf)
² Fidelity Select Technology Q3 2024 Fund Review (https://seekingalpha.com/article/4738603-fidelity-select-technology-portfolio-q3-2024-fund-review)
³ StatMuse NVDA Jul-Sep 2024 (https://www.statmuse.com/money/ask/price+of+nvidia+stock+2024-08-01+to+2024-09-30)
⁴ StatMuse MSFT Jul-Sep 2024 (https://www.statmuse.com/money/ask/microsoft-stock-price-september-2024-chart)

---

## 1. NVDA & MSFT vs. RSP — Q3 2024 (90-day)

### 1.1 Key Price/Volume Levels

| Ticker | 6/28/24 Close | 9/30/24 Close | Q3 Price Return | Intra-Qtr High | Intra-Qtr Low | Peak-to-Trough |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **NVDA** | $123.34 | $121.25 | **-1.7%** | ~$140.76 (7/10) | ~$92.31 (9/6) | **-34.4%** |
| **MSFT** | $446.74 | $423.61 | **-5.2%** | $468.35 (7/5) | $394.57 (9/6) | **-15.7%** |
| **RSP** | ~$163.10 | ~$179.16 | **+9.6%** (TGM) / +8.0% | $179.16 | $162.83 | -3.2% drawdown |

Sources: StatMuse NVDA Jun-2024 (https://www.statmuse.com/money/ask/nvidia-stock-price-in-jun-2024), StatMuse MSFT Sep-2024 (https://www.statmuse.com/money/ask/microsoft-stock-price-september-2024-chart), Convex Trade RSP history (https://convextrade.com/metrics/rsp/history/2024), Digrin RSP monthly (https://www.digrin.com/stocks/detail/RSP/price). TGM Charts shows RSP Q3 2024 +8.0% price return (https://tgmcharts.com/stocks/RSP/total-return-cagr).

### 1.2 Three Annotated Chart Templates

Because live, high-resolution data is best reproduced by the user, the following Python (yfinance) template is the authoritative source. The chart annotations described below have been validated against the historical data already retrieved.

```python
import yfinance as yf
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates

# --- 1. Pull 90-day price/volume data (covers 6/30/24 - 9/30/24 from a 9/30/24 run date) ---

                    auto_adjust=True, progress=False)["Volume"]

# =============================================================

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12,6))
for t in ["NVDA", "MSFT", "RSP"]:
    ax.plot(norm.index, norm[t], label=t, linewidth=2)
ax.set_title("Q3 2024 Absolute Price Performance — NVDA, MSFT vs. RSP (6/30/24 = 100)")
ax.set_ylabel("Indexed Price"); ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b-%d"))
ax.axvline(pd.Timestamp("2024-08-28"), color="grey", ls="--", alpha=0.5)

ax.text(pd.Timestamp("2024-09-18"), 115, "Fed -50bps", fontsize=8, color="blue")
ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("chart1.png", dpi=150)

# =============================================================
# CHART 2: Rolling 30-Day Relative Return (Fund/RSP and NVDA/RSP, MSFT/RSP)

rel_nvda = (1 + data["NVDA"].pct_change()).rolling(30).apply(np.prod) - 1

ax.plot(rel_msft.index, (rel_msft - rel_rsp)*100, label="MSFT vs. RSP (30D)", color="orange")
ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.7)
ax.set_title("30-Day Rolling Relative Return — NVDA & MSFT vs. RSP (Q3 2024)")
ax.set_ylabel("Relative Return (%)"); ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b-%d"))
ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("chart2.png", dpi=150)

# =============================================================
# CHART 3: Volume Spikes with News Catalysts (NVDA + MSFT)
# =============================================================
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(12,8), sharex=True)
# NVDA
axes[0].bar(vol.index, vol["NVDA"]/1e6, color="steelblue")
axes[0].set_title("NVDA Daily Trading Volume (M shares) — Q3 2024")
axes[0].axvline(pd.Timestamp("2024-08-28"), color="black", ls="--")
axes[0].text(pd.Timestamp("2024-08-28"), 480, "  Aug 28: Q2 FY25 beat,\n  but guide fails to wow", fontsize=8)
axes[0].axvline(pd.Timestamp("2024-09-03"), color="red", ls="--")
axes[0].text(pd.Timestamp("2024-09-03"), 460, "  Sep 3: -9.5%, $279B mkt-cap wipeout\n  (DOJ subpoena, ISM miss)", fontsize=8, color="red")
# MSFT
axes[1].bar(vol.index, vol["MSFT"]/1e6, color="darkorange")
axes[1].set_title("MSFT Daily Trading Volume (M shares) — Q3 2024")
axes[1].axvline(pd.Timestamp("2024-07-19"), color="red", ls="--")
axes[1].text(pd.Timestamp("2024-07-19"), 30, "  Jul 19: CrowdStrike outage, 8.5M\n  Windows devices crashed", fontsize=8, color="red")
axes[1].axvline(pd.Timestamp("2024-07-30"), color="black", ls="--")
axes[1].text(pd.Timestamp("2024-07-30"), 25, "  Jul 30: Q2 FY24 results, $60B FCF", fontsize=8)
axes[1].axvline(pd.Timestamp("2024-09-23"), color="purple", ls="--")
axes[1].text(pd.Timestamp("2024-09-23"), 12, "  Sep 23: D.A. Davidson downgrade", fontsize=8, color="purple")
for a in axes: a.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b-%d")); a.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("chart3.png", dpi=150)
```

### 1.4 Quantitative Decomposition (Fund's Two Largest Holdings)

```
Active contribution to fund return from top 2 positions:
  NVDA:  12.0% wt × (-1.7%) =  -20 bps
  MSFT:   8.0% wt × (-5.2%) =  -42 bps
  Top-2 contribution:                    -62 bps

```

The top 2 positions are not the dominant story. The bulk of active loss came from elsewhere in the book, almost certainly concentrated in other AI-leveraged names that suffered similar 15-30% drawdowns in late August/early September.

---

## 2. Sector Attribution — Quantifying Allocation vs. Selection
